nodes.title: Q_c is positive definite and dominates Q_{c₀} (Zwegers Lemma 2.5)
nodes.statement: For c ∈ C_Q the form Q_c(ν) := Q(ν) − B(c, ν)²/(2Q(c)) is positive definite, and Q_c(ν) ≥ λ_{c,c₀}Q_{c₀}(ν) with λ_{c,c₀} = (B(c,c₀)² − 2Q(c)Q(c₀) − |B(c,c₀)|√(B(c,c₀)² − 4Q(c)Q(c₀)))/(2Q(c)Q(c₀)) > 0; λ_{c,c₀} depends continuously on c.
hypotheses: c ∈ C_Q.
proofSteps: On span{c, ν} (ν ∉ ℝc) Q has type (1, 1), so 4Q(ν)Q(c) − B(c, ν)² < 0, giving Q_c(ν) > −B(c,ν)²/(4Q(c)) ≥ 0; for ν = λc, Q_c = −Q(c)λ² > 0.
Minimise Q_c on the ellipsoid {Q_{c₀} = 1} by Lagrange multipliers: the multiplier satisfies Q(c)Q(c₀)(λ + 1)² = λB(c, c₀)² or equals 1, and the minimum is λ₋ = λ_{c,c₀}.
acceptance: For c = c₀: λ_{c₀,c₀} = 1.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 2.5 Let c ∈ C_Q. The quadratic form Q_c : R^r → R, Q_c(ν) := Q(ν)−B(c,ν)²/(2Q(c)) is positive deﬁnite, and we have Q_c(ν) ≥ λ_{c,c0}Q_{c0}(ν) ∀ν ∈ R^r,
sources.match: The statement (λ_{c,c₀} as displayed there).

nodes.title: Q⁺ is positive definite (Zwegers Lemma 2.6)
nodes.statement: For linearly independent c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q, Q⁺(ν) := Q(ν) + B(c₁,c₂)/(4Q(c₁)Q(c₂) − B(c₁,c₂)²)·B(c₁,ν)B(c₂,ν) is positive definite.
hypotheses: c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q linearly independent.
proofSteps: For ν ∉ span{c₁, c₂}: Q has type (2, 1) on span{c₁, c₂, ν}, so the 3 × 3 Gram determinant is negative, which rewrites to Q⁺(ν) > (Q(c₂)B(c₁,ν)² + Q(c₁)B(c₂,ν)²)/(4Q(c₁)Q(c₂) − B(c₁,c₂)²) ≥ 0.
On span{c₁, c₂} equality holds and Q⁺(ν) = 0 forces B(c₁, ν) = B(c₂, ν) = 0, i.e. ν = 0.
acceptance: Bounds the sign-difference part of ρ: |sgn B(c₁,ν) − sgn B(c₂,ν)||e^{2πiQ(ν)τ}| ≤ 2e^{−2πQ⁺(ν)y}.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 2.6 Let c1, c2 ∈ C_Q be linearly independent. The quadratic form Q^+ : R^r → R, Q^+(ν) := Q(ν) + B(c1,c2)/(4Q(c1)Q(c2)−B(c1,c2)²) B(c1, ν)B(c2, ν) is positive deﬁnite.
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Convergence of the β-series (Zwegers, proof of Prop. 2.4, (2.10))
nodes.statement: For c ∈ ℝ^r with Q(c) < 0, a, b ∈ ℝ^r, τ ∈ ℍ: Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ^r} sgn(B(c,ν))β(−B(c,ν)²y/Q(c))e^{2πiQ(ν)τ+2πiB(ν,b)} converges absolutely, locally uniformly in (c, τ).
proofSteps: β(x) ≤ e^{−πx} bounds the ν-term by e^{−2πQ_c(ν)y} (2.12); Q_c is positive definite (Lemma 2.5, with c or −c in C_Q), so Σ e^{−2πQ_c(ν)y} converges; local uniformity from the continuity of λ_{c,c₀}.
acceptance: Also gives continuity in c (Prop. 2.7(4)).

sources.excerpt: We will ﬁrst show that the series (2.10) converges absolutely for all c with Q(c) < 0: We can easily see that 0 ≤ β(x) ≤ e^{−πx} for all x ∈ R≥0; hence if Q(c) < 0
sources.match: The step.

nodes.title: Convergence of the sign-difference series (Zwegers, proof of Prop. 2.4, (2.11))
nodes.statement: For c₁, c₂ ∈ C̄_Q, a ∈ R(c₁) ∩ R(c₂), b ∈ ℝ^r, τ ∈ ℍ: Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ^r}{sgn(B(c₁,ν)) − sgn(B(c₂,ν))}e^{2πiQ(ν)τ + 2πiB(ν,b)} converges absolutely.
hypotheses: a admissible for the cusp vectors among c₁, c₂.
proofSteps: Case c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q: non-zero terms have B(c₁,ν)B(c₂,ν) ≤ 0, where Q(ν) ≥ Q⁺(ν) (Lemma 2.6), bounded by 2e^{−2πQ⁺(ν)y}.

Case c₁ ∈ C_Q, c₂ ∈ S_Q: reduce to c₁ integral; write ν = μ + nc₂ with B(c₁,μ)/B(c₁,c₂) ∈ [0,1), sum the geometric series in n (possible since B(c₂, μ) is bounded away from 0 on a + ℤ^r by admissibility), leaving a positive definite theta series over ⟨c₁⟩^⊥_ℤ with bounded coefficients.
Cases c₁ ∈ S_Q, c₂ ∈ C_Q and c₁, c₂ ∈ S_Q: by antisymmetry and the cocycle relation with an auxiliary c₃ ∈ C_Q.
acceptance: For c₁, c₂ ∈ S_Q the resulting holomorphic series are Göttsche–Zagier's.

sources.excerpt: We will now show that the series (2.11) converges absolutely for all c1, c2 ∈ C̄_Q: If c1 and c2 are linearly dependent, we have ρ^{c1,c2} = 0. Hence we can assume that they are linearly independent.
sources.match: The step, with its four cases.

nodes.title: Absolute convergence of ϑ^{c₁,c₂} (Zwegers Prop. 2.4)
nodes.statement: For c₁, c₂ ∈ C̄_Q and (z, τ) ∈ D(c₁) ∩ D(c₂), the series defining ϑ^{c₁,c₂}(z; τ) (and ϑ_{a,b}(τ)) converges absolutely.
hypotheses: As stated.
proofSteps: Write ρ^{c₁,c₂} as the sum of (2.7), (2.8), (2.9) (Lemma 1.7 applied to ρ^{c_i} for c_i ∈ C_Q); (2.7), (2.8) are β-series (QM.4/indefinite-theta-beta-series-convergence) and (2.9) the sign-difference series (QM.4/indefinite-theta-sign-series-convergence).
acceptance: Makes Def. 2.1 meaningful despite Q being indefinite.

sources.excerpt: Because Q is indeﬁnite, e^{2πiQ(n)τ} isn’t bounded. Therefore it’s not immediately clear that the series deﬁning ϑ(z; τ) converges absolutely. However, using an estimate for the growth of ρ we shall ﬁnd: Proposition 2.4 The series deﬁning ϑ(z; τ) converges absolutely.
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Cocycle relations (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(1))
nodes.statement: ϑ^{c₁,c₂} + ϑ^{c₂,c₁} = 0 and ϑ^{c₁,c₂} + ϑ^{c₂,c₃} + ϑ^{c₃,c₁} = 0 on D(c₁) ∩ D(c₂) ∩ D(c₃).
hypotheses: c₁, c₂, c₃ ∈ C̄_Q.
proofSteps: From the corresponding identities for ρ and absolute convergence.
acceptance: Reduces cusp cases to cone cases.

sources.excerpt: (1) For c1, c2, c3 ∈ C̄_Q and (z, τ) ∈ D(c1) ∩ D(c2) ∩ D(c3) we have the cocycle conditions ϑ^{c1,c2} + ϑ^{c2,c1} = 0 and ϑ^{c1,c2} + ϑ^{c2,c3} + ϑ^{c3,c1} = 0.
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Elliptic transformation (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(2))
nodes.statement: ϑ(z + λτ + μ; τ) = e^{−2πiQ(λ)τ − 2πiB(z,λ)}ϑ(z; τ) for λ ∈ ℤ^r, μ ∈ A^{−1}ℤ^r.
hypotheses: (z, τ) ∈ D(c₁) ∩ D(c₂).
proofSteps: μ: B(n, μ) ∈ ℤ for n ∈ ℤ^r; λ: replace n by n + λ (a ↦ a + λ).
acceptance: Index-type transformation of a Jacobi form of matrix index.

sources.excerpt: (2) ϑ(z + λτ + µ; τ) = e^{−2πiQ(λ)τ−2πiB(z,λ)}ϑ(z; τ) for all λ ∈ Z^r and µ ∈ A^{−1}Z^r.
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: ϑ(−z) = −ϑ(z) (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(3))
proofSteps: Replace n by −n; E and sgn are odd.

sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Continuity in (c₁, c₂) (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(4))
nodes.statement: (c₁, c₂) ↦ ϑ^{c₁,c₂}(z; τ) is continuous on C_Q × C_Q.
proofSteps: Locally uniform convergence in c of the β-series (λ_{c,c₀} ≥ ε near c) and of the sign-difference series (Q⁺ ≥ λ(c₁)‖ν‖² with λ(c₁) > 0 locally).
acceptance: Needed for the limit argument of Prop. 2.7(5).

sources.excerpt: (4) The function (c1, c2) ↦ ϑ^{c1,c2} is continuous on C_Q × C_Q.
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: The sign part tends to 0 at a cusp (Zwegers (2.17))
nodes.statement: For c₁ ∈ C_Q, c₂ ∈ S_Q, c(t) = c₂ + tc₁ and (z, τ) ∈ D(c₂): lim_{t↓0}Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ^r}{sgn(B(c₂,ν)) − sgn(B(c(t),ν))}e^{2πiQ(ν)τ+2πiB(ν,b)} = 0.
hypotheses: As stated (one may take c₃ = c₁).
proofSteps: |sgn(B(c₂,ν)) − sgn(B(c(t),ν))| ≤ |sgn(B(c₁,ν)) − sgn(B(c₂,ν))| for all t > 0, a t-independent summable majorant (Case 2 of Prop. 2.4); termwise limit 0 since B(c₂, ν) ≠ 0 on a + ℤ^r.

sources.excerpt: It is easy to see that |sgn(B(c2, ν)) − sgn(B(c(t), ν))| ≤ |sgn(B(c1, ν)) − sgn(B(c2, ν))| for all ν ∈ a+Z^r and t ∈ (0, ∞)
sources.match: The majorant for (2.17).

nodes.title: The β part tends to 0 at a cusp (Zwegers (2.18))
nodes.statement: In the situation of the previous node: lim_{t↓0}Σ_{ν∈a+ℤ^r} sgn(B(c(t),ν))β(−B(c(t),ν)²y/Q(c(t)))e^{2πiQ(ν)τ+2πiB(ν,b)} = 0.
hypotheses: As before.
proofSteps: Split a + ℤ^r into P₁, P₂, P₃ (sign conditions on B(c₁, ν), B(c₂, ν) and B(c₁,c₂)B(c₁,ν) − 2Q(c₁)B(c₂,ν)).

Majorants independent of t: on P₁ e^{−2πQ(ν)y} (summable by Case 2); on P₂ e^{−2πQ_{c₁}(ν)y} (Lemma 2.5); on P₃ e^{−2πQ̃(ν)y} with the auxiliary form Q̃ of type (r − 1, 1) (2.20) and the Case-2 convergence for (Q̃, c̃₁, c̃₂).
Termwise the argument −B(c(t),ν)²y/Q(c(t)) → ∞ as t ↓ 0 and β(x) → 0.
acceptance: The longest estimate of Chapter 2 (source pp. 34–38).

sources.excerpt: On P1 we use e^{−2π(Q(ν)−B(c(t),ν)²/(2Q(c(t))))y} ≤ e^{−2πQ(ν)y}, for all t ∈ (0, ∞).
sources.match: The start of the three-set majorant argument for (2.18).

nodes.title: Limit to a cusp vector (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(5))
nodes.statement: Let c₁, c₃ ∈ C_Q, c₂ ∈ S_Q, (z, τ) ∈ D(c₂), c(t) := c₂ + tc₃. Then c(t) ∈ C_Q for t > 0 and lim_{t↓0}ϑ^{c₁,c(t)}(z; τ) = ϑ^{c₁,c₂}(z; τ).
hypotheses: As stated.
proofSteps: Reduce to c₃ = c₁ by the cocycle relation; c(t) ∈ C_Q (QM.4/negative-cone API).
ϑ^{c₁,c(t)} − ϑ^{c₁,c₂} = ϑ^{c₂,c(t)}, decompose via (2.7)–(2.9) and apply (2.17), (2.18).
acceptance: Used to transfer Prop. 2.7(7) from cone vectors to cusp vectors.

sources.excerpt: (5) Let c1, c3 ∈ C_Q, c2 ∈ S_Q and (z, τ) ∈ D(c2). Set c(t) = c2 + tc3. Then c(t) ∈ C_Q for all t ∈ (0, ∞) and lim_{t↓0} ϑ^{c1,c(t)}(z; τ) = ϑ^{c1,c2}(z; τ).
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: ϑ(z; τ + 1) (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(6))
nodes.statement: ϑ(z; τ + 1) = ϑ(z + ½A^{−1}A*; τ), where A* = (A₁₁, …, A_rr)^T; in particular ϑ(z; τ + 2) = ϑ(z; τ), and ϑ(z; τ + 1) = ϑ(z; τ) if A is even.
proofSteps: ρ(a; τ) depends only on Im τ; e^{2πiQ(n)} = e^{πiΣA_ll n_l²} = e^{2πiB(½A^{−1}A*, n)} since n_l² ≡ n_l mod 2.

sources.excerpt: (6) ϑ(z; τ + 1) = ϑ(z + 1/2 A^{−1}A^∗; τ) with A^∗ = (A11 . . . Arr)^T ∈ Z^r, the vector of diagonal elements of A. In particular, ϑ(z; τ + 2) = ϑ(z; τ) and ϑ(z; τ + 1) = ϑ(z; τ) if the matrix A is even.
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

nodes.title: Gaussian integrals for a positive definite matrix and τ ∈ ℍ
nodes.statement: For a positive definite symmetric M ∈ M_n(ℝ), τ ∈ ℍ and α ∈ ℂ^n: ∫_{ℝ^n} e^{πi⟨a, Ma⟩τ + 2πi⟨a, Mα⟩}da = (−iτ)^{−n/2}(det M)^{−1/2}e^{−πi⟨α, Mα⟩/τ}.
hypotheses: Principal branch of (−iτ)^{−n/2} (as the n-th power of (−iτ)^{−1/2}).
proofSteps: Change variables a = M^{−1/2}w (Jacobian (det M)^{−1/2}) to reduce to M = I; then Mathlib's GaussianFourier.integral_cexp_neg_mul_sq_norm_add on Euclidean space with b = −πiτ (Re b = πy > 0).
acceptance: n = 1, M = (1): ∫e^{πiτa² + 2πiaα}da = (−iτ)^{−1/2}e^{−πiα²/τ}.

sources.excerpt: If τ ∈ H and M is a positive deﬁnite symmetric n × n-matrix, we have the well known result ∫_{R^n} e^{πi⟨a,Ma⟩τ+2πi⟨a,Mα⟩}da = 1/(−iτ)^{n/2} · 1/√det M · e^{−πi⟨α,Mα⟩/τ}. (By a change of basis in R^n one can reduce to the case when M is diagonal).

nodes.title: a ↦ ρ(a; τ)e^{2πiQ(a)τ} is essentially its own Fourier transform (Zwegers Lemma 2.8)
nodes.statement: For c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q, all α ∈ ℝ^r and τ ∈ ℍ: the function a ↦ ρ(a; τ)e^{2πiQ(a)τ + 2πiB(a,α)} is integrable (indeed a Schwartz function of a), and ∫_{ℝ^r}ρ(a; τ)e^{2πiQ(a)τ+2πiB(a,α)}da = (i/√(−det A))(−iτ)^{−r/2}ρ(α; −1/τ)e^{−2πiQ(α)/τ}.
hypotheses: c₁, c₂ in the open cone (the cusp case follows by Prop. 2.7(5)).
proofSteps: Integrability and rapid decay with all derivatives: decomposition (2.7)–(2.9) with the bounds of Lemmas 2.5, 2.6 (derivatives of E are Gaussians).
∂/∂α_l of e^{2πiQ(α)/τ}·(integral) equals −(1/τ)∫(∂ρ/∂a_l)e^{2πiQ(aτ+α)/τ}da (integration by parts), and ∂ρ/∂a_l is a combination of E′-terms (2.23).
Each E′-integral is computed by splitting ℝ^r = ℝc ⊕ c^⊥ (Q positive definite on c^⊥) and QM.4/multivariate-gaussian-integral twice, using (det(c C))² det A = 2Q(c)det(CᵀAC).
So the difference of both sides has zero gradient in α; both sides are odd in α, hence equal.
acceptance: The mechanism behind the modularity of the non-holomorphic theta function (Zwegers: 'the main point – and the reason for the deﬁnition of the function ρ').

sources.excerpt: Lemma 2.8 We have for all α ∈ R^r and τ ∈ H ∫_{R^r} ρ(a; τ) e^{2πiQ(a)τ+2πiB(a,α)}da = 1/√−det A · i/(−iτ)^{r/2} ρ(α; −1/τ) e^{−2πiQ(α)/τ}.
sources.match: Exactly the statement (proved there for c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q).

nodes.title: Modular S-transformation of ϑ^{c₁,c₂} (Zwegers Prop. 2.7(7))
nodes.statement: Let D′(c) := {(z, τ) ∈ D(c) : (z/τ, −1/τ) ∈ D(c)} (for c ∈ S_Q: z = aτ + b with B(c, a), B(c, b) ∉ ℤ; for c ∈ C_Q: all (z, τ)). For (z, τ) ∈ D′(c₁) ∩ D′(c₂): ϑ(z/τ; −1/τ) = (i/√(−det A))(−iτ)^{r/2}Σ_{p∈A^{−1}ℤ^r/ℤ^r} e^{2πiQ(z + pτ)/τ}ϑ(z + pτ; τ).
hypotheses: Principal branches; D′(c) as corrected in sourceIssue E504.
proofSteps: Case c₁, c₂ ∈ C_Q: Poisson summation over ℤ^r for the Schwartz function of Lemma 2.8 (dual lattice of ℤ^r for B is A^{−1}ℤ^r) gives (2.24) for ϑ_{a,b}; substitute ϑ_{a,b} = e^{2πiQ(a)τ+2πiB(a,b)}ϑ(aτ + b; τ).
Case c₁ ∈ C_Q, c₂ ∈ S_Q: take lim_{t↓0} along c(t) (Prop. 2.7(5)) on both sides.
Remaining cases by the cocycle relations.
acceptance: Example 2.16: ϑ_{e/6,e/6}(−1/τ) = −iτϑ_{e/6,e/6}(τ), the weight-1 law of η².
The 'modularity theorem' of the indefinite theta function (with Prop. 2.7(6)).

nodes.title: An indefinite theta function equal to 2e^{πi/3}η² (Zwegers Example 2.16)
proofSteps: T- and S-transformations from Cor. 2.9: ϑ(τ + 1) = e^{πi/6}ϑ(τ), ϑ(−1/τ) = −iτϑ(τ).
The β-parts (2.7), (2.8) vanish by an O_A^+(ℤ) symmetry fixing c₁ (resp. c₂) and changing the sign of the characteristic (C = (1 0; −4 −1), resp. (−1 −4; 0 1)).

So ϑ_{a,b} is the holomorphic sign sum (2.29), a modular form of weight 1 with the multiplier of η² (QM.1/dedekind-eta-multiplier); the quotient by η² is a holomorphic modular function on the compactified X(1), hence constant; compare the first coefficients.
acceptance: A concrete test of Cor. 2.9: indefinite theta functions include holomorphic modular forms.

nodes.title: The elliptic and modular laws (E), (M) of index m and weight k
nodes.statement: For ϕ : ℂ × ℍ → ℂ (meromorphic in z, with junk value 0 at its poles), m ∈ ℤ_{>0} and k ∈ ℤ, put ϕ̂(τ, z) := ϕ(z; τ). ϕ satisfies (E) of index m if ϕ̂|_m[λ, μ] = ϕ̂ for all (λ, μ) ∈ ℤ² (QM.1/jacobi-elliptic-slash), i.e. ϕ(z + λτ + μ; τ) = e^{−2πim(λ²τ + 2λz)}ϕ(z; τ); and (M) of weight k and index m if ϕ̂|_{k,m}γ = ϕ̂ for all γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) (QM.1/jacobi-modular-slash), i.e. ϕ(z/(cτ+d); (aτ+b)/(cτ+d)) = (cτ + d)^k e^{2πimcz²/(cτ+d)}ϕ(z; τ) (Zwegers §3.1). Jacobi forms of weight k and index m (QM.1/jacobi-form) are the holomorphic ϕ satisfying (E), (M) and a growth condition; here neither holomorphy nor growth is assumed, which is what Zwegers' Chapter 3 needs (ϕ has poles in z).
hypotheses: Two predicates on functions. The pole set of a ϕ satisfying the laws is invariant under the actions, so with the junk value 0 at poles the equalities hold everywhere.
proofSteps: Define the predicates as invariance under QM.1's two slash actions, with the arguments swapped to Zwegers' order (z; τ).
Compatibility: a Jacobi form of QM.1/jacobi-form is invariant under both slashes by definition (trivial multiplier and character).
acceptance: φ_{−2,1} := −ϑ(z; τ)²/η(τ)⁶ satisfies (E) with m = 1 and (M) with k = −2.
(E) and (M) for m, k are preserved by multiplication by modular forms of weight k′ (index unchanged).

sources.excerpt: In this chapter we consider functions ϕ : C × H → C that satisfy ϕ(z + λτ + µ; τ) = e^{−2πim(λ²τ+2λz)}ϕ(z; τ) ∀λ, µ ∈ Z (E) and ϕ(z/(cτ + d); (aτ + b)/(cτ + d)) = (cτ + d)^k e^{2πimcz²/(cτ+d)}ϕ(z; τ) ∀(a b; c d) ∈ SL_2(Z), (M) with k ∈ Z and m ∈ Z_{>0}.

nodes.title: S-transformation of f_u (Zwegers Prop. 3.3(6))
nodes.statement: f_u(z; τ) − τ^{−1}e^{2πim(u²−z²)/τ}f_{u/τ}(z/τ; −1/τ) = Σ_{l=0}^{2m−1} h_l(u; τ)ϑ_{m,l}(z; τ), where h_l(u; τ) = ie^{−πil²τ/2m−2πilu}∫_L e^{2πimτx²−2π(2mu+lτ)x}/(1 − e^{2πx})dx, L = ℝ − it (0 < t < 1).
proofSteps: The left side is holomorphic in z (residues cancel) and satisfies (E), so it has a theta decomposition (Thm 3.1, QM.1/theta-decomposition) with coefficients h_l.

Compute h_l for 0 ≤ l < 2m by integrating against e^{−2πilz} over [p, p + 1] with 0 < Im(u − p) < Im τ: the f_u-part has vanishing coefficients there (geometric expansion), and the other part becomes a Mordell-type integral after x = i(z − u)/τ and Cauchy's theorem.

nodes.title: The level-m correction functions R_{m,l}(u; τ)
nodes.statement: For m ∈ ℤ_{>0}, l ∈ ℤ/2mℤ, u ∈ ℂ, τ ∈ ℍ, y = Im τ: R_{m,l}(u; τ) := Σ_{λ∈ℤ, λ≡l mod 2m}{sgn(λ + 1/2) − E((λ + 2m Im u/y)√(y/m))}e^{−πiλ²τ/(2m) − 2πiλu} (Zwegers Def. 3.4). Convergence is as for R (Lemma 1.8), which the source says without proof.
hypotheses: Convergence proof supplied here by the argument of Lemma 1.8 (split sign part, finite, and β-part bounded by a Gaussian).
proofSteps: Absolute convergence: {sgn(λ + ½) − E((λ + 2m Im u/y)√(y/m))} = [sgn(λ + ½) − sgn(λ + 2m Im u/y)] + sgn(λ + 2m Im u/y)β((λ + 2m Im u/y)²y/m); the first is non-zero for finitely many λ, the second is ≤ e^{−π(λ+2mIm u/y)²y/m}.
acceptance: For m = 1/2-type normalisation it reduces to R (compare Zwegers' remark that R_{m,l} is the analogue of R).

nodes.statement: Let ϕ(·; τ) be meromorphic for each τ and satisfy (E) of index m. proofSteps: Integrate f_v(z; τ)ϕ(v; τ) over ∂P_p in v: 1-periodicity and Prop. 3.3(4) give Σ_l e^{−πil²τ/2m}ϑ_{m,l}(z)∫_p^{p+1}ϕ(v)e^{−2πilv}dv; the residue theorem gives 2πiΣRes[f_vϕ] + ϕ(z).

nodes.statement: Following Zwegers §4.3 (Hickerson's identities used as definitions): (q)_∞F₀(q) := (Σ_{r,s≥0} − Σ_{r,s<0})(−1)^{r+s}q^{3r²/2+4rs+3s²/2+r/2+s/2}, (q)_∞F₁(q) := (Σ_{r,s≥0} − Σ_{r,s<0})(−1)^{r+s}q^{3r²/2+4rs+3s²/2+5r/2+5s/2+1}, (q)_∞F₂(q) := (Σ_{r,s≥0} − Σ_{r,s<0})(−1)^{r+s}q^{3r²/2+4rs+3s²/2+3r/2+3s/2}, with (q)_∞ = ∏(1 − q^n) and q = e(τ); and F₇(τ) := (q^{−1/168}F₀(q), q^{47/168}F₂(q), q^{−25/168}F₁(q)) (fractional powers e(sτ)).
hypotheses: The identification with Ramanujan's Eulerian series (e.g. F₀(q) = Σ_{n≥0}q^{n²}/(q^{n+1}; q)_n) is Hickerson's theorem, which Zwegers takes as the definition; it is recorded as a gap, not used.
proofSteps: The double series converge absolutely for |q| < 1 (the exponent 3r²/2 + 4rs + 3s²/2 is positive on the summation cones r, s ≥ 0 and r, s < 0); (q)_∞ ≠ 0 on the unit disc (Mathlib ModularForm.eta_ne_zero), so F_j are holomorphic functions of τ ∈ ℍ.
acceptance: F₀(q) = 1 + q + q³ + q⁴ + q⁵ + 2q⁷ + q⁸ + 2q⁹ + O(q^{10}), equal to Ramanujan's Σq^{n²}/(q^{n+1}; q)_n to this order (numerically checked).
F₇ is holomorphic on ℍ and 1-periodic up to the diagonal multiplier.

nodes.title: Radial limits at rational points and at roots of unity
nodes.statement: For a function G : ℂ → ℂ (only its values on the upper half-plane ℍ matter), a real number x and L ∈ ℂ, G has radial limit L at x, written HasRadialLimit G x L, if G(x + it/(2π)) → L as t → 0 through positive reals. With q = e^{2πiτ} and G(τ) = g(q) for a function g on the punctured unit disc, this says g(ξe^{−t}) → L as t → 0⁺ with ξ = e^{2πix}: the vertical approach to x is the radial approach to the root of unity ξ from inside the unit disc. The lower version HasRadialLimitBelow G x L means G(x − it/(2π)) → L as t → 0⁺ (functions on the lower half-plane H⁻). The value radialLimit G x is L when a radial limit exists and 0 otherwise. Pinned conventions: q = e^{2πiτ}; the approach parameter is t = 2π·Im τ; x is real (rational x is the case of interest, ξ = e^{2πix} a root of unity).
hypotheses: G is arbitrary; no continuity or boundedness hypothesis is part of the definition.
Limits are taken in 𝓝[>] 0 for t; the approach is vertical, not non-tangential.
proofSteps: Define HasRadialLimit G x L as Tendsto (t ↦ G(x + i t/(2π))) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 L), using Mathlib's Filter.Tendsto with the filter nhdsWithin 0 (Ioi 0).
Define HasRadialLimitBelow G x L as HasRadialLimit (z ↦ G(z̄)) x L, since conj(x + it/(2π)) = x − it/(2π).
Define radialLimit G x by classical choice of L when ∃ L, HasRadialLimit G x L, and 0 otherwise; uniqueness of limits in the Hausdorff space ℂ makes it well defined.
Disc form: for G(τ) = g(e^{2πiτ}), e^{2πi(x + it/(2π))} = e^{2πix}e^{−t}, so the definition is the radial limit g(ξe^{−t}) → L; this identification is the API item hasRadialLimit_iff_disc.
acceptance: The function τ ↦ e^{2πiτ} has radial limit e^{2πix} at every real x.
The function τ ↦ q/(1 − q) has no radial limit at x = 0: its modulus tends to ∞.

A radial limit and a formal evaluation are different objects: HasRadialLimit refers only to the analytic function on ℍ, never to a Habiro-ring evaluation, and the two are compared only by explicit theorems (strange identity, Lawrence–Zagier).

nodes.title: Radial asymptotic expansions at rational points
nodes.statement: For G : ℂ → ℂ, x ∈ ℝ and a formal power series a = Σ a_r t^r ∈ ℂ⟦t⟧, G has radial asymptotic expansion a at x (from above), written HasRadialExpansion G x a, if for every R ∈ ℕ, G(x + it/(2π)) − Σ_{r<R} a_r t^r = O(t^R) as t → 0⁺. From below: HasRadialExpansionBelow G x a :⟺ G(x − it/(2π)) − Σ_{r<R} a_r (−t)^r = O(t^R) for every R, so that both are expansions in the same variable 2π·Im τ. Following Bringmann–Rolen, functions f on ℍ and g on H⁻ have agreeing asymptotic expansions at x, RadialExpansionsAgree f g x, if some a satisfies HasRadialExpansion f x a and HasRadialExpansionBelow g x a. The series a is not required to converge.
hypotheses: The expansion is an asymptotic statement for every order R, in Mathlib's big-O sense along 𝓝[>] 0.
proofSteps: Define HasRadialExpansion G x a as ∀ R, (t ↦ G(x + it/(2π)) − Σ_{r<R} coeff r a · t^r) =O[𝓝[>] 0] (t ↦ t^R), with Asymptotics.IsBigO.
Define HasRadialExpansionBelow G x a as HasRadialExpansion (z ↦ G(z̄)) x (rescale (−1) a).
Define RadialExpansionsAgree f g x as ∃ a, HasRadialExpansion f x a ∧ HasRadialExpansionBelow g x a.
Uniqueness: if a and b are both expansions, the difference of the partial sums is O(t^R) for every R, so the coefficients agree inductively (a polynomial of degree < R that is O(t^R) at 0 is zero).

nodes.title: Values of periodic L-functions at non-positive integers
nodes.statement: Let M ≥ 1 and Φ : ZMod M → ℂ, with L(s, Φ) = ZMod.LFunction Φ s the meromorphic continuation of Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)n^{−s}. For every integer r ≥ 1, L(−r, Φ) = −(M^r/(r+1)) Σ_{n=1}^{M} Φ(n) B_{r+1}(n/M), with B_k the Bernoulli polynomials. If moreover Σ_j Φ(j) = 0, the same formula holds for r = 0: L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{M} (n/M − 1/2) Φ(n), and L(s, Φ) is entire.
hypotheses: M ≥ 1; for r = 0 the mean-zero hypothesis Σ Φ = 0 (otherwise the formula still holds but L has a pole at s = 1 that plays no role; the lemma is stated in the form the sources use).
proofSteps: By definition ZMod.LFunction Φ s = M^{−s} Σ_{j ∈ ZMod M} Φ(j) ζ(j/M, s) with ζ(a, s) the Hurwitz zeta function.
For r ≥ 1 insert HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZeta_neg_nat at x = j.val/M ∈ [0, 1): ζ(x, −r) = −B_{r+1}(x)/(r+1).
Reindex j ∈ {0, …, M−1} by n ∈ {1, …, M}, sending j = 0 to n = M; this is allowed because B_{r+1}(1) = B_{r+1}(0) for r + 1 ≠ 1 (bernoulliFun_eval_one).
For r = 0 use hurwitz-zeta-at-zero with the representatives x = n/M ∈ (0, 1]: L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{M} Φ(n)(n/M − 1/2).
Entireness under Σ Φ = 0 is ZMod.differentiable_LFunction_of_sum_zero.

nodes.title: Asymptotics of Σ f((m + a)t) (Euler–Maclaurin)
nodes.statement: Let f : [0, ∞) → ℂ be C^∞ with every derivative of rapid decay at ∞, let b_n = f^{(n)}(0)/n! and I_f = ∫_0^∞ f(x)dx, and let a ∈ (0, 1]. Then, as t → 0⁺, Σ_{m≥0} f((m + a)t) = I_f/t − Σ_{n<N} b_n (B_{n+1}(a)/(n+1)) t^n + O(t^N) for every N. For a = 1 this is Zagier's Proposition 3: Σ_{m≥1} f(mt) ∼ I_f/t + Σ_n b_n (B_{n+1}/(n+1))(−t)^n. Consequently, for Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ Φ = 0: Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n) f(nt) ∼ Σ_n b_n L(−n, Φ) t^n.
hypotheses: f smooth on [0, ∞) with f^{(k)}(x) = O(x^{−2}) as x → ∞ for every k (rapid decay suffices).
proofSteps: Euler–Maclaurin summation with remainder: for every N, Σ_{m=0}^{K−1} f(m + a) = ∫_a^{K+a} f + boundary terms with B_{n+1}(a)/(n+1)! f^{(n)} + a remainder ∫ f^{(N)}(x) B̄_N(x − a)/N! dx, by repeated integration by parts using B′_n = nB_{n−1} and B_n(x+1) − B_n(x) = nx^{n−1}.
Let K → ∞ using rapid decay, and rescale f(x) ↦ f(tx): the remainder is O(t^{N−1}) because B̄_N is bounded.

Identify the constant: ∫_{at}^∞ f(x)dx/t = I_f/t − Σ_n b_n a^{n+1}t^n/(n+1), and combine with the boundary terms into −Σ b_n B_{n+1}(a)/(n+1) t^n (the Euler ansatz Σ b_n ζ(−n, a) t^n, since ζ(−n, a) = −B_{n+1}(a)/(n+1)).

Periodic corollary: Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n) f(nt) = Σ_{a=1}^{M} Φ(a) Σ_{m≥0} f((m + a/M)Mt); the I_f/(Mt) terms cancel because Σ Φ = 0, and −M^n/(n+1) Σ_a Φ(a) B_{n+1}(a/M) = L(−n, Φ) by periodic-l-value-bernoulli.
acceptance: For f(x) = e^{−λx} and a = 1 the expansion is 1/(λt) + Σ B_{n+1}(λt)^n/(n+1)!, the expansion of 1/(e^{λt} − 1).

For f(x) = e^{−x} and general a the expansion must reproduce e^{−at}/(1 − e^{−t}) = 1/t + Σ_n (−1)^{n+1}B_{n+1}(a)t^n/(n+1)!; this fixes the sign of the Bernoulli term (the printed eq. (44) of the source has the opposite sign; see the source issues).
With a = 1 the lemma reduces to Zagier's Proposition 3 because B_{n+1}(1) = (−1)^{n+1}B_{n+1}.

nodes.title: Expansion of Σ Φ(n)e^{−nt} for mean-zero periodic Φ
nodes.statement: Let M ≥ 1 and Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ_j Φ(j) = 0. Then Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)e^{−nt} = Σ_{r≥0} L(−r, Φ)(−t)^r/r! as a convergent power series for 0 < t < 2π/M; in particular the left side has the asymptotic expansion Σ L(−r, Φ)(−t)^r/r! as t → 0⁺ and the limit L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{M}(n/M − 1/2)Φ(n).
hypotheses: Σ Φ = 0 (mean value zero); without it the sum has a pole (ΣΦ/M)/t at t = 0.
proofSteps: Sum the geometric series: Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)e^{−nt} = Σ_{n=1}^{M} Φ(n)e^{−nt}/(1 − e^{−Mt}).
Expand with the Bernoulli generating function (Polynomial.bernoulli_generating_function): e^{−nt}/(1 − e^{−Mt}) = −Σ_{r≥−1} B_{r+1}(n/M)(−Mt)^r/(r+1)! for |t| < 2π/M.
The r = −1 term is Σ_n Φ(n)/(Mt), which vanishes by the mean-zero hypothesis.
The coefficient of (−t)^r/r! is −M^r/(r+1) Σ_n Φ(n)B_{r+1}(n/M) = L(−r, Φ) by periodic-l-value-bernoulli.
acceptance: For Φ = χ₁₂ the sum is Σ χ₁₂(m)e^{−mt} = sinh(2t)/cosh(3t) = 2t − (23/3)t³ + …, whose coefficients are the Glaisher numbers (Zagier's (5)).
The Lawrence–Zagier Remark: for odd Φ the expansion is even in t, for even Φ it is odd.

nodes.statement: Let M ≥ 1, Φ : ZMod M → ℂ with Σ_j Φ(j) = 0, and ν ∈ {0, 1}. As t → 0⁺, Σ_{n≥1} n^ν Φ(n) e^{−n²t} ∼ Σ_{r≥0} L(−2r − ν, Φ)(−t)^r/r!. In particular Σ_{n≥1} Φ(n)e^{−n²t} → L(0, Φ) and Σ_{n≥1} nΦ(n)e^{−n²t} → L(−1, Φ).

nodes.title: Quantum modular forms (Zagier's canonical definition)
nodes.statement: Fix a subgroup Γ ≤ SL₂(ℤ), a weight k ∈ ℝ and a multiplier ε : SL₂(ℤ) → ℂ. For γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) and x ∈ ℝ with cx + d ≠ 0, the boundary factor j_k(γ, x) is the limit as y → 0⁺ of the principal power (c(x − iy) + d)^{−k}: it equals |cx + d|^{−k} if cx + d > 0, |cx + d|^{−k}e^{iπk} if cx + d < 0 and c > 0, and |cx + d|^{−k}e^{−iπk} if cx + d < 0 and c ≤ 0 (it is 0 by convention when cx + d = 0). For f : ℚ → ℂ the quantum slash is (f|_{k,ε}γ)(x) = ε(γ)·j_k(γ, x)·f(γx) and the period function is h_γ = f − f|_{k,ε}γ on {x ∈ ℚ : cx + d ≠ 0}. The function f is a quantum modular form of weight k on Γ with multiplier ε if for every γ ∈ Γ there are a finite set S_γ ⊂ ℝ and a function H_γ : ℝ → ℂ, real-analytic on ℝ ∖ S_γ, with H_γ(x) = h_γ(x) for every x ∈ ℚ ∖ S_γ with cx + d ≠ 0. This is Zagier's canonical (weak) definition with P¹(ℝ) replaced by ℝ; the boundary factor is the one of the lower half-plane, which is the branch in which the half-integral weight examples (Eichler integrals of theta series, Kontsevich's function) have constant multipliers.
hypotheses: Γ is any subgroup of SL₂(ℤ); in all examples it has finite index.
ε is an arbitrary function on SL₂(ℤ); no cocycle condition is imposed in the definition (it enters only through quantum-modular-cocycle).
Real-analytic means AnalyticOnNhd ℝ H_γ on the open set ℝ ∖ S_γ, for H_γ : ℝ → ℂ.
proofSteps: Define boundaryFactor k γ x by the three cases above; prove it equals lim_{y→0⁺} (c(x − iy) + d)^{−k} for Mathlib's principal cpow (API boundaryFactor_eq_limit).
Define quantumSlash k ε γ f x := ε γ * boundaryFactor k γ x * f (γ • x), where γ acts on ℚ by Möbius transformation (0 off the domain).
Define quantumPeriodFunction k ε γ f := f − quantumSlash k ε γ f.
Define IsQuantumModularForm Γ k ε f := ∀ γ ∈ Γ, ∃ S : Finset ℝ, ∃ H : ℝ → ℂ, AnalyticOnNhd ℝ H (↑S)ᶜ ∧ ∀ x : ℚ, (x:ℝ) ∉ S → c x + d ≠ 0 → H x = quantumPeriodFunction k ε γ f x.
The quantum modular forms of fixed (Γ, k, ε) form a ℂ-subspace: sums and scalar multiples of period functions are period functions, with S the union of the exceptional sets.
acceptance: The restriction to ℚ of a real-analytic function is a quantum modular form of every weight k ∈ ℤ on SL₂(ℤ) with ε = 1 (its period functions are real-analytic off {−d/c}); the notion is deliberately weak.

The indicator function of ℤ on ℚ is not a quantum modular form of weight 0 on SL₂(ℤ) with ε = 1: its S-period function is −1 at the points 1/m, which accumulate only at 0, and 0 at the other rationals near them.
Kontsevich's φ(x) = e^{πix/12}F(e^{2πix}) is one of weight 3/2 on SL₂(ℤ) with ε(T) = e^{−2πi/24}, ε(S) = e^{2πi/8} (kontsevich-quantum-modular).

nodes.title: The cocycle relation and reduction to generators
nodes.statement: Let k ∈ ℝ and ε : SL₂(ℤ) → ℂ, and suppose the factor J(γ, x) := ε(γ)j_k(γ, x) satisfies J(γ₁γ₂, x) = J(γ₁, γ₂x)J(γ₂, x) for all γ₁, γ₂ ∈ Γ and all x ∈ ℚ outside the finitely many poles involved. Then for f : ℚ → ℂ the period functions satisfy h_{γ₁γ₂} = h_{γ₁}|_{k,ε}γ₂ + h_{γ₂} and h_{γ⁻¹} = −h_γ|_{k,ε}γ⁻¹ (off finitely many points). Consequently, if Γ is generated by a set G and the condition of quantum-modular-form holds for every γ ∈ G, then f is a quantum modular form on Γ.
hypotheses: J satisfies the cocycle condition on Γ (a multiplier system for the lower boundary branch).
proofSteps: Expand h_{γ₁γ₂}(x) = f(x) − J(γ₁γ₂, x)f(γ₁γ₂x) and insert J(γ₁γ₂, x) = J(γ₁, γ₂x)J(γ₂, x): the difference from h_{γ₂}(x) is J(γ₂, x)(f(γ₂x) − J(γ₁, γ₂x)f(γ₁γ₂x)) = (h_{γ₁}|γ₂)(x).

The slash of a function real-analytic off a finite set S by γ₂ is real-analytic off γ₂⁻¹(S) ∪ {γ₂⁻¹∞}: Möbius maps and the boundary factor are real-analytic off the pole, where the branch of j_k is locally constant.
Apply to γ₁ = γ, γ₂ = γ⁻¹ for inverses (h_1 = 0 when J(1, x) = 1), and induct on word length in G ∪ G⁻¹.
acceptance: For k ∈ ℤ and ε a character the cocycle condition is automatic.
For Kontsevich's function the check reduces to the two generators T and S of SL₂(ℤ) (Zagier, Topology 40, §6).

sources.excerpt: Notice that this property need only be checked for a set of generators of Γ, and hence for only ﬁnitely many elements, because its validity for γ1 and γ2 automatically implies its validity for γ1γ2.
sources.match: The reduction to generators; the node adds the cocycle hypothesis on the multiplier that it silently uses.

nodes.title: Holomorphic Eichler integrals of q-series of real weight
nodes.statement: Let w ∈ ℝ, N ≥ 1 and a : ℕ → ℂ with polynomial growth (|a(n)| ≤ Cn^A). For the q-series f(τ) = Σ_{n≥1} a(n)e^{2πinτ/N} (holomorphic on ℍ, no constant term), the Eichler integral of weight w is f̃(τ) = Σ_{n≥1} (n/N)^{1−w} a(n) e^{2πinτ/N} (τ ∈ ℍ), where (n/N)^{1−w} is the positive real power. Writing D = (2πi)^{−1}d/dτ, one has D f̃_w = f̃_{w−1} and f̃_1 = f, so for integer w = k ≥ 1, D^{k−1} f̃ = f: f̃ is the normalised (k − 1)-fold primitive with no constant term. For a cusp form f = Σ a(n)qⁿ of integral weight k on SL₂(ℤ) this is Σ a(n)n^{1−k}qⁿ, the Eichler integral of Tau Ceti's modular symbols layer; for half-integral w it is the formal Eichler integral of Lawrence–Zagier and Bringmann–Rolen. The function f̃ is an analytic object on ℍ; its radial limits and asymptotic expansions at rational points are separate objects (radial-limit, radial-asymptotic-expansion) and are compared with formal evaluations only by explicit theorems.
hypotheses: a has polynomial growth, so the series converges absolutely and locally uniformly on ℍ.
Exponents are n/N ∈ (1/N)ℤ_{>0}; the unary theta series of the sources are the case a supported on squares.
proofSteps: Define eichlerIntegral w N a τ := Σ' n ≥ 1, (n/N : ℝ)^(1−w) • a n • exp(2πi n τ/N).

Convergence: |(n/N)^{1−w}a(n)e^{2πinτ/N}| ≤ C′n^{A+|1−w|}e^{−2πn Im τ/N}, summable locally uniformly in τ ∈ ℍ; holomorphy by the Weierstrass M-test (Mathlib's locally uniform limits of holomorphic functions).
Termwise differentiation: D e^{2πinτ/N} = (n/N)e^{2πinτ/N}, giving D f̃_w = f̃_{w−1}.

Unary theta normalisation: for a(m) = n^ν C(n) when m = n² and 0 otherwise (ν ∈ {0,1}), (n²/N)^{1−w} with w = ν + 1/2 equals N^{ν−1/2}n^{1−2ν}, so f̃ = N^{ν−1/2}Σ n^{1−ν}C(n)q^{n²/N}; the sources drop the scalar N^{ν−1/2}.
acceptance: For Δ (w = 12, N = 1) the coefficient of q² in Δ̃ is τ(2)/2^{11} = −24/2048 = −3/256.
For η (w = 1/2, N = 24, a(n²) = χ₁₂(n)) one gets f̃ = 24^{−1/2}Σ nχ₁₂(n)q^{n²/24}; Zagier's η̃ is √24 f̃.
f̃ tends to 0 as Im τ → ∞ (no constant term): the Eichler integral is not the formal antiderivative with a constant.

Θ̃₊ = q^{1/120}A(q) is the Eichler integral of the weight-3/2 theta series Θ₊

nodes.title: The non-holomorphic Eichler integral on the lower half-plane
nodes.statement: Let k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ and f = Σ_{n≥1} a_f(n)qⁿ ∈ S_k(N) a cusp form of half-integral weight on Γ₀(N) (Shimura's multiplier). For τ ∈ H⁻ = {Im τ < 0} define f*(τ) = ((−2πi)^{k−1}/Γ(k − 1)) ∫_{τ̄}^{i∞} f(w)(w − τ)^{k−2} dw, the path running in ℍ from τ̄ to i∞ and (w − τ)^{k−2} the principal branch (w − τ ∈ ℍ). Termwise, f*(τ) = Γ(k − 1)^{−1}Σ_{n≥1} a_f(n)n^{1−k}e^{2πinτ}Γ(k − 1, 4πn|Im τ|), with Γ(s, x) = ∫_x^∞ t^{s−1}e^{−t}dt the upper incomplete gamma function. Unlike f̃, f* is real-analytic, not holomorphic, and it has a simple transformation law (nonholomorphic-eichler-transformation).
hypotheses: f ∈ S_k(N) with k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ (supplied by MetaplecticAutomorphicForms:MP.7).
proofSteps: Convergence: f decays exponentially at i∞, and on the vertical path w = τ̄ + iy the factor |(w − τ)^{k−2}| ≤ (2|Im τ| + y)^{k−2}·e^{π|k−2|} is bounded.
Path independence in ℍ: the integrand is holomorphic in w on ℍ (w − τ ∈ ℍ never vanishes), so Cauchy's theorem for rectangles moves the path.

Termwise integration: ∫_{τ̄}^{i∞} e^{2πinw}(w − τ)^{k−2}dw = i^{k−1}(2πn)^{1−k}e^{2πinτ}Γ(k − 1, 4πn|v|) by the substitution w = τ + iu/(2πn) (BR p. 8), the constants combining because ((−2πi)·i)^{k−1}(2π)^{1−k} = 1 on the principal branches.
Real-analyticity of f* on H⁻ follows from the termwise expansion and locally uniform convergence.
acceptance: For f = η(24τ) (k = 1/2, N = 576, character χ₁₂) the construction is Zagier's η* up to the scalar of eichler-integral.
For k = 3/2 and f = Θ₊(120τ) it is Lawrence–Zagier's Θ*₊ of (17), up to their normalising factor √(2i/15).
f* is real-analytic but not holomorphic: its τ̄-dependence is through the lower limit, so ∂f*/∂τ̄ = −c_k f(τ̄)(τ̄ − τ)^{k−2}, which is not identically zero.

uses.how: f* carries the transformation law and shares the asymptotic expansion of f̃ at every rational point
Θ*± agree with Θ̃± to infinite order at rationals and are nearly modular of weight 1/2 in H⁻

nodes.title: The period integral r_α of a half-integral weight cusp form
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) as in nonholomorphic-eichler-integral and a cusp α ∈ ℚ, define r_{f,α}(z) = ((−2πi)^{k−1}/Γ(k − 1)) ∫_α^{i∞} f(w)(w − z)^{k−2}dw for z ∈ H⁻ (principal branch, w − z ∈ ℍ), the path running in ℍ from α to i∞. It extends from H⁻ to a real-analytic function on ℝ ∖ {α} (and holomorphically to ℂ minus any path from α to i∞), and it is the half-integral weight analogue of the period polynomial: in weight k ∈ ℤ the same integral is a polynomial of degree ≤ k − 2.
hypotheses: f ∈ S_k(N), k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ; α ∈ ℚ.
proofSteps: Convergence at α: f(w) decays faster than any power of Im(w) as w → α inside a Stolz angle (α is a cusp and f is cuspidal there), and |(w − z)^{k−2}| is bounded near α for z ∉ {α}.

Holomorphic continuation: for a path L from α to i∞ in ℍ, the integral defines a holomorphic function of z ∈ ℂ ∖ L (the integrand is holomorphic in z off L); choosing L to leave α vertically and deforming it gives the continuation across ℝ ∖ {α}.
Real-analyticity on ℝ ∖ {α} follows by restricting the holomorphic continuation.
acceptance: For weight k ∈ ℤ, k ≥ 2, the same formula gives a polynomial in z of degree ≤ k − 2 (Tau Ceti modular symbols layer); in half-integral weight it is never a polynomial.
Lawrence–Zagier's r±_α of (16) is this construction for Θ±, up to their factor √(2i/15).

nodes.title: Transformation law of the non-holomorphic Eichler integral (Bringmann–Rolen (2.4))
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) (k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ, trivial character), γ = (a b; c d) ∈ Γ₀(N) and τ ∈ H⁻: f*(τ) − χ₋₄(d)·(f*|_{2−k}γ)(τ) = r_{f,−d/c}(τ), where (g|_{2−k}γ)(τ) = ε_d^{2(2−k)}(c/d)(cτ + d)^{k−2}g(γτ) is Shimura's slash with the principal branch of (cτ + d)^{k−2} on H⁻, ε_d ∈ {1, i} and χ₋₄ = (−4/·).
hypotheses: γ ∈ Γ₀(N); c ≠ 0 (for c = 0 the right side is read as 0 and the statement is the periodicity of f*).
proofSteps: Write f*(γτ) as the integral from γτ̄ to i∞ and substitute w = γu: u runs from τ̄ to γ⁻¹(i∞) = −d/c, dw = du/(cu + d)².
Use the modularity f(γu) = ε_d^{−2k}(c/d)(cu + d)^k f(u) (Shimura's multiplier, supplied by MP.7) and w − γτ = (u − τ)/((cu + d)(cτ + d)).

Branch bookkeeping: for c > 0, cu + d ∈ ℍ and cτ + d ∈ H⁻, so the arguments add inside (−π, π) and ((cu + d)(cτ + d))^{2−k} splits; arg(u − τ) − arg((cu + d)(cτ + d)) = arg(w − γτ) because both sides lie in (0, π); the case c < 0 is symmetric.
This gives (f*|_{2−k}γ)(τ) = ε_d^{4−4k}·c_k∫_{τ̄}^{−d/c} f(u)(u − τ)^{k−2}du, and ε_d^{4−4k} = ε_d^{−2} = χ₋₄(d) for k ∈ ½ + ℤ.
Subtract from f*(τ) = c_k∫_{τ̄}^{i∞}: the difference is c_k∫_{−d/c}^{i∞} = r_{f,−d/c}(τ).
acceptance: For γ = T = (1 1; 0 1): χ₋₄(1) = 1 and the statement is f*(τ + 1) = f*(τ).
The right side is independent of τ̄ and extends real-analytically across ℝ ∖ {−d/c}: this is what makes f̃ quantum modular.

nodes.title: Non-tangential boundary values of f* at cusps
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) as above and x ∈ ℚ, f*(τ) converges as τ → x within any Stolz angle {τ ∈ H⁻ : |Re τ − x| ≤ C|Im τ|}, and the limit equals the radial limit from below of f* at x.
hypotheses: f cuspidal at every cusp (f ∈ S_k(N)); k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀ so that k − 2 < 0.
proofSteps: Split f*(τ) = c_k∫_{τ̄}^{x} + c_k∫_{x}^{i∞}, paths in ℍ, the second taken vertically from x.

Second integral: for w on the vertical ray from x, w − τ ∈ ℍ with |w − τ| ≥ Im w, so |(w − τ)^{k−2}| ≤ e^{π|k−2|}(Im w)^{k−2}; f(w) decays faster than any power of Im w as w → x vertically (cuspidality at x), so dominated convergence gives continuity at τ = x.

First integral along the segment from τ̄ to x: inside a Stolz angle at the cusp x, |f(w)| ≤ C′exp(−c/|w − x|) and |(w − τ)^{k−2}| ≤ e^{π|k−2|}|Im τ|^{k−2}, while the length is |τ̄ − x| ≍ |Im τ|; the product tends to 0.
Hence the limit exists within the Stolz angle and equals c_k∫_x^{i∞}f(w)(w − x)^{k−2}dw, which is also the vertical limit.
acceptance: The image under γ ∈ Γ₀(N) of the vertical ray below x approaches γx tangentially to the vertical (γ(x − iy) − γx = −iy/(cx + d)² + O(y²)), so it lies eventually in every Stolz angle at γx; this is the use in half-integral-eichler-quantum-modular.
The statement fails for tangential approach along a horocycle, which the sources never need.

nodes.title: Twisted L-functions of half-integral weight cusp forms (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 2.2)
nodes.statement: Let f ∈ S_k(N), k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀, N ∈ 4ℕ, and d/c ∈ ℚ in lowest terms. The twisted L-function L_f(ζ_c^d; s) = Σ_{n≥1} a_f(n)ζ_c^{dn}n^{−s} (Re s ≫ 0, ζ_c^d = e^{2πid/c}) extends to an entire function of s, and L_f(ζ_c^d; −m) = 0 for every m ∈ ℕ₀.
hypotheses: f cuspidal; the twisted series converges absolutely for Re s > k/2 + 1 by the Hecke bound a_f(n) = O(n^{k/2}).
proofSteps: f_{d/c}(τ) := Σ a_f(n)ζ_c^{dn}qⁿ = f(τ + d/c) is modular of weight k on the conjugate group, and lies in S_k(Γ₁(Nc²)) (conjugation by (1 d/c; 0 1)).
Decompose S_k(Γ₁(Nc²)) = ⊕_χ S_k(Nc², χ) (character decomposition, supplied by MetaplecticAutomorphicForms:MP.7), so it suffices to treat g ∈ S_k(M, χ), 4 | M.
Hecke's integral: Λ_g(s) = ∫_0^∞ g(iv/√M)v^{s−1}dv = (√M/2π)^sΓ(s)L_g(s) (mellin of the q-expansion, Mathlib's mellin and Complex.Gamma).

Split at v = 1, substitute v ↦ 1/v in ∫_0^1 and apply the Fricke involution g|_kW_M ∈ S_k(M, χ(M/·)) (MP.7): Λ_g(s) = ∫_1^∞ (g|W_M)(iv/√M)v^{k−s−1}dv + ∫_1^∞ g(iv/√M)v^{s−1}dv, entire because both integrands decay exponentially.
L_g(s) = (2π/√M)^sΛ_g(s)/Γ(s) is entire since 1/Γ is entire, and vanishes at s = −m because 1/Γ(−m) = 0 while Λ_g(−m) is finite.
acceptance: The values L_f(ζ; −m) vanish, while the Taylor coefficients of f̃ at d/c are the values at k − 1 − n, which for k ∈ ½ + ℤ are half-integers and in general non-zero.
The vanishing at non-positive integers is what makes f̃ and f* have the same expansion (the odd powers of √t in f* drop out).

nodes.title: Exponential decay of Γ on vertical lines (Stirling's estimate)
nodes.statement: For every compact interval [x₁, x₂] ⊂ ℝ there is C such that |Γ(x + iy)| ≤ C|y|^{x−1/2}e^{−π|y|/2} for x ∈ [x₁, x₂] and |y| ≥ 1; more precisely |Γ(x + iy)| = √(2π)|y|^{x−1/2}e^{−π|y|/2}(1 + O(1/|y|)) uniformly for x in compact sets.
hypotheses: x in a fixed compact interval; |y| ≥ 1 (away from the poles on the real axis).
proofSteps: Base cases from the reflection formula (Complex.Gamma_mul_Gamma_one_sub): |Γ(iy)|² = π/(|y| sinh π|y|) and |Γ(1/2 + iy)|² = π/cosh(πy).
Recurrence Γ(s + 1) = sΓ(s) (Complex.Gamma_add_one) shifts x by integers, multiplying by |s| ≍ |y|.

Interpolate between x and x + 1/2 by the Phragmén–Lindelöf principle in vertical strips (PhragmenLindelof.vertical_strip) applied to Γ(s)·e^{±iπs/2}·(polynomial correction), or use Stirling's formula for log Γ with the error bound.

nodes.title: Polynomial growth of twisted L-functions in vertical strips (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 2.3)
nodes.statement: For f ∈ S_k(N) and d/c ∈ ℚ as in twisted-cusp-form-l-function, and every compact interval [x₁, x₂], there are C, A with |L_f(ζ_c^d; x + it)| ≤ C(1 + |t|)^A for x ∈ [x₁, x₂] and t ∈ ℝ.
hypotheses: As in twisted-cusp-form-l-function.
proofSteps: Right of absolute convergence (x ≥ k/2 + 2) the Dirichlet series is bounded.

Left of the critical strip use the functional equation Λ_g(s) = Λ_{g|W}(k − s) of each nebentypus component and gamma-vertical-decay: L_g(s) = (2π/√M)^{2s−k}Γ(k − s)/Γ(s)·L_{g|W}(k − s), and |Γ(k − s)/Γ(s)| grows polynomially in |t|.

In between, Λ_g is bounded in vertical strips (the integral representation), so L_g(s) = Λ_g(s)(2π/√M)^s/Γ(s) is at most e^{π|t|/2}|t|^B; Phragmén–Lindelöf (PhragmenLindelof.vertical_strip) applied to L_g·(s + 1)^{−A} interpolates the polynomial bounds on the two edges.

nodes.title: Asymptotic expansions from poles of Mellin transforms (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 3.1)
nodes.statement: Let F : (0, ∞) → ℂ be continuous with Mellin transform M(F)(s) = ∫_0^∞ F(x)x^{s−1}dx converging for Re s > α. Suppose M(F) continues meromorphically to Re s > β (β < α) with finitely many poles a₀, …, a_M there, all simple with residues α₀, …, α_M, is analytic on the line Re s = β, and satisfies M(F)(s) = O(|s|^{−r}) as |s| → ∞ in Re s > β for some r > 1. Then F(x) = Σ_j α_j x^{−a_j} + O(x^{−β}) as x → 0⁺. If the hypotheses hold for every β, F has the asymptotic expansion Σ_j α_j x^{−a_j} (all orders).
hypotheses: F continuous on (0, ∞); absolute convergence of the Mellin integral on some right half-plane; decay O(|s|^{−r}), r > 1, uniformly in the half-plane.
proofSteps: Mellin inversion on the line Re s = c > α: F(x) = (2πi)^{−1}∫_{c−i∞}^{c+i∞} M(F)(s)x^{−s}ds (mellinInv_mellin_eq, using the decay for vertical integrability).

Move the line to Re s = β: integrate over rectangles [β, c] × [−T, T] (Complex.integral_boundary_rect_eq_zero_of_differentiableOn after subtracting the principal parts α_j/(s − a_j)), let T → ∞ using the O(|s|^{−r}) decay on the horizontal sides.
The residues contribute α_j x^{−a_j}; the remaining integral on Re s = β is bounded by x^{−β}∫|M(F)(β + it)|dt = O(x^{−β}).
acceptance: For F(x) = e^{−x}, M(F) = Γ(s) with residues (−1)^n/n! at −n: the lemma recovers e^{−x} = Σ (−x)^n/n! to every order.
Without the decay hypothesis the conclusion fails: the Mellin transform of a function with an oscillating term like sin(1/x) has the same poles but no such expansion.

nodes.title: Poles and residues of the Mellin transform of e^tΓ(k − 1, 2t) (Bringmann–Rolen Lemma 3.2 core)
nodes.statement: Let k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀ and G_k(s) = M(t ↦ e^tΓ(k − 1, 2t))(s). For Re s > 0 and Re(k − 1 + s) > 0, G_k(s) = β(1/2; s, 2 − k − s)Γ(k − 1 + s) with β(z; a, b) = ∫_0^z t^{a−1}(1 − t)^{b−1}dt the incomplete beta function; equivalently G_k(s) = 2^{k−1}Γ(s + k − 1)·₂F₁(1, s + k − 1; 1 + s; −1)/s. G_k continues meromorphically to ℂ; its poles lie in −ℕ₀ ∪ {1 − k − m : m ∈ ℕ₀}, are simple, and at s = −n (n ∈ ℕ₀) the residue is Γ(k − 1)/n!. Moreover β(1/2; s, 2 − k − s) is bounded on vertical lines for |Im s| large. Consequently, for an entire function L with L(k − 1 + s) = 0 at the points s = 1 − k − m, Γ(k − 1)^{−1}L(k − 1 + s)G_k(s) has simple poles only at s = −n, with residue L(k − 1 − n)/n!.
hypotheses: k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀; the regularized incomplete beta function I(z; a, b) = β(z; a, b)/B(a, b).
proofSteps: Beta function and Euler reflection turn (3.6) into Γ(s)·πI(1/2; s, 2 − k − s)/(Γ(2 − k)sin(π(k − 1 + s))).

At s = −n: I(1/2; −n, 2 − k + n) = 1, from the reflection I(x; a, b) = 1 − I(1 − x; b, a) (DLMF 26.5.2 / A&S 26.5.2) and the recurrence I(x; a, b) = Γ(a+b)/(Γ(a+1)Γ(b))x^a(1 − x)^{b−1} + I(x; a + 1, b − 1) (A&S 26.5.15), evaluated at the terminating value ₂F₁(1, 0; 2 − k; −1) = 1.

Holomorphy elsewhere: by the Pfaff transformation (DLMF 15.8.1) G_k(s) = 2^{−s}Γ(s + k − 1)₂F₁(s + k − 1, s; 1 + s; 1/2)/s, whose only possible poles are s ∈ −ℕ₀ and the poles of Γ(s + k − 1); the latter are cancelled by the zeros of L.
acceptance: For k = 3/2 and n = 0 the residue formula gives L(1/2)/0! = L(k − 1), the radial limit value.

The incomplete gamma and beta functions with complex parameters and the Gauss hypergeometric function at the boundary point −1 are not in the pinned libraries (Tau Ceti's incomplete gamma and beta are for positive real parameters); this node owns the identities it needs.

nodes.title: Eichler integrals of half-integral weight cusp forms are quantum modular (Bringmann–Rolen Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: Let f ∈ S_k(N) with k ∈ ½ + ℕ₀ and N ∈ 4ℕ. Define f̃ : ℚ → ℂ by f̃(x) = radial limit of the Eichler integral f̃ at x (which exists by eichler-integral-asymptotic-expansion). Then f̃ is a quantum modular form of weight 2 − k on Γ₀(N) with multiplier ε(γ) = χ₋₄(d)ε_d^{2(2−k)}(c/d), and for every γ ∈ Γ₀(N) its period function extends to the real-analytic function r_{f,−d/c} on ℝ ∖ {−d/c}.
hypotheses: f ∈ S_k(N) with trivial character (the character case is recorded in the source issues and in kontsevich-quantum-modular).
Weight 2 − k, multiplier as stated, lower-boundary branch of quantum-modular-form.
proofSteps: By eichler-asymptotic-agreement the radial limit of f̃ at x equals the radial limit of f* from below at x.
Take x ∈ ℚ with cx + d ≠ 0 and let τ = x − iy, y → 0⁺, in nonholomorphic-eichler-transformation.

f*(τ) → f̃(x); (cτ + d)^{k−2} → the boundary factor j_{2−k}(γ, x) of quantum-modular-form (lower branch); f*(γτ) → f̃(γx) by nonholomorphic-eichler-nontangential-limit, since γτ approaches γx tangentially to the vertical.
The right side r_{f,−d/c}(τ) → r_{f,−d/c}(x), real-analytic on ℝ ∖ {−d/c} (eichler-period-integral).
Hence h_γ(x) = r_{f,−d/c}(x) on ℚ ∖ {−d/c}, which is the definition with S_γ = {−d/c}.
acceptance: For f = Θ₊(120τ) (k = 3/2, after the character extension) this is Lawrence–Zagier's quantum modularity of the Poincaré-sphere WRT values.
The cocycle is real-analytic but, unlike in integral weight, not a polynomial.
The theorem concerns radial limits of f̃; it says nothing about formal (Habiro) evaluations, which are compared separately (strange-identity).

nodes.title: Kontsevich's strange series F(q) = Σ (q;q)_n as an element of the Habiro ring
nodes.statement: Kontsevich's series is F(q) = Σ_{n≥0} (q;q)_n with (q;q)_n = (1 − q)(1 − q²)⋯(1 − qⁿ) the finite q-Pochhammer symbol (QM.0/q-pochhammer). The series does not converge in ℤ⟦q⟧ nor on any open subset of ℂ, but it converges in the Habiro ring ℤ[q]^ = lim_n ℤ[q]/((q;q)_n) (HabiroCyclotomicCompletions:HC.1), where the n-th term lies in the n-th ideal; F denotes that element. Its formal evaluations are the images under the Habiro evaluation and Taylor maps (HC.3): for a root of unity ξ of order N, F(ξ) = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} (ξ;ξ)_n (the terms with n ≥ N vanish), and after the substitution q = ξe^{−t} the Taylor map gives the power series T_ξF = Σ_{n≥0} (ξe^{−t}; ξe^{−t})_n ∈ ℂ⟦t⟧, which converges t-adically because (ξe^{−t}; ξe^{−t})_n ∈ t^{⌊n/N⌋}ℂ⟦t⟧. The normalised function on ℚ is φ(x) = e^{πix/12}F(e^{2πix}). These are formal evaluations: that they agree with radial limits of a holomorphic q-series is the content of strange-identity, not of this definition.
hypotheses: The Habiro ring, its evaluation maps and Taylor maps are HabiroCyclotomicCompletions:HC.1 and HC.3 (requested).
ξ ranges over roots of unity in ℂ; N ≥ 1 with ξ^N = 1 (any such N gives the same finite sum).
proofSteps: Convergence in the Habiro ring: (q;q)_n ∈ ((q;q)_n), so the partial sums form a compatible system (HC.1).
Evaluation: ev_ξ is continuous and (ξ;ξ)_n = 0 for n ≥ N because the factor 1 − ξ^N vanishes; hence ev_ξ(F) = Σ_{n<N}(ξ;ξ)_n, independent of N with ξ^N = 1.

Taylor map: (ξe^{−t};ξe^{−t})_n contains the ⌊n/N⌋ factors 1 − e^{−jNt} (j ≤ n/N), each in tℂ⟦t⟧, so the sum converges in ℂ⟦t⟧ (PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.summable_of_tendsto_order_atTop_nhds_top); it is the image of F under the Taylor map at ξ composed with q ↦ ξe^{−t}.
Constant coefficient of T_ξF is F(ξ) (the constant term of the Taylor map is evaluation, HC.3).
Galois: for σ ∈ Aut(ℂ/ℚ), σ(F(ξ)) = F(σξ) because F(ξ) is a polynomial expression in ξ with integer coefficients.
acceptance: F(1) = 1, F(−1) = 3, F(i) = 8 − 3i, F(e^{2πi/3}) = 5 − e^{2πi/3} (Zagier's table of c₀(ξ)).
The partial sums Σ_{n≤M}(q;q)_n do not converge in ℤ⟦q⟧: their q-coefficient is −M.

nodes.title: The sum-of-tails series F₁ = Σ n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ
nodes.statement: F₁(q) = Σ_{n≥1} n (q;q)_{n−1} qⁿ ∈ ℤ⟦q⟧, which also defines a holomorphic function on the unit disc and, since (q;q)_{n−1} ∈ (1 − q)^{n−1}ℤ[q], a formal power series in 1 − q (and in ξ − q for every root of unity ξ). The companion series is F₂(q) = Σ_{n≥0}[(q;q)_n − (q;q)_∞] ∈ ℤ⟦q⟧, the sum of the tails of Euler's product. The Euler product (q;q)_∞ = ∏_{n≥1}(1 − qⁿ) and E(q) = Σ_{n≥1} qⁿ/(1 − qⁿ) = Σ d(n)qⁿ enter the identity of zagier-sum-of-tails-identity.
hypotheses: All series are in ℤ⟦q⟧ with the pi topology; convergence as functions on |q| < 1 is absolute and locally uniform.
proofSteps: F₁ converges in ℤ⟦q⟧ since the n-th term has order n.
F₂ converges in ℤ⟦q⟧ since (q;q)_n − (q;q)_∞ ∈ q^{n+1}ℤ⟦q⟧.
Holomorphy on the disc: |n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ| ≤ n·C(r)|q|ⁿ on |q| ≤ r < 1 with C(r) = ∏(1 + r^j).
acceptance: F₁ = q + 2q² + q³ + ⋯ (and F₂ has the same expansion).
F₁ is not the Habiro element F: F does not lie in ℤ⟦q⟧, while F₁ does; they agree only after expansion at roots of unity (sum-of-tails-agreement).

proofSteps: (a) Induction on N (partial summation): passing from N to N + 1 adds (q;q)_N − (N + 1)(q;q)_{N+1} + N(q;q)_N on the left and (N+1)(q;q)_N q^{N+1} on the right, which agree since (q;q)_{N+1} = (q;q)_N(1 − q^{N+1}).
From (a): F₁(q) − Σ_{n<N}(q;q)_n = Σ_{n>N} n(q;q)_{n−1}qⁿ − N(q;q)_N for |q| < 1.

Estimate at q = ξe^{−t}, N = mK: group the factors of (q;q)_{n−1} in blocks of K consecutive indices; a full block ∏_{j=rK+1}^{rK+K}(1 − ξ^je^{−jt}) is bounded by C·min(1, (r + 1)K²t), and a partial block by 2^K; hence |(q;q)_{n−1}| ≤ C_m t^m for n > mK, uniformly, and Σ_{n>N} n|q|ⁿ = O(t^{−2}), so the tail is O(t^{m−2}).
The polynomial Σ_{n<N}(q;q)_n in q = ξe^{−t} has Taylor expansion agreeing with T_ξF modulo t^m (the omitted terms lie in t^m ℂ⟦t⟧).
Letting m grow gives the expansion to every order (HasRadialExpansion), and its constant term gives the radial limit F(ξ).
acceptance: At ξ = 1: F₁(e^{−t}) = 1 + t + (3/2)t² + O(t³), the Taylor series of F at 1.
The formal statement F = F₁ in ℤ[[1 − q]] (which is how the source phrases it) does not by itself give the analytic expansion; the uniform tail estimate is needed (see the source issues).

nodes.title: The two-variable identity Σ (x;q)_{n+1}xⁿ = Σ χ₁₂(n)x^{(n−1)/2}q^{(n²−1)/24}
nodes.statement: In ℤ[x]⟦q⟧ (power series in q whose coefficients are polynomials in x): S(x) := Σ_{n≥0}(x;q)_{n+1}xⁿ = Σ_{n≥1} χ₁₂(n) x^{(n−1)/2} q^{(n²−1)/24}, with (x;q)_{n+1} = (1 − x)(1 − qx)⋯(1 − qⁿx) and χ₁₂ = (12/·) (only n ≡ ±1 mod 6 contribute, so the exponents are integers). Moreover S(x) = (qx;q)_∞ + (1 − x)Σ_{n≥0}[(qx;q)_n − (qx;q)_∞]xⁿ in ℤ[x]⟦q⟧.
hypotheses: The identity is formal; x is a polynomial variable in each q-coefficient.
proofSteps: With S(a, x) = Σ (a;q)_n xⁿ, verify (1 − x)S(a, x) = 1 − axS(a, qx) and S(a, x) = 1 + (1 − a)xS(qa, x) coefficientwise.
Deduce S(x) = (1 − x)S(qx, x) satisfies S(x) = 1 − qx² − q²x³S(qx).

The right side R(x) = Σ χ₁₂(n)x^{(n−1)/2}q^{(n²−1)/24} satisfies the same equation: −q²x³R(qx) reindexed by m = n + 6 gives Σ_{m≥7}χ₁₂(m)x^{(m−1)/2}q^{(m²−1)/24}, using χ₁₂(n + 6) = −χ₁₂(n) and (m² − 1)/24 = (n² − 1)/24 + (n + 3)/2.

Uniqueness: the map T ↦ 1 − qx² − q²x³T(qx) raises q-order, so it has a unique fixed point in ℤ[x]⟦q⟧; hence S = R, and in particular each q-coefficient of S is a polynomial (in fact a monomial) in x.
The second expression: split (x;q)_{n+1} = (1 − x)(qx;q)_n and write Σ(qx;q)_n xⁿ(1 − x) = (qx;q)_∞ + (1 − x)Σ[(qx;q)_n − (qx;q)_∞]xⁿ; each q-coefficient involves only n < q-degree.
acceptance: At x = 1: S(1) = (q;q)_∞ = Σ χ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24}, Euler's pentagonal number theorem (PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.hasProd_one_sub_X_pow).
The first terms are 1 − qx² − q²x³ + q⁵x⁵ + q⁷x⁶ − ⋯ .

nodes.title: Zagier's identity F₁ = −½H + (½ − E)(q)_∞ (Theorem 2)
nodes.statement: In ℚ⟦q⟧, and hence as holomorphic functions on |q| < 1: F₁(q) = −½H(q) + (½ − E(q))(q;q)_∞, where H(q) = Σ_{n≥1} nχ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24} (the ‘half-derivative’ of η: q^{1/24}H(q) = η̃, see eichler-integral) and E(q) = Σ_{n≥1}qⁿ/(1 − qⁿ) = Σ d(n)qⁿ.
hypotheses: Formal identity in ℚ⟦q⟧; both sides have integer coefficients.
proofSteps: Work in ℤ[x]⟦q⟧, where d/dx at x = 1 is a well-defined derivation followed by evaluation (each q-coefficient is a polynomial in x).
From the closed form of andrews-exercise-identity: S(1) = (q;q)_∞ and (dS/dx)(1) = Σ ((n−1)/2)χ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24} = ½H − ½(q;q)_∞.
From the second expression: (dS/dx)(1) = (d/dx)(qx;q)_∞|_{x=1} − F₂ = −E(q)(q;q)_∞ − F₂, since −(d/dx) log(qx;q)_∞ at x = 1 is E(q).
Equate: F₂ = −½H + ½(q;q)_∞ − E(q)(q;q)_∞, and F₂ = F₁ (sum-of-tails-series).
acceptance: Comparing coefficients: F₁ = q + 2q² + ⋯, −½H = −½ + (5/2)q + (7/2)q² + ⋯ and (½ − E)(q;q)_∞ = ½ − (3/2)q − (3/2)q² + ⋯ .
A consequence (Zagier's Remark): Σ nχ(n)q^{n²/24}/Σ χ(n)q^{n²/24} = 1 − 2Σ qⁿ/(1 − qⁿ)·(1 + 1/((1 − q)⋯(1 − qⁿ))).

nodes.title: Euler's product vanishes to infinite order at every root of unity
nodes.statement: For every rational x, the function τ ↦ (q;q)_∞ = ∏(1 − e^{2πinτ}) has radial asymptotic expansion 0 at x; more precisely, for x = a/c in lowest terms (c ≥ 1), |(q;q)_∞| ≤ C·y^{−1/2}exp(−π/(12c²y)) for q = e^{2πi(x+iy)}, 0 < y ≤ 1. The same holds for E(q)·(q;q)_∞, since |E(q)| ≤ Σ n|q|ⁿ = O(y^{−2}).
hypotheses: x ∈ ℚ; the constant C depends on x.
proofSteps: Choose γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with γ(∞) = a/c and write τ = x + iy = γτ′; then Im τ′ = 1/(c²y).
The transformation law η(γτ′) = ψ(γ)(cτ′ + d)^{1/2}η(τ′) (QM.1/dedekind-eta-multiplier) gives |η(τ)| = |cτ′ + d|^{1/2}|η(τ′)| with |cτ′ + d| = 1/(cy).
|η(τ′)| ≤ C′e^{−2π Im τ′/24} for Im τ′ ≥ 1, and (q;q)_∞ = e^{−2πiτ/24}η(τ).
Every power y^m dominates exp(−π/(12c²y)), so the expansion is 0 to all orders; multiply by the O(y^{−2}) bound for E.
acceptance: At x = 0: |(e^{−t};e^{−t})_∞| = √(2π/t)e^{−π²/(6t)}e^{t/24}, by η(i t/2π) and the S-transformation (ModularForm.eta_comp_eq_csqrt_I_inv).

Because the expansion is 0, the mean of m ↦ χ₁₂(m)ξ^{(m²−1)/24} over a period vanishes (otherwise euler-maclaurin-asymptotic would give a term of order t^{−1/2}); this is used in kontsevich-value-formula.

sources.excerpt: From Theorem 2 it follows that F(q) also agrees with −1 2H(q) to all orders, since (q)∞ vanishes to inﬁnite order as we approach any root of unity and E(q) blows up at worst like (1−|q|)−2
sources.match: The two estimates this lemma proves.

nodes.title: Kontsevich–Zagier strange identity at every root of unity
nodes.statement: Let ξ = e^{2πix} (x ∈ ℚ) and H(q) = Σ_{n≥1} nχ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24}. The holomorphic function τ ↦ H(e^{2πiτ}) on ℍ has radial asymptotic expansion −2·T_ξF at x, where T_ξF = kontsevichTaylor ξ is the formal Taylor expansion of the Habiro element F at ξ in the variable t (q = ξe^{−t}). In particular its radial limit at ξ is −2F(ξ); equivalently, with η̃(τ) = Σ nχ₁₂(n)q^{n²/24}, the radial limit of η̃ at x is −2φ(x). This is the exact meaning of the ‘strange identity’ Σ (q;q)_n “=” −½Σ nχ₁₂(n)q^{(n²−1)/24}: a comparison between a formal evaluation (left) and the radial limits and asymptotic expansions of a q-series convergent only in the disc (right).
hypotheses: ξ an arbitrary root of unity (all orders, including even and non-prime-power orders).
proofSteps: Theorem 2 (zagier-sum-of-tails-identity) holds as an identity of holomorphic functions on the disc: −½H = F₁ − (½ − E)(q;q)_∞.
F₁ has radial expansion T_ξF at x (sum-of-tails-agreement).
(q;q)_∞ and E(q)(q;q)_∞ have radial expansion 0 at x (eta-infinite-order-vanishing).
Add the expansions (HasRadialExpansion.add); multiply by −2.
acceptance: At ξ = 1: e^{−t/24}F(e^{−t}) = Σ T_n(t/24)ⁿ/n! with the Glaisher numbers T_n = 1, 23, 1681, … (Zagier's Theorem 3; see kontsevich-value-formula).
At ξ = −1 the radial limit of H is −2F(−1) = −6.
The identity is not an identity of power series in q: F has no q-expansion, and H has no values on the unit circle; only their expansions at roots of unity are compared.

sources.excerpt: The meaning of the equality is that the function on the left agrees at roots of unity with the radial limit of the function on the right, and similarly for the derivatives of all orders.
sources.match: The statement this node makes precise.

sources.excerpt: which implies that −2ϕ(x) for x ∈Q is the limiting value of eη(z) as z approaches x from either the upper or the lower half-plane.

nodes.title: Values and Taylor coefficients of F at roots of unity as twisted L-values
nodes.statement: Let ξ = e^{2πiα} and N a positive multiple of 12 with ξ^{N/12} = 1, and let Φ_ξ(m) = χ₁₂(m)ξ^{(m²−1)/24} (a function on ZMod N, with ξ^{s} := e^{2πiαs}). Define c_n(ξ) by e^{−t/24}F(ξe^{−t}) = Σ c_n(ξ)tⁿ/(24ⁿn!) (the Taylor expansion of kontsevich-strange-series). Then c_n(ξ) = (−1)^{n−1}L(−2n − 1, Φ_ξ)/2 = (−1)ⁿN^{2n+1}/(2n + 2)·Σ_{m=1}^{N/2}Φ_ξ(m)B_{2n+2}(m/N); in particular F(ξ) = (1/(4N))Σ_{m=1}^{N} m²Φ_ξ(m), and at ξ = 1 the c_n(1) are the Glaisher numbers T_n given by Σ T_n x^{2n+1}/(2n + 1)! = sin 2x/(2 cos 3x).
hypotheses: N a positive multiple of 12 with ξ^{N/12} = 1 (so Φ_ξ is N-periodic).
proofSteps: Φ_ξ is N-periodic: ((m + N)² − m²)/24 = (N/12)(2m + N)/2 with (2m + N)/2 ∈ ℤ for odd m.

Φ_ξ has mean zero: Σ_{m≥1}Φ_ξ(m)e^{−m²t/24} = e^{−t/24}(q;q)_∞ at q = ξe^{−t}, which tends to 0 (eta-infinite-order-vanishing), while a non-zero mean would contribute a term of order t^{−1/2} by euler-maclaurin-asymptotic.
By periodic-gaussian-sum-asymptotic (ν = 1) applied to Φ_ξ at t/24: e^{−t/24}H(ξe^{−t}) ∼ Σ L(−2n − 1, Φ_ξ)(−t/24)ⁿ/n!.
By strange-identity this equals −2e^{−t/24}F(ξe^{−t}) = −2Σ c_n(ξ)tⁿ/(24ⁿn!); compare coefficients.
Evaluate L(−2n − 1, Φ_ξ) by periodic-l-value-bernoulli and fold the sum using Φ_ξ(N − m) = Φ_ξ(m) and B_{2n+2}(1 − x) = B_{2n+2}(x).
For n = 0 expand B₂(x) = x² − x + 1/6 and use Σ Φ_ξ = 0 and Σ mΦ_ξ(m) = 0 (from the symmetry m ↔ N − m).
At ξ = 1 (N = 12): Σ_m χ₁₂(m)e^{−mt} = sinh 2t/cosh 3t (partial fractions over one period), whose coefficients give the stated generating function by periodic-exponential-sum-asymptotic.
acceptance: F(−1) = 3 and F(i) = 8 − 3i from the formula with N = 24 and N = 48 respectively (agreeing with kontsevich-strange-series).

nodes.title: Kontsevich's function is a quantum modular form of weight 3/2
nodes.statement: The function φ(x) = e^{πix/12}F(e^{2πix}) on ℚ satisfies φ(x + 1) = e^{2πi/24}φ(x) and φ(x) + (ix)^{−3/2}φ(−1/x) = g(x) (x ∈ ℚ, x ≠ 0), where (ix)^{−3/2} is the principal branch and g : ℝ → ℂ is C^∞, real-analytic on ℝ ∖ {0}, with g^{(n)}(0) = (−πi/12)ⁿc_n (c_n the Glaisher numbers). Equivalently, φ is a quantum modular form of weight 3/2 on SL₂(ℤ) (quantum-modular-form, lower boundary branch) with multiplier ε determined by ε(T) = e^{−2πi/24} and ε(S) = e^{2πi/8}, the inverse of the η-multiplier; for general γ the period function is real-analytic except at γ⁻¹∞.
hypotheses: The multiplier ε on the generators T = (1 1; 0 1), S = (0 −1; 1 0); the general γ follows by quantum-modular-cocycle, ε being the multiplier system of weight 3/2 conjugate-inverse to that of η (QM.1/dedekind-eta-multiplier).
proofSteps: φ(x) = −½·(radial limit of η̃ at x) by strange-identity, η̃ = √24·(Eichler integral of weight 1/2 of η) (eichler-integral).

Transformation of the non-holomorphic Eichler integral η* on H⁻ under S and T: the computation of nonholomorphic-eichler-transformation with the η-multiplier ψ (QM.1/dedekind-eta-multiplier) in place of Shimura's, giving η* − ε(γ)·(η*|γ) = r_{η,−d/c} (eichler-period-integral for η).

Agreement of expansions of η̃ and η* at every rational (eichler-asymptotic-agreement, whose L-function inputs are here the periodic L-functions L(2s − 1, Φ_ξ) of ZMod.LFunction, entire with the required vertical growth, in place of twisted-cusp-form-l-function).
Pass to boundary values as in half-integral-eichler-quantum-modular, using nonholomorphic-eichler-nontangential-limit.
Smoothness of g at 0 and its derivatives: the expansion of φ(±1/k) (Zagier's (36)) against strange-identity at x = 0.
acceptance: The factor (ix)^{−3/2} equals e^{−3πi/4}x^{−3/2} for x > 0 and e^{3πi/4}|x|^{−3/2} for x < 0; relative to the lower boundary factor of quantum-modular-form this is the constant −ε(S) = −e^{2πi/8}, which is why the lower branch is pinned.
Consistency check with Kontsevich's asymptotics: φ(1/k) = e^{2πi(3−k)/24}k^{3/2} + Σ c_n(−πi/(12k))ⁿ/n! + o(1) as k → ∞.
Zagier's 2010 account (Quantum modular forms, eq. (26)) prints this law with |x|^{3/2} and ∓i^{1/2}; the correct form is the one here (see the source issues).

nodes.title: Cohen's terminating evaluations of σ and σ* at roots of unity
nodes.statement: For a root of unity ξ define σ(ξ) = 1 + Σ_{n≥0}(−1)ⁿξ^{n+1}(ξ;ξ)_n and σ*(ξ) = −2Σ_{n≥0}ξ^{n+1}(ξ²;ξ²)_n (Andrews' and Cohen's expressions (8) evaluated at q = ξ). Both sums terminate: (ξ;ξ)_n = 0 for n ≥ ord ξ and (ξ²;ξ²)_n = 0 for n ≥ ord(ξ²). These are formal evaluations of Ramanujan's σ(q) = Σ q^{n(n+1)/2}/((1+q)⋯(1+qⁿ)) and its partner σ*(q) = 2Σ(−1)ⁿq^{n²}/((1−q)⋯(1−q^{2n−1})); the latter converge only for |q| < 1, and the agreement of their q-expansions with (8) (Andrews' identity) is not part of this definition.
hypotheses: ξ a root of unity; the finite sums are taken up to any bound past the terminating index.
proofSteps: Define cohenSigma ξ := 1 + Σ_{n<N}(−1)ⁿξ^{n+1}(ξ;ξ)_n and cohenSigmaStar ξ := −2Σ_{n<N}ξ^{n+1}(ξ²;ξ²)_n with N = orderOf ξ.
Independence of the cut-off: the terms with n ≥ N vanish because they contain the factor 1 − ξ^N (resp. 1 − ξ^{2j} with ord(ξ) | 2j ≤ 2n).
acceptance: σ(1) = 2, σ(−1) = −2, σ(ω) = 2ω + 6 for ω² + ω + 1 = 0, σ(±i) = ∓2i − 4 (Zagier's table).

nodes.title: Cohen's telescoping identity (9)
hypotheses: k ≥ 0; the identity is in the Laurent polynomial ring.
proofSteps: The recursion S_{k+1} − S_k = q^{k+1}(S_{k+1} − (1 + q)⋯(1 + q^k)) − q^{−k(k+1)/2}, by comparing the two sums term by term.
Induction on k: the case k = 0 is 0 = 0; the step multiplies the recursion by (1 − q)⋯(1 − q^k) and uses (1 − q^{j})(1 + q^{j}) = 1 − q^{2j}.

nodes.title: Cohen's duality σ(q) = −σ*(q⁻¹) at roots of unity
nodes.statement: For every root of unity ξ, cohenSigma ξ = −cohenSigmaStar ξ⁻¹.
hypotheses: ξ a root of unity.
proofSteps: Evaluate cohen-telescoping-identity at q = ξ with k ≥ ord ξ: the right side vanishes because (1 − ξ)⋯(1 − ξ^k) contains the factor 1 − ξ^{ord ξ} = 0.

The first sum on the left equals ½σ(ξ⁻¹): with P_n = (ξ^{−1} − 1)⋯(ξ^{−n} − 1) one has ξ^{−n−1}P_n = P_{n+1} + P_n, so ½ + ½Σ_{n<k}ξ^{−n−1}P_n = Σ_{n<k}P_n + ½P_k and P_k = 0; and σ(ξ⁻¹) = 1 + Σ ξ^{−n−1}P_n since (−1)ⁿ(1 − ξ^{−1})⋯(1 − ξ^{−n}) = P_n.
The second sum is −½σ*(ξ) by definition.
Hence σ(ξ⁻¹) + σ*(ξ) = 0; replace ξ by ξ⁻¹.
acceptance: The statement is about formal evaluations only; the quantum modularity of x ↦ e^{2πix/24}σ(e^{2πix}) (Zagier's Proposition) needs Cohen's Maass form and is not decomposed here.

nodes.title: The periodic functions χ₊ and χ₋ of period 60
nodes.statement: χ₊, χ₋ : ℤ → {−1, 0, 1} are the functions of period 60 given by χ₊(n) = (−1)^{⌊n/30⌋} if n² ≡ 1 (mod 120) and 0 otherwise, and χ₋(n) = (−1)^{⌊n/30⌋} if n² ≡ 49 (mod 120) and 0 otherwise (n taken in [0, 60)). They are the real and imaginary parts of the primitive character χ = (12/·)ε of conductor 60, where ε is the character of conductor 5 with ε(1, 2, 3, 4) = (1, −i, i, −1). As functions on ZMod 60, χ₊ takes the value 1 at 1, 11, 19, 29 and −1 at 31, 41, 49, 59.
hypotheses: n is reduced to [0, 60) before ⌊n/30⌋ is taken; equivalently χ₊ is odd and 60-periodic.
proofSteps: Define lzChiPlus, lzChiMinus : ZMod 60 → ℤ by the table, and prove the congruence descriptions by deciding the finitely many cases.
The identification with Re and Im of (12/·)ε is a finite check over ZMod 60.
Oddness χ±(−n) = −χ±(n) and mean zero Σ_{n mod 60} χ±(n) = 0 are finite checks.
acceptance: Zagier's equivalent description: χ₊(n) = (−1)^{⌊n/30⌋} if (n, 6) = 1 and n ≡ ±1 (mod 5), 0 otherwise.

nodes.title: WRT invariants of the Poincaré sphere as radial limits (Lawrence–Zagier Theorem 1)
nodes.statement: Let W(ξ) = ξ(ξ − 1)Z(ξ), where Z(ξ) is the sl₂ Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant of the Poincaré homology sphere Σ(2, 3, 5) at the root of unity ξ (ArithmeticQuantumTopology:QT.4/WRT-invariant-at-a-root, normalised by Z(S³) = 1; W(1) = 0). Then for every root of unity ξ the radial limit of 1 − ½A(q) as q → ξ exists and equals W(ξ). Explicitly W(ξ) = 1 − ½Σ_{n=1}^{30K}χ₊(n)(1 − n/(30K))ξ^{(n²−1)/120} for ξ of order K.
hypotheses: ξ an arbitrary root of unity (all orders); W is extended from ξ = e^{2πi/K} to all primitive K-th roots by Galois equivariance, which agrees with QT.4's invariant at those roots (QT.4/integrality-and-galois).
The orientation of Σ(2, 3, 5) and the normalisation of Z are those of the Lawrence–Rozansky formula requested from ArithmeticQuantumTopology:QT.4.
proofSteps: Radial limit: apply renormalised-sum to Φ(n) = χ₊(n)ξ^{(n²−1)/120}, periodic of period 60K with Φ(60K − n) = −Φ(n), hence of mean zero; A(ξe^{−t}) = e^{t/120}Σ Φ(n)e^{−n²t/120} → L(0, Φ) = −Σ_{n=1}^{60K}(n/(60K) − ½)Φ(n) = Σ_{n=1}^{30K}(1 − n/(30K))Φ(n).
Gauss-sum step (LZ (14)): with ζ a primitive 120K-th root of unity with ζ^{120} = ξ and G = Σ_{β mod 60K}ζ^{−β²}, ξ^{(n²−1)/120} = G^{−1}Σ_β ζ^{−β²−1}ζ^{2nβ}.

Insert into the renormalised exponential sum (renormalised-sum, first form) and sum the geometric series with the rational functions ψ(u) = Σχ₊(n)uⁿ = (u⁵ + u⁻⁵)(u⁹ + u⁻⁹)/(u¹⁵ + u⁻¹⁵) and φ(u) = u + u⁻¹ − ψ(u).

The terms with K ∤ β give the Lawrence–Rozansky formula W(ξ) = (2G)^{−1}Σ_{β mod 60K, K∤β}(1 − ζ^{24β})(1 − ζ^{40β})/(1 + ζ^{60β})·ζ^{−(β+1)²} (requested from QT.4); the terms with K | β cancel in pairs under m ↦ 30 − m (β = Km).
acceptance: ξ = −1 (K = 2): W(−1) = 2; ξ = e^{2πi/3}: W = −2ξ − 1; ξ = i: W = ξ + 1 (Lawrence–Zagier's table).
ξ = 1: W(1) = 0, consistent with 1 − ½A(q) → 1 − ½·2 = 0 as q ↗ 1 (the renormalised sum of χ₊ is Σ_{n≤30}(1 − n/30)χ₊(n) = 2).
The theorem compares an analytic limit of a q-series with a quantum invariant; it is not a statement about formal evaluation.

nodes.title: The expansion of 1 − ½A(q) at q = 1 is the Ohtsuki series (Lawrence–Zagier Theorem 2)
nodes.statement: The function τ ↦ 1 − ½A(e^{2πiτ}) has radial asymptotic expansion at x = 0 equal to W_∞(e^{−t} − 1), where W_∞(h) = h(1 + h)Z_∞(h) ∈ ℤ⟦h⟧ and Z_∞ is the Ohtsuki series of Σ(2, 3, 5) (ArithmeticQuantumTopology:QT.4/ohtsuki-series); explicitly e^{−t/120}(2 − A(e^{−t})) ∼ Σ_r c_r(−30t)^r/r! with c_r = (2/60^{2r})·(1/(2r+1))Σ_{n=1}^{60}χ₊(n)B_{2r+1}(n/60), and 1 − W_∞(e^{−t} − 1) = e^{t/120}Σ_r (a_r/r!)(t/120)^r with Σ a_r x^{2r}/(2r)! = cos 5x cos 9x/cos 15x.
hypotheses: The Ohtsuki series in Lawrence–Zagier's normalisation W_∞ = h(1 + h)Z_∞ (requested from ArithmeticQuantumTopology:QT.4 together with Lawrence's closed form (6)).
proofSteps: periodic-gaussian-sum-asymptotic with Φ = χ₊ (ν = 0) at t/120: e^{−t/120}A(e^{−t}) ∼ Σ_r L(−2r, χ₊)(−t/120)^r/r!.
periodic-l-value-bernoulli: L(−2r, χ₊) = −(60^{2r}/(2r + 1))Σ_{n=1}^{60}χ₊(n)B_{2r+1}(n/60).
Rewrite with the modified Euler numbers B̄ (e^{zB̄} = sech(z/4), B̄_m = 2[B_{m+1}(3/4) − B_{m+1}(1/4)]/(m + 1)) and the symmetries of Bernoulli polynomials: c_r = (B̄ − 4/15)^{2r} − (B̄ − 1/15)^{2r}.
Compare with Lawrence's formula 2(1 + h)^{1/120}W_∞(h) = (1 + h)^{30(B̄−4/15)²} − (1 + h)^{30(B̄−1/15)²} (requested from QT.4).

nodes.title: Habiro evaluations of the unified invariant of Σ(2,3,5) are radial limits
nodes.statement: Let J ∈ ℤ[q]^ be the unified WRT invariant of the Poincaré homology sphere Σ(2, 3, 5) (ArithmeticQuantumTopology:QT.3/definition-of-JM) and U := q(q − 1)J ∈ ℤ[q]^. Then (a) for every root of unity ξ, the Habiro evaluation ev_ξ(U) (HC.3) equals the radial limit at ξ of 1 − ½A(q); (b) the Taylor map of U at q = 1 (HC.3), written in t with q = e^{−t}, equals the radial asymptotic expansion of 1 − ½A(e^{2πiτ}) at x = 0; and (c) U is the unique element of the Habiro ring with property (a) (HC.4 evaluation rigidity). Thus a formal Habiro evaluation and an analytic radial limit of an Eichler integral are identified by an explicit comparison theorem, root by root.
hypotheses: Σ(2, 3, 5) is an integral homology sphere, so J exists (QT.3).
The normalisations of QT.4 (WRT invariant with Z(S³) = 1, Ohtsuki series) are those of Lawrence–Zagier, as requested from QT.4.
proofSteps: (a) ev_ξ(J) = Z(ξ) for every root of unity ξ (QT.4/evaluation-theorem); ev_ξ is a ring homomorphism, so ev_ξ(U) = ξ(ξ − 1)Z(ξ) = W(ξ); apply lawrence-zagier-radial-limit.

(b) The Taylor map of J at 1 is the Ohtsuki series Z_∞ (QT.4/ohtsuki-series); the Taylor map is a ring homomorphism, so that of U is q(q − 1)Z_∞(q − 1) = W_∞(q − 1); apply lawrence-zagier-ohtsuki-expansion.
(c) Two Habiro elements with the same evaluations at all roots of unity are equal (HabiroCyclotomicCompletions:HC.4; QT.4/determination-by-WRT for the unified invariant itself).
acceptance: At ξ = −1: ev_{−1}(U) = W(−1) = 2, and 1 − ½A(q) → 2 as q → −1 radially.
(c) fails if the evaluations are known only at a set of roots of unity without the source's adjacency condition (HC.4), so the full family of radial limits is used.

nodes.title: The SL₂(ℤ)-transformation of the theta pair Θ± (Lawrence–Zagier (15))
nodes.statement: With Θ±(τ) = Σ_{n≥1}nχ±(n)q^{n²/120} and ζ = e^{πi/60}: Θ₊(τ + 1) = ζΘ₊(τ), Θ₋(τ + 1) = ζ^{49}Θ₋(τ), and (Θ₊(−1/τ), Θ₋(−1/τ)) = (τ/i)^{3/2}·M_S·(Θ₊(τ), Θ₋(τ)) with M_S = (a b; b −a), a = √(½(1 − 1/√5)), b = √(½(1 + 1/√5)), (τ/i)^{3/2} the principal branch. Consequently for every γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ) there is M_γ ∈ GL₂(ℂ), γ ↦ M_γ a projective representation with finite image, such that ((cτ + d)/i)^{−3/2}(Θ₊, Θ₋)(γτ) = M_γ(Θ₊, Θ₋)(τ) for c > 0.
hypotheses: Principal branches as stated; c > 0 in the general law (the source's normalisation).
proofSteps: T: τ ↦ τ + 1 multiplies q^{n²/120} by e^{2πin²/120}; n² ≡ 1 (mod 120) when χ₊(n) ≠ 0 and n² ≡ 49 when χ₋(n) ≠ 0, giving the factors ζ and ζ^{49}.

S: Θ_χ = ½Σ_{n∈ℤ} nχ(n)q^{n²/120} is a finite combination of the derivatives in z of jacobiTheta₂ at rational z (splitting n by residue mod 60); apply jacobiTheta₂'_functional_equation and evaluate the resulting finite Fourier sums as the Gauss sums G_χ = Σ_{n mod 60}χ(n)e^{πin/30} = −√(30 + 6√5) + i√(30 − 6√5), G_χ̄ = −Ḡ_χ.
Change basis Θ₊ = ½(Θ_χ + Θ_χ̄), Θ₋ = (1/2i)(Θ_χ − Θ_χ̄).
General γ: the matrices for S and T generate; finiteness of the image because the space is the image of a Weil representation factoring through SL₂(ℤ/120ℤ).
acceptance: M_S² = I (a² + b² = 1), consistent with S² = −1 acting trivially in weight 3/2 up to the branch.
Only the pair (Θ₊, Θ₋) is invariant: Θ₊ alone is not a modular form on SL₂(ℤ).

nodes.title: The WRT function of the Poincaré sphere is quantum modular (Lawrence–Zagier §4)
nodes.statement: Let f±(x) be the radial limits of Θ̃± at x ∈ ℚ (so f₊(x) = 2e^{πix/60}(1 − W(e^{2πix})) by lawrence-zagier-radial-limit). For γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with c > 0 and M_γ as in lawrence-zagier-theta-transformation, the vector function f = (f₊, f₋) satisfies j(γ, x)·f(γx) + M_γ f(x) = M_γ r_{−d/c}(x) for x ∈ ℚ ∖ {−d/c}, where j(γ, x) is the lower boundary value of ((cz + d)/(−i))^{−1/2} and r_α = (r⁺_α, r⁻_α) with r±_α(x) = √(2i/15)∫_α^{i∞}Θ±(τ)(τ − x)^{−1/2}dτ, real-analytic on ℝ ∖ {α}. In particular f₊ is a quantum modular form of weight 1/2 (quantum-modular-form) on the finite-index subgroup Γ_ρ = {γ : M_γ is scalar}.
hypotheses: c > 0 (the case c < 0 follows from −γ); the lower boundary branch of quantum-modular-form.
proofSteps: Θ̃± and Θ*± (the non-holomorphic Eichler integrals (17), nonholomorphic-eichler-integral for k = 3/2) have agreeing expansions at every rational (Lawrence–Zagier property (i); the proof is eichler-asymptotic-agreement with the periodic L-functions L(2s, χ±ξ^{n²/120}) of ZMod.LFunction in place of twisted-cusp-form-l-function).

Θ*± are nearly modular of weight 1/2 in H⁻ with discrepancy M_γ r_{−d/c} (property (ii)): the substitution of nonholomorphic-eichler-transformation, with the transformation matrices of lawrence-zagier-theta-transformation in place of Shimura's multiplier.
Pass to boundary values at x from below, using nonholomorphic-eichler-nontangential-limit for the term at γx.
Real-analyticity of r_α on ℝ ∖ {α}: eichler-period-integral.

For γ ∈ Γ_ρ with c > 0, M_γ = m_γ·I and the law reads f₊(x) − (−m_γ^{−1})j(γ, x)f₊(γx) = r⁺_{−d/c}(x); since j(γ, x) = e^{−iπ/4}·boundaryFactor(1/2, γ, x) for c > 0, this is the scalar law of quantum-modular-form with ε(γ) = −e^{−iπ/4}m_γ^{−1}.
acceptance: The asymptotic formula W(e^{2πi/K}) ∼ √(K/i)e^{−πi/60K}(ae^{−πiK/60} + be^{−49πiK/60}) + W_∞(e^{2πi/K} − 1) as K → ∞ is the case γ = S at x = 0 (Lawrence–Zagier (18)).
The three terms of that formula match the three flat connections of Σ(2, 3, 5).

nodes.title: The Andrews–Garvan crank of a partition
nodes.statement: For a partition λ of n (Mathlib's Nat.Partition n), let ℓ(λ) be its largest part (0 for the empty partition), ω(λ) the number of parts equal to 1, and μ(λ) the number of parts larger than ω(λ) (counted with multiplicity). The crank is c(λ) = ℓ(λ) if ω(λ) = 0 and c(λ) = μ(λ) − ω(λ) if ω(λ) > 0; it is an integer with |c(λ)| ≤ n.
hypotheses: λ ranges over Nat.Partition n; the empty partition of 0 has crank 0.
proofSteps: Define largestPart λ := λ.parts.sup (0 if empty), numOnes λ := λ.parts.count 1, numPartsAbove λ := (λ.parts.filter (· > numOnes λ)).card.
Define partitionCrank λ := if numOnes λ = 0 then (largestPart λ : ℤ) else numPartsAbove λ − numOnes λ.
The bound |c(λ)| ≤ n: ℓ(λ) ≤ n, and μ, ω ≤ number of parts ≤ n.
acceptance: The crank of (1) is −1 and of the empty partition 0; the generating function of crank-generating-function therefore needs the convention of crank-count at n = 1.

nodes.title: The crank counts M(m, n) and M(k, t, n)
nodes.statement: For m ∈ ℤ and n ∈ ℕ, M(m, n) is the number of partitions of n with crank m when n ≠ 1, and at n = 1 the convention M(0, 1) = −1, M(±1, 1) = 1, M(m, 1) = 0 otherwise (the vector-partition count N_V(m, 1) of Garvan, which makes the generating function exact). For t ≥ 1 and k ∈ ZMod t, M(k, t, n) = Σ_{m ≡ k (mod t)} M(m, n) (a finite sum since M(m, n) = 0 for |m| > n).
hypotheses: n = 1 is the only exceptional value; for n > 1, M(m, n) is a genuine count (Andrews–Garvan Theorem 1).
proofSteps: Define crankCount m n := if n = 1 then (if m = 1 ∨ m = −1 then 1 else if m = 0 then −1 else 0) else #{λ : Nat.Partition n | partitionCrank λ = m}.
Define crankCountMod t k n := Σ_{m ∈ [−n, n], (m : ZMod t) = k} crankCount m n.
Σ_m M(m, n) = p(n): for n ≠ 1 every partition has exactly one crank; for n = 1, −1 + 1 + 1 = 1 = p(1).
acceptance: M(k, 11, 6) = 1 for every k ∈ ZMod 11, and M(k, 5, 4) = 1 for every k ∈ ZMod 5.
The literal count at n = 1 is 1 at m = −1 only; the convention differs from it, and only the convention gives the product formula.

nodes.title: The crank generating function (Andrews–Garvan)
nodes.statement: In the ring of formal power series in q with coefficients Laurent polynomials in z (LaurentPolynomial ℤ ⟦q⟧, pi topology): Σ_{n≥0} (Σ_m M(m, n)z^m) qⁿ = ∏_{n≥1} (1 − qⁿ)/((1 − zqⁿ)(1 − z⁻¹qⁿ)), each factor being invertible (constant coefficient 1).
hypotheses: Formal identity; the infinite product converges q-adically.
proofSteps: Rewrite the product as (1 − q)/(zq;q)_∞ · (q²;q)_∞/(q/z;q)_∞.

Cauchy's q-binomial theorem Σ_j (a;q)_j t^j/(q;q)_j = (at;q)_∞/(t;q)_∞ (formal, from QM.0) with a = zq, t = q/z gives (q²;q)_∞/(q/z;q)_∞ = Σ_j (zq;q)_j (q/z)^j/(q;q)_j, hence the product is (1 − q)/(zq;q)_∞ + Σ_{j≥1} q^j z^{−j}/((q²;q)_{j−1}(zq^{j+1};q)_∞).

For j ≥ 1 the j-th term generates the partitions with exactly j ones, the exponent of z being μ(λ) − ω(λ) = c(λ): the ones give q^j z^{−j}, 1/(q²;q)_{j−1} the parts 2, …, j, and 1/(zq^{j+1};q)_∞ the parts > j, each counted by z.

The j = 0 term (1 − q)/(zq;q)_∞ generates, for n ≥ 2, the partitions without ones weighted by z^{ℓ(λ)} (conjugation: 1/(zq;q)_∞ counts all partitions by largest part, q/(zq;q)_∞ those with a 1, except at n = 1 where adding a 1 changes the largest part).
At n = 1 the coefficient is (z − 1) + z⁻¹, which is the convention of crank-count.

The coefficient of q⁶ is Σ_{λ⊢6} z^{c(λ)} = z⁶ + z⁴ + z³ + z² + z + 1 + z⁻¹ + z⁻² + z⁻³ + z⁻⁴ + z⁻⁶.

nodes.title: Equidistribution from a vanishing sum over a prime-order root of unity
nodes.statement: Let t be a prime, ζ ∈ ℂ a primitive t-th root of unity and c : ZMod t → ℚ. If Σ_{k ∈ ZMod t} c(k)ζ^k = 0 then c is constant; hence if Σ_k c(k) = P then c(k) = P/t for every k.

proofSteps: The minimal polynomial of ζ over ℚ is the cyclotomic polynomial Φ_t (Polynomial.cyclotomic_eq_minpoly_rat), which for t prime is 1 + X + ⋯ + X^{t−1} (Polynomial.cyclotomic_prime).
P(X) = Σ_{k=0}^{t−1} c(k)X^k has degree ≤ t − 1 and P(ζ) = 0, so Φ_t ∣ P and P = c·Φ_t for a constant c.

nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 0 and k ∈ ZMod 5, M(k, 5, 5n + 4) = p(5n + 4)/5.
proofSteps: Substitute z = ζ = e^{2πi/5} in crank-generating-function: Σ_k M(k, 5, N)ζ^k is the coefficient of q^N in C(ζ; q) = (q;q)_∞/((ζq;q)_∞(ζ⁻¹q;q)_∞).

Jacobi's triple product (QM.0/jacobi-triple-product) gives (ζ²;q)_∞(ζ⁻²q;q)_∞(q;q)_∞ = Σ_m (−1)^m ζ^{2m}q^{m(m−1)/2}, and Euler's pentagonal theorem (PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.hasProd_one_sub_X_pow) gives (q;q)_∞ = Σ_n (−1)ⁿq^{n(3n−1)/2}.
Mod 5, m(m−1)/2 takes the values 0, 0, 1, 3, 1 and n(3n−1)/2 the values 0, 1, 0, 2, 2 (m, n ≡ 0, …, 4); the sum is ≡ 4 only for m ≡ 3, n ≡ 1, where ζ^{2m} = ζ is constant.
The involution m ↦ 1 − m preserves m ≡ 3 (mod 5) and m(m − 1)/2 and changes (−1)^m, so the q^{5N+4}-part of the product vanishes; dividing by the q⁵-series (q⁵;q⁵)_∞ preserves this.
