nodes.title: Dyson's rank and the rank counts N(m, n)
nodes.statement: The rank of a partition λ is ℓ(λ) − #parts(λ) (largest part minus number of parts; 0 for the empty partition). N(m, n) is the number of partitions of n with rank m (so N(0, 0) = 1, the convention of Folsom–Ono–Rhoades (1.4); Atkin–Swinnerton-Dyer and Garvan set N(0, 0) = 0), and N(k, t, n) = Σ_{m ≡ k (mod t)} N(m, n).
hypotheses: The two conventions for N(0, 0) differ only in the constant term of the generating function.
proofSteps: Define dysonRank λ := (largestPart λ : ℤ) − card λ.parts, dysonRankCount m n := #{λ ⊢ n | dysonRank λ = m}, dysonRankCountMod t k n := Σ_{m ≡ k} dysonRankCount m n.
Conjugation (Tau Ceti's TauCeti.conjugate, an involution by TauCeti.conjugate_conjugate) exchanges largest part and number of parts, so rank(λ′) = −rank(λ) and N(−m, n) = N(m, n).
acceptance: The rank of 4 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 is 4 − 7 = −3 (Garvan's example).

The ranks of the five partitions of 4 are 3, 1, 0, −1, −3, one in each class mod 5; the ranks of the partitions of 6 are 5, 3, 2, 1, 1, 0, −1, −1, −2, −3, −5, not equidistributed mod 11 (Dyson's observation that led to the crank).

nodes.title: The rank generating function R(z; q) (Durfee square)
nodes.statement: In LaurentPolynomial ℤ ⟦q⟧: Σ_{n≥0}Σ_m N(m, n)z^m qⁿ = 1 + Σ_{n≥1} q^{n²}/((zq;q)_n(z⁻¹q;q)_n) =: R(z; q). In particular R(−1; q) = Σ_{n≥0} q^{n²}/(−q;q)_n² is Ramanujan's third-order mock theta function f(q), whose coefficient of qⁿ is N(0, 2, n) − N(1, 2, n).
hypotheses: Formal identity; the series converges q-adically since the n-th term has order n².
proofSteps: Decompose a non-empty partition by its Durfee square, the largest n × n square in its Young diagram: the square contributes q^{n²}.
The part to the right of the square is a partition with at most n parts; by conjugation its generating function with z marking its largest part is 1/(zq;q)_n.
The part below the square is a partition with parts ≤ n; with z⁻¹ marking its number of parts its generating function is 1/(z⁻¹q;q)_n.
The rank is (n + largest part of the right piece) − (n + number of parts of the lower piece), matching the exponent of z; the empty partition gives the constant 1.
acceptance: At z = 1: 1 + Σ q^{n²}/(q;q)_n² = 1/(q;q)_∞ (the Durfee-square identity).
R(−1; q) = 1 + q − 2q² + 3q³ − 3q⁴ + 3q⁵ − 5q⁶ + ⋯ (the coefficients of f(q)).

nodes.title: Uniform bounds for q-Pochhammer symbols near roots of unity
nodes.statement: Let ξ = e^{2πih/k} with gcd(h, k) = 1 and let w ∈ ℂ with w^k = 1 and w ∈ ⟨ξ⟩. For q = ξe^{−t} (0 < t ≤ 1): (i) |(wq;q)_n| ≤ C_k for all n; (ii) for every m ≥ 1 there is C_{k,m} with |(wq;q)_n| ≤ C_{k,m}t^m for all n ≥ (m + 1)k. The constants do not depend on n or t.
hypotheses: w a root of unity lying in the cyclic group generated by ξ (for w = 1 this covers (q;q)_n itself).
proofSteps: Group the factors 1 − wq^j into blocks of k consecutive indices j = rk + 1, …, rk + k; with x_r = e^{−rkt} a block equals ∏_{i=1}^{k}(1 − wξ^i x_r e^{−it}).
Unperturbed, ∏_{i=1}^{k}(1 − wξ^i x) = 1 − w^kx^k = 1 − x^k because {wξ^i} is the full group of k-th roots of unity; the perturbation e^{−it} changes the block by at most C′_k x_r t.
Hence |block_r| ≤ min(1, (r + 1)k²t) + C′_k x_r t; the product over r ≥ m of (1 + C′_k x_r t) is at most exp(C′_k t Σ_r e^{−rkt}) ≤ exp(2C′_k/k), bounded.
The first m blocks give O(t^m); the last incomplete block is bounded by 2^k. Combine.
acceptance: For w = 1 and ξ = 1: |(e^{−t};e^{−t})_n| ≤ n!tⁿ from 1 − e^{−jt} ≤ jt.
Termwise bounds by ∏(1 + |q|^j) are useless here (they grow like e^{c/t}); the block cancellation is essential.

nodes.title: The unimodal-sequence series U(w; q) and its values at roots of unity
nodes.statement: U(w; q) = Σ_{n≥0}(wq;q)_n(w⁻¹q;q)_n q^{n+1} ∈ LaurentPolynomial ℤ ⟦q⟧, the generating function Σ u(m, n)(−w)^m qⁿ of strongly unimodal sequences of size n and rank m. For a root of unity w = ζ_b^a and ζ = ζ_k^h with b | k, gcd(a, b) = gcd(h, k) = 1, the formal value U(w; ζ) = Σ_{n=0}^{k−1}(wζ;ζ)_n(w⁻¹ζ;ζ)_nζ^{n+1} is a finite sum (the terms with n ≥ k vanish, since some factor 1 − wζ^j is 0). This formal value is distinct from the radial limit of U(w; q) as q → ζ; they are equal by pochhammer-root-of-unity-bound, which is a theorem and not part of the definition.
hypotheses: b | k for the formal value; for b ∤ k the series does not terminate (e.g. U(−1; e^{2πi/3}), where no factor 1 + ζ^j vanishes).
proofSteps: Define unimodalSeries w as Σ_n (wq;q)_n(w⁻¹q;q)_n q^{n+1}, convergent q-adically (the n-th term has order n + 1).
Define unimodalValue a b h k := Σ_{n<k}(ζ_b^aζ_k^h;ζ_k^h)_n(ζ_b^{−a}ζ_k^h;ζ_k^h)_nζ_k^{h(n+1)}.
Termination: since b | k, ζ_b^a = ζ_k^{ha′} for some a′, so 1 − ζ_b^{−a}ζ_k^{hj} = 0 for j ≡ a′ (mod k), which occurs among j ≤ k.
Relation: Σ_{n≥1}qⁿ(w;q)_n(w⁻¹;q)_n = (1 − w)(1 − w⁻¹)U(w; q), from (w;q)_{n} = (1 − w)(wq;q)_{n−1}.

U(−1; −1) = −1 and U(−1; i) = −i, so −4U(−1; ζ) = 4 and 4i: the constants in Ramanujan's claim (ramanujan-radial-limit-claim).

nodes.title: Choi's identity relating the rank function to an Appell–Lerch sum
nodes.statement: For q = e^{2πiz} (z ∈ ℍ) and α = e^{2πiu}, β = e^{2πiv} with u, v ∉ ℤz + ℤ: Σ_{n≥0}(αβ)ⁿq^{n²}/((αq;q)_n(βq;q)_n) + Σ_{n≥1}qⁿ(α⁻¹;q)_n(β⁻¹;q)_n = iq^{1/8}(1 − α)(βα⁻¹)^{1/2}(qα⁻¹;q)_∞(β⁻¹;q)_∞µ(u, v; z), with µ Zwegers' Appell–Lerch sum (QM.4/appell-lerch-sum). With α = ζ_b^{−a}, β = ζ_b^a it reads R(ζ_b^a; q) + (1 − ζ_b^a)(1 − ζ_b^{−a})U(ζ_b^a; q) = m(a, b; z)µ(−a/b, a/b; z).

proofSteps: The identity is quoted by Folsom–Ono–Rhoades from Choi and from Ramanujan's lost notebook (Entry 3.4.7 in Andrews–Berndt); its proof is not in a read source.

nodes.title: Positive definite forms of discriminant −d, their CM points and weights
nodes.statement: For an integer d > 0 with d ≡ 0 or 3 (mod 4), Q_d is the set of positive definite integral binary quadratic forms Q = [a, b, c] = aX² + bXY + cY² (a > 0) with b² − 4ac = −d, primitive or not, with the action of Γ = PSL₂(ℤ) by (Q∘γ)(X, Y) = Q(aX + bY, cX + dY). Its CM point is the unique root α_Q = (−b + i√d)/(2a) ∈ ℍ of Q(X, 1), and w_Q = |Γ_Q| is the order of its stabiliser in PSL₂(ℤ): w_Q = 2 if Q ∼ [a, 0, a], 3 if Q ∼ [a, a, a], 1 otherwise. Q_d/Γ is finite (every class contains a unique reduced form |b| ≤ a ≤ c, with b ≥ 0 if |b| = a or a = c), and the weighted count Σ_{Q∈Q_d/Γ}1/w_Q is the Hurwitz–Kronecker class number H(d).
hypotheses: d > 0, d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4); for d ≡ 1, 2 (mod 4), Q_d is empty.
The class number H(d) of Tau Ceti's ModularForms layer 11 (reduced forms, weights 1/2 and 1/3) is the same weighted count.
proofSteps: Define heegnerForms d as {Q : Fin 3 → ℤ | Q 0 > 0 ∧ Q 1² − 4·Q 0·Q 2 = −d} with the right action of SL₂(ℤ) through its image in PSL₂(ℤ).
cmPoint Q := (−b + i√d)/(2a) ∈ ℍ; it satisfies α_{Q∘γ} = γ⁻¹α_Q (Möbius action), so it depends only on the orbit up to the action.
Finiteness: reduction theory (a ≤ √(d/3)), giving the reduced representatives.
stabiliserOrder Q := card of the stabiliser of Q in PSL₂(ℤ), equal to the stabiliser of α_Q, which is trivial except at the orbits of i and ρ = e^{2πi/3}.

the points α_Q are the fixed points of integral matrices of determinant n and trace r with r² − 4n = −d

nodes.title: The recursions for the coefficients of g (Zagier §2)
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 0: Σ_{r∈ℤ}B(4n − r²) = 0 and Σ_{r>0}r²B(4n − r²) = 240σ₃(n), with σ₃(0) := 1/240 and B(d) := 0 for d < −1. These determine all B(d) recursively from B(−1) = 1: B(4n − 1) = 240σ₃(n) − Σ_{2≤r≤√(4n+1)}r²B(4n − r²) and B(4n) = −2Σ_{1≤r≤√(4n+1)}B(4n − r²).
proofSteps: gθ, with θ = Σq^{n²}, is a weakly holomorphic form of weight 2 on Γ₀(4) whose U₄-image lies in M^!₂(SL₂(ℤ)) (Kohnen's plus-space lemma, requested from MP.7); its constant term is B(0) + 2B(−1) = 0 and it has no polar terms, so (gθ)|U₄ ∈ M₂(SL₂(ℤ)) = 0 (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_two_rank_zero).

The Rankin–Cohen bracket [g, θ] = g′θ − 3gθ′ (′ = q d/dq) is modular of weight 4 (the first Rankin–Cohen bracket of weights 3/2 and 1/2: the correction terms of the derivatives cancel), and [g, θ]|U₄ ∈ M₄(SL₂(ℤ)) = ℂE₄ (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_four_rank_one).

Its q^{4n}-coefficient is Σ_r(4n − 4r²)B(4n − r²) = −8Σ_{r>0}r²B(4n − r²) (using the first identity); the constant term is −8B(−1) = −8, so [g, θ]|U₄ = −8E₄, and the coefficients 1, 240σ₃(n) of E₄ give Σ_{r>0}r²B(4n − r²) = 240σ₃(n) (with σ₃(0) = 1/240).
Read off Fourier coefficients: the coefficient of qⁿ in (gθ)|U₄ is Σ_r B(4n − r²); in [g, θ]|U₄ it is a multiple of Σ_{r>0}r²B(4n − r²).
Solving the r = 1 and r = 0 terms gives the recursion.
acceptance: The recursion uses only B(−1) and B(0) as initial values.

nodes.title: The weight-two logarithmic derivative Λ_d of the class polynomial
nodes.statement: For d > 0, d ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4): Λ_d(τ) = Σ_{Q∈Q_d/Γ}(1/w_Q)·j′(τ)/(j(τ) − j(α_Q)), a meromorphic modular form of weight 2 on SL₂(ℤ), holomorphic at ∞, with a simple pole at each α ∈ ℍ satisfying a quadratic equation over ℤ of discriminant −d, of residue 1 as a function on ℍ (Zagier's ‘residue 1/|Γ_α|’ is the residue of Λ_d dτ in the local coordinate of the quotient curve, which differs by the factor |Γ_α| at the elliptic points i and ρ), and with q-expansion −(2πi)⁻¹Λ_d = H(d) + t(d)q + O(q²). It is the logarithmic derivative of H_d(j(τ)) = ∏(j(τ) − j(α_Q))^{1/w_Q}, and it is uniquely characterised by its poles and residues because M₂(SL₂(ℤ)) = 0.
hypotheses: j′ = dj/dτ; Λ_d avoids the fractional powers in H_d.
proofSteps: Define heegnerLogDeriv d τ := Σ_{Q ∈ heegnerClasses d} (1/w_Q)·deriv j τ/(j τ − j α_Q).
Modularity of weight 2: j′ has weight 2 and j is invariant.
Residues: j − j(α_Q) vanishes at α_Q to order |Γ_{α_Q}| = w_Q (to order 2 at i, since j − 1728 = E₆²/Δ, and to order 3 at ρ, since j = E₄³/Δ), so (1/w_Q)j′/(j − j(α_Q)) has residue 1.
Expansion at ∞: −(2πi)^{−1}j′ = q^{−1} − 196884q + ⋯ and j − j(α) = q^{−1} − J(α) + O(q), so each term is 1 + J(α_Q)q + O(q²).
Uniqueness: two meromorphic weight-2 forms with the same principal parts differ by a holomorphic weight-2 form, which is 0 (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_two_rank_zero).

nodes.title: The logarithmic derivative of Φ_n(j, j) (Zagier (9))
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 not a square let D_n(τ) = ∏_{ad=n, a,d>0}∏_{b=0}^{d−1}(j(τ) − j((aτ + b)/d)) (= Φ_n(j(τ), j(τ)) for the n-th modular polynomial). Then D′_n/D_n = Σ_{|r|<2√n}Λ_{4n−r²} as meromorphic functions on ℍ. For n = m² a square the same holds for D_n/D₁-type quotients: the factor with a = d = m, b = 0 is omitted on the left and Σ_{|r|<2}Λ_{4−r²} is subtracted on the right.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; the square case as stated.
proofSteps: Γ-invariance of D_n: right multiplication by γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ) permutes Γ\M_n, whose representatives are the matrices (a b; 0 d), ad = n, 0 ≤ b < d (the coset argument of HeckeRing.GL2.heckeSlashSum_slash_invariant), so D_n is a weakly holomorphic modular function and D′_n/D_n a meromorphic weight-2 form, holomorphic at ∞.

Zeros: D_n(τ) = 0 iff j(τ) = j(Mτ) for some M ∈ M_n iff τ is fixed by some M ∈ M_n (j is injective on Γ\ℍ); the fixed points of M with trace r are the α_Q with disc(Q) = r² − 4n, |r| < 2√n (n not a square excludes scalar M).

Multiplicities: each pair ±M ∈ M_n fixing α contributes a simple zero, and the matrices fixing α with trace r correspond to the |Γ_α| elements of the stabiliser, so the residue of D′_n/D_n at α equals that of Σ_rΛ_{4n−r²}.
Equality: the difference is a holomorphic weight-2 form on SL₂(ℤ), hence 0 (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_two_rank_zero).
acceptance: The multiplicity bookkeeping at elliptic points (w_Q = 2, 3) is what the weights 1/w_Q in Λ_d account for.

nodes.title: The first recursion for t(d) and the Kronecker–Hurwitz relation (Zagier (5), (7))
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 1: Σ_{|r|<2√n} t(4n − r²) = −4 if n is a square, 2 if 4n + 1 is a square, and 0 otherwise; and Σ_{|r|<2√n}H(4n − r²) = Σ_{d|n}max(d, n/d) + (1/6 if n is a square, 0 otherwise).
hypotheses: n ≥ 1 (n and 4n + 1 cannot both be squares).
proofSteps: Expand D_n at ∞ with the representatives (a b; 0 d): j(τ) − j((aτ + b)/d) = q⁻¹ − e^{−2πib/d}q^{−a/d} + O(q^{>0}); the product over b is q^{−d} − q^{−a}(1 + O(q^{>1})) = ±q^{−max(a,d)}(1 − ε_aq + O(q²)) with ε_a = 1 iff |a − d| = 1.
Hence, with A = Σ_{ad=n}max(a, d) and ε the number of factorisations n = ad with |a − d| = 1 (2 if 4n + 1 is a square, else 0): −(2πi)⁻¹D′_n/D_n = −q(d/dq)log D_n = A + εq + O(q²).
By modular-diagonal-log-derivative and heegnerLogDeriv_qExpansion the left side is Σ_r(H(4n − r²) + t(4n − r²)q) + O(q²); compare the q⁰ and q¹ coefficients.

Square n = m²: use the quotient form of modular-diagonal-log-derivative. The factors with a = d = m, b ≠ 0 contribute ∏_{b=1}^{m−1}(1 − ζ_m^{−b})q^{−1}(1 + O(q²)) = m·q^{−(m−1)}(1 + O(q²)), so the q⁰ comparison gives Σ_r H(4n − r²) − (H(4) + 2H(3)) = Σ_{d|n}max(d, n/d) − 1, i.e. the extra term 1/6 = H(4) + 2H(3) − 1, and the q¹ comparison gives Σ_r t(4n − r²) = t(4) + 2t(3) = −4.

nodes.title: The weight-two identity behind the second recursion (Zagier Proposition (12))
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 not a square and τ ∈ ℍ: (E₄E₆/Δ)(τ)·Σ_{M∈Γ\M_n}(E₄|₄M)(τ)/(j(τ) − j(Mτ)) = (1/(4πi))Σ_{|r|<2√n}(r² − n)Λ_{4n−r²}(τ), where (E₄|₄M)(τ) = n³(cτ + d)^{−4}E₄(Mτ) for M = (a b; c d).
hypotheses: n not a square.
proofSteps: Both sides are meromorphic weight-2 forms on SL₂(ℤ), holomorphic at ∞, with at most simple poles; it suffices to compare residues (ModularForm.levelOne_weight_two_rank_zero).

At a fixed point α of M with c > 0, λ = cα + d is a quadratic integer of trace r = tr M and norm n, and the residue of the left summand is (2πi)^{−1}·(−λ̄³/(λ − λ̄)), computed from Dj = −E₄²E₆/Δ, E₄(Mα) = E₄(α) and (d/dτ)(Mτ) = n(cτ + d)^{−2} (source p. 5).
Pair M with nM⁻¹ (same fixed point, conjugate λ): the residues add to (2πi)^{−1}·½(λ³ − λ̄³)/(λ − λ̄) = (2πi)^{−1}·½(r² − n).
At elliptic points (α a root of E₄ or E₆) the same comparison holds with the stabiliser weights; this case is left to the reader in the source.
acceptance: For non-square n the q⁰ coefficient gives the classical identity Σ_{|r|<2√n}(n − r²)H(4n − r²) = Σ_{d|n}min(d, n/d)³.
The identity is between weight-2 forms, so it is again rigid by M₂(SL₂(ℤ)) = 0.

nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 1: Σ_{1≤r<2√n} r²t(4n − r²) = −240σ₃(n) + (−8n if n is a square; 4n + 1 if 4n + 1 is a square; 0 otherwise).

Expand: for a < d, S_{a,d} = 1 + (240δ_{a,1}σ₃(n) + δ_{a,d−1})q + O(q²); for a > d, S_{a,d} = −δ_{a,d+1}q + O(q²) (only the pairs (l, m) listed in the source contribute).
So the q-coefficient is C₁ = 240σ₃(n) − (3n + 1 if 4n + 1 is a square), while by the proposition and heegnerLogDeriv_qExpansion C₁ = ½Σ_{|r|<2√n}(n − r²)t(4n − r²).

proofSteps: Extend t by t(−1) := −1 and t(0) := 2 (so that −t(−1) = B(−1), −t(0) = B(0)); then (5) and (6) (trace-first-recursion, trace-second-recursion) become Σ_{r∈ℤ}(−t)(4n − r²) = 0 and Σ_{r>0}r²(−t)(4n − r²) = 240σ₃(n) for all n ≥ 1, the boundary terms r² = 4n and r² = 4n + 1 accounting for −4, −8n and 2, 4n + 1.

nodes.title: Vertex algebra (Borcherds' axioms)
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring and V an R-module. A vertex algebra structure on V is a pair (Y, 1) with Y : V →ₗ[R] VertexOperator R V (Mathlib's vertex operators: R-linear maps from V to Laurent series in z with coefficients in V, support bounded below) and a vacuum vector 1 ∈ V. Write u_n := VertexOperator.ncoeff (Y u) n ∈ End_R(V), so that Y(u,z) = Σ_{n∈ℤ} u_n z^{−n−1}. The axioms are: (creation) u_n 1 = 0 for n ≥ 0 and u_{−1} 1 = u; (Borcherds identity) for all u, v, w ∈ V and m, n, q ∈ ℤ, Σ_{i≥0} C(m,i) (u_{q+i} v)_{m+n−i} w = Σ_{i≥0} (−1)^i C(q,i) ( u_{m+q−i}(v_{n+i} w) − (−1)^q v_{n+q−i}(u_{m+i} w) ), where C(m,i) = m(m−1)⋯(m−i+1)/i! ∈ ℤ is Mathlib's Ring.choose m i. The truncation axiom (for u, v there is N with u_n v = 0 for all n ≥ N) holds automatically because the support of Y(u,z)v is bounded below in z; hence both sums in the Borcherds identity are finite. Convention: index n of u_n is the 'mode' of Borcherds and Matsuo–Nagatomo; (u_n) for n ≥ 0 are the annihilation modes.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring
V is an R-module
proofSteps: Package the data as a structure whose field Y has type V →ₗ[R] VertexOperator R V and whose field vac is the vacuum; the two creation equations and the Borcherds identity are Prop fields stated with VertexOperator.ncoeff and Ring.choose.

Truncation: HVertexOperator.coeff_isPWOsupport gives that the support of the Laurent series Y(u,z)v is partially well ordered, hence bounded below in ℤ; since VertexOperator.ncoeff A n = HVertexOperator.coeff A (−n−1) (VertexOperator.ncoeff_apply), u_n v = 0 for n large.

Finiteness of the sums: the i-th term on the left vanishes once q+i exceeds the truncation bound of (u,v); on the right once n+i and m+i exceed the bounds of (v,w) and (u,w). State the identity with finite sums over ℕ (finsum) and record the finiteness as an API lemma.
acceptance: For a commutative ℚ-algebra A with derivation ∂, u_n v := (∂^{−n−1}u/(−n−1)!)·v for n ≤ −1 and u_n v := 0 for n ≥ 0 is a vertex algebra with vacuum 1 (Borcherds 1992 §3; Matsuo–Nagatomo Note 3.1.3).
The definition agrees with Matsuo–Nagatomo Definition 3.1.1 (B0)–(B2) under (p,q,r) = (m,n,q).

nodes.title: Vacuum, translation and derivation rules in a vertex algebra
nodes.statement: Let (V, Y, 1) be a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R. Define D : V → V by D v := v_{−2}1 and, for k ≥ 0, D^{(k)} v := v_{−k−1}1. Then: (a) 1_n v = δ_{n,−1} v for all n (Y(1,z) = id); (b) D 1 = 0; (c) (Dv)_n = −n v_{n−1} for all n; (d) [D, v_n] = −n v_{n−1}, i.e. D(v_n w) = (Dv)_n w + v_n(Dw), so D is a derivation of every product; (e) k·D^{(k)} v = D(D^{(k−1)} v) for k ≥ 1, hence k!·D^{(k)} = D^k; (f) u_n 1 = D^{(−n−1)} u for n ≤ −1.
hypotheses: (V, Y, 1) is a vertex algebra over R
proofSteps: (b): put u = v = w = 1 and m = n = q = −1 in the Borcherds identity (Matsuo–Nagatomo (18)).
(e),(f): put v = w = 1, m = 0, n = −2, q = n; the creation axiom gives (u_n 1)_{−2}1 = −n u_{n−1}1, which is (e) after reindexing (Matsuo–Nagatomo (19)).
(a): put v = w = 1, m = −1, n = q', q = 0 and use (b) (Matsuo–Nagatomo (20)).
(c): put v = 1, m = n', n = 0, q = −2 and use (a) (Matsuo–Nagatomo (21)).
(d): put w = 1, m = 0, n = −2, q = n (Matsuo–Nagatomo (22)); compare with (c).

Over a ℚ-algebra, Y(u,z)1 = e^{zD}u as formal power series.

nodes.title: Commutator and associativity formulas
nodes.statement: In a vertex algebra over a commutative ring, for all u, v ∈ V and m, n, q ∈ ℤ: (commutator formula) [u_m, v_n] = Σ_{i≥0} C(m,i) (u_i v)_{m+n−i}; (associativity formula) (u_q v)_n = Σ_{i≥0} (−1)^i C(q,i) ( u_{q−i} v_{n+i} − (−1)^q v_{n+q−i} u_i ) as endomorphisms of V. In particular [u_0, v_n] = (u_0 v)_n, so u ↦ u_0 acts by derivations of all products.
hypotheses: (V, Y, 1) is a vertex algebra
proofSteps: Set q = 0 in the Borcherds identity: the right side is u_m v_n w − v_n u_m w since C(0,i) = δ_{i,0} (Matsuo–Nagatomo (25)).
Set m = 0 in the Borcherds identity: the left side is (u_q v)_n w since C(0,i) = δ_{i,0} (Matsuo–Nagatomo (26)).
For m = 0 the commutator formula reads [u_0, v_n] = (u_0 v)_n.
acceptance: For VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation all commutators vanish, consistent with u_i v = 0 for i ≥ 0.
Borcherds 1986 §8 states the commutator formula [u_m, v_n] = Σ_j C(m,j)(u_j v)_{m+n−j}.

nodes.title: Skew symmetry
nodes.statement: In a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R, for all u, v ∈ V and n ∈ ℤ: v_n u = Σ_{i≥0} (−1)^{n+i+1} D^{(i)}(u_{n+i} v), where D^{(i)}x := x_{−i−1}1 (a finite sum by truncation). In particular v_0 u + u_0 v = Σ_{i≥1} (−1)^{i+1} D^{(i)}(u_i v) lies in the R-span DV_div := Σ_{i≥1} D^{(i)}(V), and u_0 u ∈ DV_div.
hypotheses: (V, Y, 1) is a vertex algebra
proofSteps: Put w = 1, m = −1, n = 0, q = n in the Borcherds identity and simplify with the creation axiom and the vacuum-translation lemma (Matsuo–Nagatomo (23)).
For n = 0 separate the i = 0 term: v_0 u = −u_0 v + Σ_{i≥1}(−1)^{i+1}D^{(i)}(u_i v).

nodes.title: The Lie algebra V/DV of a vertex algebra
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R and let DV := Σ_{i≥1} D^{(i)}(V) (the R-span of all D^{(i)}w, i ≥ 1; over a ℚ-algebra this is the image of D). Then DV is a two-sided ideal for the product (u, v) ↦ u_0 v, and V/DV is a Lie algebra over R with bracket [u + DV, v + DV] := u_0 v + DV. The map u ↦ u_0 makes V a module over the Lie algebra V/DV (DV acts by 0: (D^{(i)}w)_0 = 0 for i ≥ 1), and each u_0 acts by derivations of all products.
hypotheses: V is a vertex algebra over a commutative ring R
proofSteps: (D^{(i)} w)_0 = 0 for i ≥ 1: iterate (Dv)_n = −n v_{n−1} (vacuum-translation lemma (c)); hence DV · V ⊆ 0 on the left for the 0-product.

u_0 (D^{(i)} w) = D^{(i)}(u_0 w): u_0 commutes with D by [D, u_n] = −n u_{n−1} at n = 0, and with divided powers by the same identity applied to w_{−i−1}1 and the commutator formula; so DV is a right ideal.
Antisymmetry modulo DV: skew symmetry gives u_0 v + v_0 u ∈ DV and u_0 u ∈ DV.
Jacobi identity: the commutator formula at m = n = 0 gives u_0(v_0 w) − v_0(u_0 w) = (u_0 v)_0 w.

nodes.title: Homomorphisms and automorphisms of vertex algebras
nodes.statement: For vertex algebras (V, Y, 1) and (W, Y', 1') over R, a homomorphism is an R-linear map f : V → W with f(1) = 1' and f(u_n v) = f(u)_n f(v) for all u, v, n (equivalently f ∘ Y(u,z) = Y'(f u, z) ∘ f). The automorphisms of V form a group Aut(V) under composition. If V carries a conformal vector ω (node conformal-vector) the conformal automorphisms are those with g(ω) = ω; if V carries a bilinear form (,) the isometric conformal automorphisms are those with (gu, gv) = (u, v). For a group G, an action of G on V by vertex algebra automorphisms is a group homomorphism G →* Aut(V).
hypotheses: V, W vertex algebras over the same commutative ring R
proofSteps: Define VertexAlgebra.Hom as a structure extending V →ₗ[R] W with the two compatibility fields; composition and identity are immediate.
Define Aut(V) as the group of invertible homomorphisms (bundled as R-linear equivalences satisfying the two conditions); the inverse of a bijective homomorphism is a homomorphism.
Define the subgroups of conformal and of conformal isometric automorphisms as stabilizers.

nodes.title: Existence theorem for vertex algebras (locality criterion)
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0, V a k-vector space, 1 ∈ V nonzero, T ∈ End_k(V), and S a set of fields on V (formal series A(z) = Σ A_n z^{−n−1} with A_n ∈ End(V) and A(z)w ∈ V((z)) for every w) such that: (S1) the fields in S are pairwise local: for A, B ∈ S there is N with (y−z)^N [A(y), B(z)] = 0; (S2) the vectors A^{λ1}_{−j1−1}⋯A^{λk}_{−jk−1}1 (k ≥ 0, j_i ≥ 0, A^{λi} ∈ S) span V; (S3) each A ∈ S is creative (A_n 1 = 0 for n ≥ 0) and translation covariant: [T, A(z)] = ∂_z A(z), with T1 = 0. Then there is a unique vertex algebra structure on V with vacuum 1 such that Y(A_{−1}1, z) = A(z) for every A ∈ S; its translation operator is T.
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0
S pairwise local, creative, translation covariant, generating V from 1
proofSteps: Let O be the space of creative fields; the residual products A(z)_{(m)}B(z) of local fields are local (Dong's lemma, Matsuo–Nagatomo Proposition 1.5.5) and creative (Lemma 4.1.2).

The space ⟨S⟩ of fields generated by S under residual products is pairwise local and contains the identity field; by Li's theorem (Matsuo–Nagatomo Theorem 3.3.1, via the Borcherds identity for local fields, Corollary 2.2.2 and Theorem 2.4.1) it is a vertex algebra.
Translation covariance and (S2) make the state map A(z) ↦ A_{−1}1 bijective from ⟨S⟩ onto V (Theorem 5.3.3); transport the structure along it.
Uniqueness: a vertex algebra structure is determined by the fields of a generating set, by the associativity formula (node vertex-algebra-commutator-formula).
acceptance: The vertex algebra structure of VertexAlgebra.ofDerivation is recovered from S = {Y(a, z) : a ∈ A} with T = ∂.
Applied to S = {Y(a⊗1), Y(1⊗b)} it produces the tensor product vertex algebra (node vertex-algebra-tensor-product).

nodes.title: Tensor product of vertex algebras
nodes.statement: Let V, W be vertex algebras over a field k of characteristic 0. The k-vector space V ⊗_k W carries a unique vertex algebra structure with vacuum 1 ⊗ 1 and (a ⊗ b)_n (c ⊗ d) = Σ_{i∈ℤ} (a_i c) ⊗ (b_{n−1−i} d) (a finite sum by truncation), i.e. Y(a⊗b, z) = Y(a,z) ⊗ Y(b,z). The maps a ↦ a ⊗ 1 and b ↦ 1 ⊗ b are vertex algebra homomorphisms whose images commute: [(a⊗1)_m, (1⊗b)_n] = 0.
hypotheses: V, W vertex algebras over a field k of characteristic 0
proofSteps: Define the fields Y(a⊗1, z) := Y(a,z) ⊗ id and Y(1⊗b, z) := id ⊗ Y(b,z) on V ⊗ W; they are creative for 1⊗1 and translation covariant for T := D_V ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ D_W.
Locality: fields from the same factor are local by locality in V or W (Matsuo–Nagatomo (27)); fields from different factors commute.

The products (a⊗1)_{−1}(1⊗b)_{−1}(1⊗1) = a⊗b span, so the existence theorem gives the vertex algebra; normal ordering identifies Y(a⊗b, z) with Y(a,z)⊗Y(b,z), which yields the displayed formula for the modes.
The two inclusions are homomorphisms by uniqueness in the existence theorem.
acceptance: Borcherds 1992 §3 formula (a ⊗ b)_n(c ⊗ d) = Σ_i (a_i c) ⊗ (b_{n−1−i} d).
V ⊗ k (k the one-dimensional vertex algebra with 1_{−1} = id) is isomorphic to V.

sources.excerpt: If V and W are vertex algebras, then their tensor product V ⊗ W as vector spaces is also a vertex algebra, if (a ⊗ b)n(c ⊗ d) is defined to be Σi∈Z(aic) ⊗ (bn−1−id) and the identity 1 is defined to be 1⊗1. (See [18].)

sources.excerpt: Tensor products of vertex operator algebras are again vertex operator algebras (see [9]), and more generally, by [8], the tensor product of vertex algebras is also a vertex algebra.

nodes.title: The Virasoro algebra and modules of given central charge
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0. The Virasoro algebra Vir_k is the Lie algebra over k with basis {L_n : n ∈ ℤ} ∪ {C} and bracket [L_m, L_n] = (m − n) L_{m+n} + ((m³ − m)/12) δ_{m+n,0} C, [C, x] = 0 for all x. For c ∈ k, a Virasoro module of central charge c is a Lie module M over Vir_k on which C acts as multiplication by c; equivalently a family of operators L_n ∈ End(M) with [L_m, L_n] = (m−n)L_{m+n} + c(m³−m)/12 δ_{m+n,0}.
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0 (the coefficient 1/12 must make sense)
proofSteps: Define Vir_k as the k-module with basis ℤ ⊕ {C} (Finsupp) and the bracket extended bilinearly; check antisymmetry ((m³−m) is odd in m) and the Jacobi identity on basis elements (the cocycle ψ(m,n) = (m³−m)/12 δ_{m+n,0} satisfies the 2-cocycle identity).
Define the module predicate as a LieModule together with the scalar action of C.
acceptance: (L_{−1}, L_0, L_1) span a copy of sl₂: (2L_0, L_{−1}, −L_1) is an sl₂-triple.

sources.excerpt: These operators satisfy the relations [Li, Lj] = (i − j)Li+j + (i+1 choose 3) c/2 δi−j and so make V into a module over the Virasoro algebra.
sources.match: The Virasoro relations with central charge c; (i+1 choose 3)/2 = (i³−i)/12.

nodes.title: Conformal vector of a vertex algebra
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with translation D (node vertex-algebra-vacuum-translation). A conformal vector of central charge c ∈ k is ω ∈ V such that: ω_0 v = Dv for all v; ω_1 ω = 2ω; ω_2 ω = 0; ω_3 ω = (c/2)·1; ω_i ω = 0 for i ≥ 4; and L_0 := ω_1 is diagonalizable with integer eigenvalues: V = ⊕_{n∈ℤ} V_n (internal direct sum) with V_n := ker(L_0 − n). Put L_n := ω_{n+1}. The eigenvalue n of v ∈ V_n is its (conformal) weight. Convention (Borcherds): in the moonshine module the space of weight n + 1 is Borcherds' V_n (degree n).
hypotheses: V vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0
c ∈ k
proofSteps: Structure with fields ω, c and the six conditions, the last as DirectSum.IsInternal of the eigenspaces Module.End.eigenspace L_0 (n : k), n ∈ ℤ.
acceptance: For the zero derivation commutative vertex algebra, ω = 0 is a conformal vector of central charge 0.
For the lattice vertex algebra of a nondegenerate even lattice of rank d, ω = ½ Σ_i h_i(−1)h^i(−1)1 (dual bases) is a conformal vector of central charge d (node lattice-vertex-algebra).

sources.excerpt: A conformal vector of dimension (or “central charge”) c ∈ R of a vertex algebra V is defined to be an element ω of V such that ω0v = D(v) for any v ∈ V , ω1ω = 2ω, ω3ω = c/2, ωiω = 0 if i = 2 or i > 3, and any element of V is a sum of eigenvectors of the operator L0 = ω1

nodes.title: Modes of a conformal vector form a Virasoro module
nodes.statement: Let ω be a conformal vector of central charge c in a vertex algebra V over a field of characteristic 0, and L_n := ω_{n+1}. Then (a) [L_m, L_n] = (m − n)L_{m+n} + c (m³ − m)/12 δ_{m+n,0} for all m, n ∈ ℤ, so V is a Virasoro module of central charge c; (b) L_{−1} = D; (c) for v ∈ V_h with L_n v = 0 for all n > 0 (a primary vector of weight h), [L_m, v_n] = ((m+1)(h−1) − n) v_{m+n}; in particular for v ∈ P^1 (h = 1), [L_m, v_0] = 0, so v_0 commutes with the Virasoro action; (d) (L_{−1}v)_n = −n v_{n−1}.
hypotheses: ω conformal vector of central charge c
proofSteps: (a): apply the commutator formula [ω_{m+1}, ω_{n+1}] = Σ_i C(m+1,i)(ω_i ω)_{m+n+2−i} and substitute ω_0 ω = Dω, ω_1ω = 2ω, ω_2ω = 0, ω_3ω = (c/2)1, ω_iω = 0 (i ≥ 4), with (Dω)_k = −k ω_{k−1} and 1_k = δ_{k,−1}.
(b) is the axiom ω_0 = D.
(c): commutator formula [ω_{m+1}, v_n] = Σ_i C(m+1,i) (ω_i v)_{m+n+1−i}; for primary v, ω_i v = L_{i−1} v vanishes for i ≥ 2, ω_1 v = hv and ω_0 v = Dv, and (Dv)_k = −k v_{k−1}.
(d) is the vacuum-translation lemma (c).
acceptance: For the rank-d lattice vertex algebra the central charge is d (Borcherds 1986 §5).
Borcherds 1986 §5: [L_j, u_k] = ((j+1)(i−1) − k)u_{j+k} for u ∈ P^i (the source prints P^1, see sourceIssues).

nodes.title: Vertex operator algebra
nodes.statement: A vertex operator algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 is a vertex algebra V over k with a conformal vector ω of central charge c such that each weight space V_n = ker(L_0 − n) is finite-dimensional and V_n = 0 for all sufficiently negative n (V = ⊕_{n ≥ N} V_n). It is nonnegatively graded when V_n = 0 for n < 0 (Borcherds' definition: all L_0-eigenvalues are nonnegative integers), and of CFT type when moreover V_0 = k·1. A homomorphism of vertex operator algebras is a vertex algebra homomorphism sending ω to ω; Aut(V, ω) is the group of conformal automorphisms, and each of its elements preserves every V_n.
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0
proofSteps: Structure extending the vertex algebra by a conformal vector and the two finiteness conditions (FiniteDimensional k (V_n) for all n; ∃ N, ∀ n < N, V_n = ⊥).
Nonnegative grading and CFT type are predicates, not fields.
Conformal automorphisms preserve weight spaces because they commute with L_0 = ω_1.
acceptance: A finite-dimensional commutative k-algebra with the zero derivation and ω = 0 is a vertex operator algebra of central charge 0 concentrated in weight 0.

The lattice vertex algebra of a positive definite even lattice of rank d is a nonnegatively graded vertex operator algebra of CFT type and central charge d; the lattice vertex algebra of II_{1,1} is not a vertex operator algebra.
Agreement with Jurisich 1998 Definition 4 (V1)–(V10) and with Borcherds 1992 §3 (nonnegative case).

sources.excerpt: A vertex operator algebra is a vertex algebra with a conformal vector such that the eigenspaces of L0 are all finite dimensional with nonnegative integral eigenvalues.

nodes.title: Invariant bilinear forms compatible with the conformal vector
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vector ω, and θ a vertex algebra automorphism of V with θ² = 1 and θ(ω) = ω (the Cartan involution; θ = id for the moonshine module). A symmetric bilinear form (·,·) on V is θ-invariant (compatible with ω in Borcherds' sense) if for every u ∈ V_i (L_0-weight i), all n ∈ ℤ and all v, w ∈ V: (u_n v, w) = (−1)^i Σ_{j≥0} (1/j!) (v, (L_1^j θ(u))_{2i−j−n−2} w). For θ = id this is the Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky invariance (Y(u,z)v, w) = (v, Y(e^{zL_1}(−z^{−2})^{L_0}u, z^{−1})w). The associated contravariant form is (u, v)_0 := −(u, θ v).
hypotheses: V vertex algebra over k with conformal vector ω
θ ∈ Aut(V), θ² = 1, θω = ω
proofSteps: Define the predicate IsInvariantForm θ B by the displayed identity for homogeneous u; extend to all u by linearity using the weight decomposition.
Derived properties: taking u = ω (weight 2, L_1ω = 0, θω = ω) gives L_n* = L_{−n}; taking n = −1, v = 1 gives (V_i, V_j) = 0 for i ≠ j (use L_0* = L_0); for u ∈ P^1 the formula gives u_0* = −θ(u)_0.
acceptance: The zero form is invariant for every θ.

For the lattice vertex algebra of an even unimodular lattice, the Fock-space form with r(i)* = r(−i) and (e^r, e^s) = δ_{r,s} (Borcherds 1986 §2(v)) is invariant for the Cartan involution θ(e^r) = (−1)^{(r,r)/2}e^{−r}, θ(r(i)) = −r(i).

nodes.title: Conformal vector and invariant form of a tensor product
nodes.statement: Let V, W be vertex algebras over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vectors ω_V, ω_W of central charges c_V, c_W, involutions θ_V, θ_W and θ-invariant symmetric forms B_V, B_W. Then ω := ω_V ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ ω_W is a conformal vector of V ⊗ W of central charge c_V + c_W, L_n^{V⊗W} = L_n^V ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ L_n^W, (V⊗W)_n = ⊕_{a+b=n} V_a ⊗ W_b, θ_V ⊗ θ_W is an involution fixing ω, and B_V ⊗ B_W is a (θ_V ⊗ θ_W)-invariant symmetric form, nondegenerate when B_V and B_W are.

proofSteps: Mode formula of the tensor product: (ω_V ⊗ 1)_{n+1} = L_n^V ⊗ 1 and (1 ⊗ ω_W)_{n+1} = 1 ⊗ L_n^W; check the six conformal-vector conditions factorwise (the cross terms vanish because the two factors commute).
Invariance: the adjoint formula is multiplicative for a ⊗ b with a, b homogeneous since L_1 and L_0 act as derivations of the tensor product; check on pure tensors.

nodes.title: Graded trace (graded character) of an endomorphism
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex operator algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 and g ∈ End_k(V) with g(V_n) ⊆ V_n for all n (for example g ∈ Aut(V, ω)). The graded trace of g is Z_V(g) := Σ_{n∈ℤ} tr(g|V_n) q^n ∈ k((q)) (a Laurent series because V_n = 0 for n ≪ 0). The graded dimension is Z_V(1) = Σ_n dim(V_n) q^n. Convention: no factor q^{−c/24} is included here (it is added in node mckay-thompson-series for c = 24).

g preserves every weight space
proofSteps: For each n, restrict g to the finite-dimensional V_n (LinearMap.restrict) and take LinearMap.trace; the resulting ℤ-indexed family has support bounded below, so it defines a HahnSeries ℤ k = LaurentSeries k.
acceptance: Z_V(g) depends only on the conjugacy class of g in Aut(V, ω).

nodes.title: McKay–Thompson series
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex operator algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 and g ∈ Aut(V, ω). The McKay–Thompson series of g is T_g := q^{−1}·Z_V(g) = Σ_{n∈ℤ} tr(g|V_{n+1}) q^n ∈ k((q)), and c_g(n) := tr(g|V_{n+1}) (Borcherds' Thompson series Σ Tr(g|V_n)q^n with Borcherds' V_n = V_{n+1} here). The factor q^{−1} is q^{−c/24} for central charge c = 24, the case used in this stage. For a group G acting on V by conformal automorphisms, T_g for g ∈ G is a class function of g. When V is nonnegatively graded with V_0 = k·1 and V_1 = 0, T_g = q^{−1} + Σ_{n≥1} c_g(n) q^n.
hypotheses: V vertex operator algebra of central charge 24
g ∈ Aut(V, ω)
proofSteps: Define as HahnSeries.single (−1) 1 * gradedTrace V g in LaurentSeries k.
The normalized shape follows from tr(g|k·1) = 1 (g1 = 1) and V_1 = 0.
acceptance: T_1 is q^{−1} times the graded dimension; for the moonshine module T_1 = J (node moonshine-identity-thompson-series).
For the rank-24 Heisenberg vertex operator algebra, T_1 = q^{−1}Π(1 − q^n)^{−24} = q^{−1} + 24 + 324q + 3200q² + ⋯.

nodes.title: Double cover of an even lattice and its twisted group algebra
nodes.statement: Let (L, ⟨·,·⟩) be an even lattice: a finitely generated free ℤ-module with a symmetric ℤ-valued bilinear form with ⟨α,α⟩ ∈ 2ℤ for all α (in Tau Ceti: the carrier of a TauCeti.IntegralLattice satisfying IsEven). A lattice cocycle is a bimultiplicative map ε : L × L → {±1} with ε(α,α) = (−1)^{⟨α,α⟩/2} for all α; it satisfies ε(α,β)ε(β,α) = (−1)^{⟨α,β⟩}. Cocycles exist: for a ℤ-basis e_1, …, e_d put ε(e_i,e_j) = (−1)^{⟨e_i,e_j⟩} for i < j, (−1)^{⟨e_i,e_i⟩/2} for i = j, 1 for i > j, and extend bimultiplicatively. For a field k, the twisted group algebra k_ε[L] has k-basis {e^α : α ∈ L} and product e^α e^β = ε(α,β) e^{α+β}; it is associative with unit e^0. The group L̂ = {±e^α} is a central extension 1 → {±1} → L̂ → L → 1 with commutator (−1)^{⟨α,β⟩}, unique up to isomorphism; two cocycles give isomorphic twisted group algebras.
hypotheses: L free of finite rank
⟨·,·⟩ symmetric, ℤ-valued and even
proofSteps: Bimultiplicativity makes ε a 2-cocycle, so k_ε[L] is associative (build it on AddMonoidAlgebra k L with the twisted product).
ε(α,β)ε(β,α) = (−1)^{⟨α,β⟩}: expand ε(α+β, α+β) = (−1)^{⟨α+β,α+β⟩/2} using bimultiplicativity.
Existence: the displayed values on a basis define a bimultiplicative map with ε(e_i,e_i) = (−1)^{⟨e_i,e_i⟩/2}; the diagonal condition for general α follows from the commutator identity and evenness.

Uniqueness: two cocycles with the same diagonal differ by a symmetric bimultiplicative map η with η(α,α) = 1, which is a coboundary η(α,β) = f(α+β)f(α)^{−1}f(β)^{−1}; rescaling e^α ↦ f(α)e^α gives the isomorphism.
acceptance: For L = ℤα with ⟨α,α⟩ = 2, ε(α,α) = −1 and (e^α)² = −e^{2α}.
Borcherds 1986 §2: e^r e^s = ε^{(r,s)} e^s e^r and e^r e^{−r} = ε^{(r,r)/2}.

nodes.title: The vertex algebra of an even lattice
nodes.statement: Let L be an even lattice with cocycle ε, k a field of characteristic 0, h := L ⊗_ℤ k with the k-bilinear extension of ⟨·,·⟩. Put V_L := S(ĥ⁻) ⊗_k k_ε[L], where S(ĥ⁻) is the symmetric algebra of ⊕_{n≥1} h ⊗ t^{−n} (write α(−n) := α ⊗ t^{−n}). For α ∈ h, n ∈ ℤ define α(n) ∈ End(V_L): multiplication by α(n) for n < 0; α(0)(s ⊗ e^γ) = ⟨α,γ⟩ s ⊗ e^γ; for n > 0 the derivation of S(ĥ⁻) with α(n)β(−m) = n⟨α,β⟩δ_{n,m}; so [α(m), β(n)] = m⟨α,β⟩δ_{m+n,0}. Then there is a unique vertex algebra structure on V_L with vacuum 1 := 1 ⊗ e^0 such that Y(α(−1)1, z) = Σ_n α(n) z^{−n−1} and Y(1 ⊗ e^β, z) = exp(Σ_{n≥1} β(−n)z^n/n) exp(−Σ_{n≥1} β(n)z^{−n}/n) e^β z^{β(0)}, where e^β acts by left multiplication in k_ε[L] and z^{β(0)}(s ⊗ e^γ) = z^{⟨β,γ⟩} s ⊗ e^γ. It is L-graded (V_{L,γ} := S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^γ, u_n v ∈ V_{L,α+β} for u ∈ V_{L,α}, v ∈ V_{L,β}). If ⟨·,·⟩ is nondegenerate with dual bases (h_i), (h^i) of h, then ω := ½ Σ_i h_i(−1)h^i(−1)1 is a conformal vector of central charge d = rank L, and L_0(α_1(−n_1)⋯α_k(−n_k) ⊗ e^γ) = (Σ n_i + ⟨γ,γ⟩/2)·(same vector). The Cartan involution θ(α(n)) = −α(n), θ(e^γ) = (−1)^{⟨γ,γ⟩/2} e^{−γ} (for a cocycle with ε(γ,−γ) = ε(γ,γ)) is an automorphism fixing ω. If L is positive definite, V_L is a vertex operator algebra of CFT type.
hypotheses: L even lattice, ε a lattice cocycle
k field of characteristic 0
conformal vector only for nondegenerate ⟨·,·⟩
proofSteps: The operators α(n) form a representation of the Heisenberg Lie algebra ĥ on V_L; α(n)1 = 0 for n ≥ 0.
The fields α(z) and Y(e^β, z) are creative and translation covariant for T(s ⊗ e^γ) := (T_S s) ⊗ e^γ + γ(−1)s ⊗ e^γ with T_S the derivation α(−n) ↦ nα(−n−1).

Locality: [α(z), β(w)] = ⟨α,β⟩∂_wδ(z−w); [α(z), Y(e^β,w)] = ⟨α,β⟩Y(e^β,w)δ(z−w); and Y(e^α,z)Y(e^β,w) = ε(α,β)(z−w)^{⟨α,β⟩} :Y(e^α,z)Y(e^β,w):, so (z−w)^N[Y(e^α,z), Y(e^β,w)] = 0 for N ≥ −⟨α,β⟩, the sign ε(α,β)ε(β,α)(−1)^{⟨α,β⟩} = 1 making the two orders agree.
The vectors α_1(−n_1)⋯α_k(−n_k) ⊗ e^γ are obtained from 1 by the modes of these fields, so the existence theorem gives the vertex algebra; the grading statement is read off the fields.
Conformal vector: compute ω_{n+1} = ½Σ_i Σ_m :h_i(m)h^i(n−m): (Sugawara/Segal operators) and check the six conditions; the central charge equals the trace of the identity of h, i.e. d.
θ preserves the defining fields up to the stated signs, hence is an automorphism by uniqueness in the existence theorem.
Positive definite L: weights Σn_i + ⟨γ,γ⟩/2 ≥ 0 with finitely many vectors of each weight, and weight 0 only for 1.
acceptance: For L = ℤα with ⟨α,α⟩ = 2, (e^α)_0 e^{−α} = ε(α,−α) α(−1)1 and V_1 (with bracket u_0 v) is isomorphic to sl₂ (Borcherds 1986 §5).
For positive definite L of rank d, the graded dimension is Σ_{γ∈L} q^{⟨γ,γ⟩/2} / Π_{n≥1}(1−q^n)^d.

nodes.title: Invariant form on the vertex algebra of an even unimodular lattice
nodes.statement: Let L be an even unimodular lattice (for example II_{1,1}) and V_L its vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vector ω and Cartan involution θ. Then V_L carries a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form (·,·), invariant in the Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky sense (θ = id in node invariant-bilinear-form), unique up to a nonzero scalar; it satisfies (V_{L,r}, V_{L,s}) = 0 unless r + s = 0, (α(n)u, v) = −(u, α(−n)v), θ preserves it, and with the normalization (1,1) = −1 one has (e^r, θ(e^r)) = −1 for every r ∈ L. Consequently, for a vertex algebra V with id-invariant form (·,·)_V, the product form on V ⊗ V_L satisfies (u ⊗ e^r, θ(u ⊗ e^r)) = −(u,u)_V.
hypotheses: L even unimodular
k field of characteristic 0
proofSteps: V_L is an irreducible module over itself and every irreducible V_L-module is isomorphic to V_L (Dong 1993, cited in Jurisich 1998 Lemma 6.1); the contragredient module V_L' (restricted dual with respect to the L × ℤ grading) is irreducible, hence isomorphic to V_L; an isomorphism V_L ≅ V_L' is a nondegenerate invariant form, and symmetry holds by Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky Remark 5.3.3 (Jurisich 1998 Lemma 6.1).
Orthogonality of degrees: invariance with u = α(−1)1 gives (α(0)x, y) = −(x, α(0)y), so (x,y) = 0 unless the degrees add to 0.

(e^r, θe^r) = (1,1): apply the invariance formula to u = e^r, which is primary of weight ⟨r,r⟩/2, with v = 1: (e^r, θe^r) = ((e^r)_{−1}1, θe^r) = (−1)^{⟨r,r⟩/2}(1, (e^r)_{⟨r,r⟩−1} θe^r); by the expMode formula (e^r)_{⟨r,r⟩−1}e^{−r} = ε(r,−r)1, and the signs (−1)^{⟨r,r⟩/2} from θ and from the adjoint formula and ε(r,−r) = ε(r,r) = (−1)^{⟨r,r⟩/2} cancel (Jurisich 1998, proof of Theorem 6.1).
The product-form statement is the tensor-product lemma applied to V ⊗ V_L.
acceptance: The form restricted to the weight-one degree-zero space span{α(−1)1} is ±⟨·,·⟩, of signature (1,1) for II_{1,1}.

nodes.statement: II_{1,1} is ℤ² with the symmetric bilinear form ⟨(m,n),(m',n')⟩ = −(mn' + m'n) (Gram matrix [[0,−1],[−1,0]] in the standard basis); the norm of (m,n) is ⟨(m,n),(m,n)⟩ = −2mn. It is even, unimodular (Gram determinant −1) and of signature (1,1). Its norm-2 vectors are exactly ±(1,−1); the reflection in (1,−1) is (m,n) ↦ (n,m). Convention: Borcherds' sign; Gannon uses the form mn' + m'n, which differs by the isometry (m,n) ↦ (m,−n).

Norm 2: −2mn = 2 iff mn = −1 iff (m,n) = ±(1,−1).

nodes.title: Physical spaces P^i of a vertex algebra with conformal vector
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vector ω and L_n = ω_{n+1}. For i ∈ ℤ the physical space of weight i is P^i := {v ∈ V : L_0 v = i v and L_n v = 0 for all n ≥ 1} (the lowest-weight vectors of the Virasoro action of weight i). If V is graded by an abelian group Λ compatibly with the vertex algebra structure and with L_0 ∈ End of degree 0, then P^i = ⊕_{r∈Λ} P^i_r.
hypotheses: V vertex algebra with conformal vector ω over a field of characteristic 0
proofSteps: Define P^i as the intersection of the L_0-eigenspace of eigenvalue i with the kernels of L_n, n ≥ 1 (a k-submodule); since L_n for n ≥ 3 lies in the Lie algebra generated by L_1 and L_2, it suffices to impose L_1 v = L_2 v = 0.
u, v ∈ P^1 ⇒ u_0 v ∈ P^1: by the Virasoro-representation theorem (c), [L_m, u_0] = 0 for u ∈ P^1, and u_0 commutes with L_0.
acceptance: 1 ∈ P^0; ω ∈ P^2 only when c = 0, since L_2ω = (c/2)1.
For the lattice vertex algebra of ℤα with ⟨α,α⟩ = 2: e^α, e^{−α}, α(−1)1 ∈ P^1.

nodes.title: The Lie algebra of physical states
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex algebra over a field k of characteristic 0 with conformal vector ω, an involution θ ∈ Aut(V) fixing ω, and a symmetric bilinear form (·,·) that is invariant (Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky sense, node invariant-bilinear-form with θ = id) and θ-stable. Let N := {p ∈ P^1 : (p, P^1) = 0}. Then g(V) := P^1/N is a Lie algebra over k with bracket [u + N, v + N] := u_0 v + N; (·,·) induces on g(V) a nondegenerate symmetric invariant form ([x,y],z) = −(y,[x,z]); θ induces a Lie algebra involution; the contravariant form is (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy). P^1 ∩ DV ⊆ N, so g(V) is a quotient of the Lie subalgebra P^1/(P^1 ∩ DV) of V/DV. If V is graded by an abelian group Λ (compatibly with products, L_0 of degree 0, (V_r, V_s) = 0 unless r + s = 0, θ(V_r) = V_{−r}), then g(V) = ⊕_{r∈Λ} g(V)_r is a Λ-graded Lie algebra. Every g ∈ Aut(V) fixing ω, commuting with θ and preserving (·,·) induces an automorphism of g(V) preserving the grading and both forms.
hypotheses: V vertex algebra with conformal vector ω over a field of characteristic 0
θ involutive automorphism fixing ω
(·,·) symmetric, invariant, θ-stable
proofSteps: P^1 is closed under u_0 (physical-space API).
P^1 ∩ DV ⊆ N: for p = Dv ∈ P^1 and q ∈ P^1, (Dv, q) = (L_{−1}v, q) = (v, L_1 q) = 0 using L_n* = L_{−n}.

N is an ideal: for u ∈ P^1, r ∈ N, q ∈ P^1: (u_0 r, q) = −(r, u_0 q) = 0 by the adjoint formula for weight-one primaries (u_0* = −u_0); r_0 u = −u_0 r + (element of DV) by skew symmetry, and this element lies in P^1 ∩ DV ⊆ N.
Antisymmetry: u_0 u ∈ DV ∩ P^1 ⊆ N by skew symmetry. Jacobi identity: commutator formula (u_0 v)_0 = [u_0, v_0].
Invariance of the induced form is (u_0 v, w) = −(v, u_0 w); nondegeneracy holds by construction; θ-stability of (·,·) and θω = ω give the involution.
Grading: each P^1_r is stable under the construction and N = ⊕_r N_r because the form pairs degree r with −r.
Functoriality: automorphisms preserve P^1, N and the bracket.
acceptance: For a vertex operator algebra of CFT type with nondegenerate invariant form, g(V) = V_1 with bracket u_0 v (for the A_1 lattice: sl₂).

nodes.title: No-ghost theorem, step 1: adjoints, commutators and nondegeneracy
nodes.statement: Setting: V is a vertex operator algebra over ℝ with conformal vector of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·)_V, and a group G acting by automorphisms preserving ω and (·,·)_V. L := II_{1,1}; W := V ⊗ V_L with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ := id ⊗ θ_L, product form (·,·) (with (1,1)_{V_L} = −1) and contravariant form (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy); G acts trivially on V_L. For 0 ≠ r ∈ L fix w ∈ L with ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, and put K_i := (1 ⊗ w(−1)1)_i = 1 ⊗ w(i). H := V ⊗ S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^r (the degree-r subspace), 𝒜 the Lie algebra spanned by all L_i, K_i, 𝒲 = span{L_i}, 𝒴 = span{K_i}, with ± and 0 parts by the sign of i. P := {v ∈ H : L_i v = 0 for i > 0}, T := {v ∈ H : L_i v = K_i v = 0 for i > 0}, N := rad((·,·)_0|_P), K := U(𝒴)T, S := 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T; a subscript 1 means the L_0-weight-one part. Claim: (a) with respect to (·,·)_0, L_i* = L_{−i} and K_i* = K_{−i} for all i; (b) [L_i, K_j] = −j K_{i+j} and [K_i, K_j] = 0; (c) (·,·)_0 restricted to H is nondegenerate; (d) H = ⊕_{n ≥ ⟨r,r⟩/2} H_n with each L_0-weight space H_n finite-dimensional.
hypotheses: Setting as stated
proofSteps: (a): apply the adjoint formula to ω (weight 2, L_1ω = 0, θω = ω) and to 1 ⊗ w(−1)1 (weight 1, L_1 = 0, θ = −1).
(b): [L_m, w(n)] = −n w(m+n) in V_L and w(i), w(j) commute because ⟨w,w⟩ = 0.
(c): the form on W is nondegenerate and pairs degree r with degree r only (for the contravariant form), so its radical on H lies in the radical on W.
(d): weights of v ⊗ α_1(−n_1)⋯ ⊗ e^r are wt(v) + Σn_i + ⟨r,r⟩/2 with wt(v) ≥ 0; finitely many vectors of each weight because V has finite-dimensional weight spaces and the partitions are finite.
acceptance: For r = (1,1), H has lowest weight ⟨r,r⟩/2 = −1 with H_{−1} = V_0 ⊗ e^r one-dimensional.

nodes.title: No-ghost theorem, step 2: H is generated by transverse states
nodes.statement: Setting: V is a vertex operator algebra over ℝ with conformal vector of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·)_V, and a group G acting by automorphisms preserving ω and (·,·)_V. L := II_{1,1}; W := V ⊗ V_L with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ := id ⊗ θ_L, product form (·,·) (with (1,1)_{V_L} = −1) and contravariant form (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy); G acts trivially on V_L. For 0 ≠ r ∈ L fix w ∈ L with ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, and put K_i := (1 ⊗ w(−1)1)_i = 1 ⊗ w(i). H := V ⊗ S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^r (the degree-r subspace), 𝒜 the Lie algebra spanned by all L_i, K_i, 𝒲 = span{L_i}, 𝒴 = span{K_i}, with ± and 0 parts by the sign of i. P := {v ∈ H : L_i v = 0 for i > 0}, T := {v ∈ H : L_i v = K_i v = 0 for i > 0}, N := rad((·,·)_0|_P), K := U(𝒴)T, S := 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T; a subscript 1 means the L_0-weight-one part. Claim: H = U(𝒜)T, i.e. every vector of H is obtained from vectors annihilated by all L_i, K_i (i > 0) by applying the operators L_i, K_i.
hypotheses: Setting as stated
proofSteps: By step 1 the form on each finite-dimensional H_n is nondegenerate and distinct weight spaces are orthogonal, so H_n = (U(𝒜)T)_n ⊕ ((U(𝒜)T)^⊥)_n and H = U(𝒜)T ⊕ (U(𝒜)T)^⊥ as 𝒜-modules (the orthogonal complement is 𝒜-stable because 𝒜 is closed under adjoints).

If (U(𝒜)T)^⊥ ≠ 0, take its lowest weight n (weights are bounded below by step 1 (d)); since L_i, K_i (i > 0) lower weight, its weight-n part is annihilated by them, so lies in T ⊆ U(𝒜)T, a contradiction.
acceptance: For V = V♮ and r = (1,1), the lowest weight space H_{−1} = V_0 ⊗ e^r lies in T.

nodes.title: No-ghost theorem, step 3: the transverse space is isomorphic to V ⊗ e^r
nodes.statement: Setting: V is a vertex operator algebra over ℝ with conformal vector of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·)_V, and a group G acting by automorphisms preserving ω and (·,·)_V. L := II_{1,1}; W := V ⊗ V_L with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ := id ⊗ θ_L, product form (·,·) (with (1,1)_{V_L} = −1) and contravariant form (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy); G acts trivially on V_L. For 0 ≠ r ∈ L fix w ∈ L with ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, and put K_i := (1 ⊗ w(−1)1)_i = 1 ⊗ w(i). H := V ⊗ S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^r (the degree-r subspace), 𝒜 the Lie algebra spanned by all L_i, K_i, 𝒲 = span{L_i}, 𝒴 = span{K_i}, with ± and 0 parts by the sign of i. P := {v ∈ H : L_i v = 0 for i > 0}, T := {v ∈ H : L_i v = K_i v = 0 for i > 0}, N := rad((·,·)_0|_P), K := U(𝒴)T, S := 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T; a subscript 1 means the L_0-weight-one part. Claim: (a) K = T ⊕ rad(K) with (·,·)_0 nondegenerate on T; (b) K = (V ⊗ e^r) ⊕ rad(K), and K is exactly the space of lowest-weight vectors of the abelian Lie algebra 𝒴 in H; (c) consequently the projections give a G-equivariant isometric isomorphism V ⊗ e^r ≅ T respecting L_0-weights, so T_1 ≅ V_{1−⟨r,r⟩/2} as G-modules with forms, where (u ⊗ e^r, u ⊗ e^r)_0 = (u,u)_V.
hypotheses: Setting as stated
PBW theorem for U(𝒴) and U(𝒜)
proofSteps: (a): by PBW, K = U(𝒴⁻)U(𝒴⁺)U(𝒴⁰)T = U(𝒴⁻)T = T ⊕ 𝒴⁻U(𝒴⁻)T; the second summand is orthogonal to K (adjoints K_i* = K_{−i}), hence in rad(K); T ∩ rad = 0 by step 1 (c) and step 2.

(b): H = U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T by PBW and step 2, and no nonzero vector of 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T is a 𝒴-lowest-weight vector, so K is the space of 𝒴-lowest-weight vectors. Since ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, (w, r) is a basis of ℝ²; writing S(ĥ⁻) = ℝ[x_i] ⊗ ℝ[z_i] with x_i = w(−i), z_i = r(−i), K_k = 1 ⊗ w(k) acts on ℝ[z_i] as k⟨r,w⟩∂/∂z_k (k > 0) and commutes with ℝ[x_i]; ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0 forces the lowest-weight vectors to be V ⊗ ℝ[x_i] ⊗ e^r, of which the part of positive x-degree is null.
(c): both V ⊗ e^r and T map isomorphically onto K/rad(K); the maps commute with G (G acts trivially on V_L) and with L_0 on the weight-one parts.
acceptance: For r = (1,−1) (norm 2), T_1 ≅ V_0 is one-dimensional: the root space of the real simple root.

nodes.title: No-ghost theorem, step 4: spurious states in critical dimension
nodes.statement: Setting: V is a vertex operator algebra over ℝ with conformal vector of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·)_V, and a group G acting by automorphisms preserving ω and (·,·)_V. L := II_{1,1}; W := V ⊗ V_L with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ := id ⊗ θ_L, product form (·,·) (with (1,1)_{V_L} = −1) and contravariant form (x,y)_0 := −(x, θy); G acts trivially on V_L. For 0 ≠ r ∈ L fix w ∈ L with ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, and put K_i := (1 ⊗ w(−1)1)_i = 1 ⊗ w(i). H := V ⊗ S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^r (the degree-r subspace), 𝒜 the Lie algebra spanned by all L_i, K_i, 𝒲 = span{L_i}, 𝒴 = span{K_i}, with ± and 0 parts by the sign of i. P := {v ∈ H : L_i v = 0 for i > 0}, T := {v ∈ H : L_i v = K_i v = 0 for i > 0}, N := rad((·,·)_0|_P), K := U(𝒴)T, S := 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T; a subscript 1 means the L_0-weight-one part. Claim: H = S ⊕ K, and the operators L_1 and L_2 + (3/2)L_1², which generate the associative algebra generated by all L_i with i > 0, map S_1 into S. This uses that the central charge of W is 26.
hypotheses: Setting as stated
central charge of V ⊗ V_{II_{1,1}} equal to 26
proofSteps: H = S ⊕ K from H = U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T (PBW) and K = U(𝒴⁻)T.
Every s ∈ S_1 can be written s = L_{−1}f_1 + L_{−2}f_2 with L_0 f_1 = 0 and L_0 f_2 = −f_2, since every L_{−m} (m > 0) is a polynomial in L_{−1}, L_{−2}.

Compute with the Virasoro relations of central charge c: L_1 s = L_{−1}(L_1f_1 + 3f_2) + L_{−2}L_1f_2 and (L_2 + (3/2)L_1²)s = L_{−1}(L_2 + (3/2)L_1²)f_1 + L_{−2}(L_2 + (3/2)L_1²)f_2 + 9L_{−1}L_1f_2 + (c/2 − 13)f_2. Since S = L_{−1}H + L_{−2}H, both lie in S exactly because c = 26 kills the last term.
L_1 and L_2 + (3/2)L_1² generate the associative algebra generated by the L_i, i > 0 (L_2 is obtained, then L_{i+1} = [L_i, L_1]/(i−1) for i ≥ 2).
acceptance: For c ≠ 26 the computation leaves the term (c/2 − 13)f_2 and the lemma fails (the no-ghost theorem needs central charge 24 for V).

nodes.statement: Setting: V is a vertex operator algebra over ℝ with conformal vector of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·)_V, and a group G acting by automorphisms preserving ω and (·,·)_V. For 0 ≠ r ∈ L fix w ∈ L with ⟨w,w⟩ = 0 and ⟨r,w⟩ ≠ 0, and put K_i := (1 ⊗ w(−1)1)_i = 1 ⊗ w(i). H := V ⊗ S(ĥ⁻) ⊗ e^r (the degree-r subspace), 𝒜 the Lie algebra spanned by all L_i, K_i, 𝒲 = span{L_i}, 𝒴 = span{K_i}, with ± and 0 parts by the sign of i. P := {v ∈ H : L_i v = 0 for i > 0}, T := {v ∈ H : L_i v = K_i v = 0 for i > 0}, N := rad((·,·)_0|_P), K := U(𝒴)T, S := 𝒲⁻U(𝒲⁻)U(𝒴⁻)T; a subscript 1 means the L_0-weight-one part. proofSteps: Write p ∈ P_1 as p = k + s with k ∈ K_1, s ∈ S_1 (step 4).

For a generator u ∈ {L_1, L_2 + (3/2)L_1²}: 0 = up = uk + us with uk ∈ K (K is stable under L_i, i > 0, being U(𝒴)T with [L_i, K_j] ∈ 𝒴) and us ∈ S (step 4); directness of H = S ⊕ K gives uk = us = 0.
Hence k ∈ K ∩ P = T and s ∈ S ∩ P; S is orthogonal to P (adjoints: (L_{−m}f, p) = (f, L_m p) = 0), so s ∈ N_1; T_1 ∩ N_1 = 0 by step 3 (a).

nodes.title: The no-ghost theorem (Goddard–Thorn, Borcherds)
nodes.statement: Let V be a vertex operator algebra over ℝ of central charge 24, nonnegatively graded with dim V_0 = 1, with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form, and let G be a group acting on V by automorphisms preserving ω and the form. Let W := V ⊗ V_{II_{1,1}} with its conformal vector (central charge 26), involution θ = id ⊗ θ_{II_{1,1}}, product form and contravariant form (x,y)_0 = −(x,θy); let P^1_r ⊆ W be the physical space of weight 1 and degree r ∈ II_{1,1}, with G acting through V. Then the quotient of P^1_r by the radical of (·,·)_0 restricted to P^1_r is isomorphic, as a G-module with invariant bilinear form, to V_{1−⟨r,r⟩/2} if r ≠ 0, and to V_1 ⊕ ℝ² (G acting trivially on ℝ²) if r = 0. In particular, if (·,·)_V is positive definite then the induced contravariant form on P^1_r/rad is positive definite for r ≠ 0.
hypotheses: V vertex operator algebra over ℝ, c = 24
V nonnegatively graded, dim V_0 = 1
nondegenerate symmetric invariant form on V
G acts by automorphisms preserving ω and the form
proofSteps: r ≠ 0: combine step 3 (V_{1−⟨r,r⟩/2} ⊗ e^r ≅ T_1, weights: wt(v ⊗ e^r) = wt(v) + ⟨r,r⟩/2 = 1) with step 5 (P^1_r/N_1 ≅ T_1); all maps are G-equivariant and preserve the forms.
Positivity: for x = u ⊗ e^r, (x, θx) = −(u,u)_V (lattice invariant-form lemma), so (x,x)_0 = (u,u)_V > 0 for u ≠ 0.

r = 0: the weight-one degree-zero space of W is V_1 ⊗ 1 ⊕ V_0 ⊗ span{α(−1)1 : α ∈ ℝ²}; since dim V_0 = 1, L_1V_1 ⊆ V_0 = ℝ1 and (L_1v, 1) = (v, L_{−1}1) = 0 give L_1V_1 = 0, and L_n (n ≥ 2) kills it by weight; the form on this space is nondegenerate, so P^1_0/rad ≅ V_1 ⊕ ℝ².
acceptance: For V = V♮ (moonshine module) and r = (a,b) ≠ 0: P^1_r/rad ≅ V♮_{1+ab}, of dimension c(ab).
Without the hypothesis dim V_0 = 1 the r = 0 case fails (for V♮ × V♮ the quotient is V_1 ⊕ ℝ⁴); see sourceIssues E705.

sources.excerpt: Then the quotient of Pr(1) by the nullspace of its bilinear form is isomorphic as a G-module with G-invariant bilinear form to V(1−⟨r,r⟩/2) if r ≠ 0 and to V(1) ⊕ R2 if r = 0.
sources.match: Statement with hypotheses i–iv (including dim V(0) = 1); proof in Appendix A.

sources.excerpt: Then the quotient of P 1r by the nullspace of its bilinear form is naturally isomorphic, as a G module with an invariant bilinear form, to V 1−(r,r)/2 if r ≠ 0 and to V 1 ⊕ R2 if r = 0.

nodes.title: Borcherds' axioms for a moonshine module
nodes.statement: A moonshine module (Borcherds' properties (1)–(2)) is a vertex operator algebra V over ℝ such that: (1) the central charge is 24 and V carries a positive definite symmetric bilinear form that is invariant in the Frenkel–Huang–Lepowsky sense (θ = id in node invariant-bilinear-form); (2) V is nonnegatively graded and q^{−1}·gradedDimension(V) = J, the Laurent series q^{−1} + Σ_{n≥1} c(n)qⁿ of j − 744 (node j-laurent-series); equivalently dim V_{n+1} = c(n) for all n ≥ −1, so V_0 = ℝ·1, V_1 = 0, dim V_2 = 196884. A moonshine module with symmetry group G is moreover a group homomorphism ρ : G →* Aut(V, ω, (·,·)) into the conformal automorphisms preserving the form (Borcherds' property (3) for G the Monster).
hypotheses: V vertex operator algebra over ℝ
proofSteps: Structure (Prop-valued) on a vertex operator algebra with a bilinear form: centralCharge = 24, form symmetric, invariant, positive definite, IsNonnegGraded, and mckayThompsonSeries V 1 = J.
Derived: dim V_0 = c(−1) = 1 and 1 ∈ V_0 is nonzero (positive definiteness and (1,1) > 0 once V ≠ 0), so V_0 = ℝ1; dim V_1 = c(0) = 0.
The no-ghost hypotheses (dim V_0 = 1, c = 24, nondegenerate invariant form, group action) follow.
acceptance: For the Frenkel–Lepowsky–Meurman module V♮ these properties are FLM's theorems (recorded as the gap 'FLM moonshine module').
The Leech lattice vertex operator algebra has graded dimension q^{−1}+24+196884q+⋯ and is not a moonshine module.

nodes.title: The Monster Lie algebra m(V)
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module (node moonshine-module-axioms) and G ≤ Aut(V, ω, (·,·)). Let W := V ⊗ V_{II_{1,1}} with conformal vector of central charge 26, involution θ = id ⊗ θ_{II_{1,1}} and product form (normalized (1,1)_{V_{II_{1,1}}} = −1). The Monster Lie algebra is m(V) := g(W), the physical Lie algebra of W (P^1 modulo the radical of the form). It satisfies: (1) m = ⊕_{r∈II_{1,1}} m_r is II_{1,1}-graded; (2) θ maps m_r onto m_{−r} and the contravariant form (x,y)_0 = −(x,θy) is positive definite on m_r for r ≠ 0; (3) G acts on m by graded Lie algebra automorphisms, and m_{(a,b)} ≅ V_{ab+1} as G-modules for (a,b) ≠ (0,0) (so dim m_{(a,b)} = c(ab)), while m_{(0,0)} = span{1 ⊗ α(−1)1 : α ∈ ℝ²} ≅ ℝ² with trivial G-action; (4) m_{(0,0)} is abelian and 1 ⊗ α(−1)1 acts on m_r by the scalar ⟨α, r⟩.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
proofSteps: W is a vertex algebra with conformal vector (tensor-product lemma) and invariant product form; it is II_{1,1}-graded through V_{II_{1,1}}.
Apply the physical Lie algebra construction; the grading and G-action are its API.
No-ghost theorem with r = (a,b): 1 − ⟨r,r⟩/2 = 1 + ab gives m_{(a,b)} ≅ V_{ab+1}; r = 0 gives V_1 ⊕ ℝ² = ℝ² since V_1 = 0.
Positivity: for x = u ⊗ e^r, (x,x)_0 = (u,u)_V > 0 (lattice invariant-form lemma).
acceptance: m_{(a,b)} = 0 whenever ab < −1.

nodes.title: Borcherds (generalized Kac–Moody) algebra of a matrix
nodes.statement: Let I be a countable set and A = (a_ij)_{i,j∈I} a real matrix with (C1) A symmetric, (C2) a_ij ≤ 0 for i ≠ j, (C3) 2a_ij/a_ii ∈ ℤ whenever a_ii > 0. The Borcherds algebra g(A) is the real Lie algebra generated by h_i, e_i, f_i (i ∈ I) with relations [h_i,h_j] = 0, [h_i,e_k] = a_ik e_k, [h_i,f_k] = −a_ik f_k, [e_i,f_j] = δ_ij h_i, (ad e_i)^{1−2a_ij/a_ii} e_j = 0 = (ad f_i)^{1−2a_ij/a_ii} f_j for i ≠ j with a_ii > 0, and [e_i,e_j] = [f_i,f_j] = 0 whenever a_ij = 0. It is graded by the root lattice Q := ⊕_{i∈I} ℤα_i ((α_i,α_j) := a_ij; deg e_i = α_i, deg f_i = −α_i, deg h_i = 0). A simple root α_i is real if a_ii > 0 and imaginary otherwise. The Chevalley involution η acts as −1 on span{h_i} and maps e_i ↦ −f_i, f_i ↦ −e_i. When A is a symmetrized generalized Cartan matrix, g(A) is the (derived) Kac–Moody algebra.
hypotheses: I countable
A satisfies (C1)–(C3)
proofSteps: Define g(A) as the quotient of Mathlib's FreeLieAlgebra ℝ (I ⊕ I ⊕ I) by the Lie ideal generated by the relations (the pattern of Mathlib's Matrix.ToLieAlgebra).
The Q-grading exists because every relation is homogeneous; η is well defined because the relations are stable under it.
acceptance: For A = (2): g(A) ≅ sl₂(ℝ). For A = (0): g(A) is the three-dimensional Heisenberg algebra.
For A a Cartan matrix of finite type (a_ii = 2, integer entries) g(A) agrees with Matrix.ToLieAlgebra.

nodes.title: Triangular and root space decomposition of a Borcherds algebra
nodes.statement: For A satisfying (C1)–(C3): g(A) = n⁻ ⊕ h ⊕ n⁺ as vector spaces, where h = span{h_i} is abelian with basis {h_i}_{i∈I}, n⁺ (resp. n⁻) is the subalgebra generated by the e_i (resp. f_i) and is the quotient of the free Lie algebra on {e_i} (resp. {f_i}) by the ideal generated by the relations of degree > 0 (resp. < 0). Every root space g_α (α ∈ Q∖{0}) is finite-dimensional and nonzero only for α ∈ Q_+ ∪ (−Q_+) (Q_+ = ⊕ℕα_i); g_{α_i} = ℝe_i. There is a unique symmetric invariant bilinear form with (e_i, f_j) = δ_ij, (h_i,h_j) = a_ij; it pairs g_α with g_{−α} nondegenerately for α ≠ 0.
hypotheses: A satisfies (C1)–(C3)
proofSteps: For the algebra g_0 (relations without the Serre-type ones) construct the module X (free associative algebra on symbols x_i) of Jurisich 1998 Proposition 3.1 to prove g_0 = n_0⁻ ⊕ h ⊕ n_0⁺ with n_0^± free and {h_i} independent.
The Serre-type relations generate an ideal k_0 = k_0⁺ ⊕ k_0⁻ contained in n_0^+ ⊕ n_0^− (Jurisich 1998 Propositions 3.2–3.3), so the decomposition descends to g(A).
Finite-dimensionality: g_α ⊆ image of the degree-α part of the free Lie algebra, finite-dimensional for α ∈ Q_+.

The invariant form: construct inductively on height as for Kac–Moody algebras (Jurisich 1998 §2.1); nondegenerate pairing of g_α and g_{−α} for α ≠ 0 after quotienting by the radical, which is zero for the matrices of Jurisich 1998 Corollary 5.3.
acceptance: For A = (2) the decomposition is sl₂ = ℝf ⊕ ℝh ⊕ ℝe.

sources.excerpt: The Lie algebra g0 has triangular decomposition g0 = n−0 ⊕ h ⊕ n+0. The abelian subalgebra h has a basis consisting of {hi}i∈I, and n±0 is the free Lie algebra generated by the ei (resp. the fi) i ∈ I.

nodes.title: The canonical central extension ĝ(A)
nodes.statement: For A satisfying (C1)–(C3), ĝ(A) is the real Lie algebra with generators e_i, f_i, h_ij (i, j ∈ I) and relations [h_ij, h_kl] = 0, [h_ij, e_k] = δ_ij a_ik e_k, [h_ij, f_k] = −δ_ij a_ik f_k, [e_i, f_j] = h_ij, (ad e_i)^{1−2a_ij/a_ii}e_j = 0 = (ad f_i)^{1−2a_ij/a_ii}f_j (i ≠ j, a_ii > 0), [e_i,e_j] = [f_i,f_j] = 0 when a_ij = 0 (Borcherds' universal generalized Kac–Moody algebra). Then h_ij = 0 unless the i-th and j-th columns of A are equal; the h_ij with equal columns form a basis of an abelian subalgebra ĥ; ĝ = n⁻ ⊕ ĥ ⊕ n⁺ with n^± as in g(A); c := span{h_ij : i ≠ j} is central, and ĝ(A)/c ≅ g(A).
hypotheses: A satisfies (C1)–(C3)
proofSteps: Lemma: h_ij acts on e_k by δ_ij a_ik and on f_k by −δ_ij a_ik; applying the Jacobi identity to [e_i, f_j] with e_k, f_k shows h_ij = 0 unless columns i and j agree (Jurisich 1998 Lemma 3.1).
Triangular decomposition via the module X with λ vanishing on h_ij for unequal columns (Jurisich 1998 Proposition 3.1); the relations of degree ≠ 0 generate ideals k^± (Propositions 3.2–3.3).
The map ĝ → g(A), h_ij ↦ δ_ij h_i, is surjective with kernel c (Theorem 3.1).
acceptance: For a Kac–Moody matrix (all a_ii > 0) no two columns agree, c = 0 and ĝ = g(A).
For Jurisich's matrix M of the Monster Lie algebra, the c(n) columns of block n agree, so c contains h_ij for all i ≠ j in one block and is infinite-dimensional (c(n) ≥ 2 for n ≥ 1).

nodes.title: Borcherds' characterisation of generalized Kac–Moody algebras
nodes.statement: Let g be a real Lie algebra such that: (1) g = ⊕_{i∈ℤ} g_i is ℤ-graded with g_i finite-dimensional for i ≠ 0, and g is diagonalizable with respect to g_0; (2) g has an involution ω with ω(g_i) = g_{−i} acting as −1 on the noncentral elements of g_0 (so g_0 is abelian); (3) g has an ω-invariant symmetric invariant bilinear form (·,·) with (g_i, g_j) = 0 unless i + j = 0, such that (x,y)_0 := −(x, ω(y)) is positive definite on g_m for every m ≠ 0; (4) g_0 ⊆ [g,g]. Then there is a matrix A satisfying (C1)–(C3) and a surjective Lie algebra homomorphism π : ĝ(A) → g whose kernel is central. If moreover (·,·) is nondegenerate, then g ≅ l/c for a Borcherds algebra l = g(A) with c the centre of l. The generators e_i can be chosen as g_0-weight vectors forming orthonormal bases (for (·,·)_0) of the orthogonal complements e_m of the subalgebra generated by ⊕_{0<n<m} g_n in g_m, with f_i = −ω(e_i).
hypotheses: g real Lie algebra with (1)–(4)
proofSteps: For m > 0 let l_m be the subalgebra generated by the g_n, 0 < n < m, and e_m := (l_m ∩ g_m)^⊥ in g_m for (·,·)_0; e_m is g_0-stable and has an orthonormal basis of g_0-weight vectors; their union {e_i} generates ⊕_{n>0} g_n; put f_i := −ω(e_i), h_ij := [e_i, f_j].
h_ij ∈ g_0 and h_ij = 0 unless deg e_i = deg e_j (contravariance and positivity); by (4) g_0 is spanned by the h_ij.
The radical of (·,·) is central; for i ≠ j, h_ij lies in the radical.

[h, e_i] = (h, h_ii)e_i, and (x,y)_0-positivity gives a_ij := (h_ii,h_jj) ≤ 0 for i ≠ j, with [e_i, e_j] = 0 iff a_ij = 0 (Jurisich 1998 equation (10)); for a_ii > 0 the sl₂-representation theory gives 2a_ij/a_ii ∈ ℤ and the Serre relations (using Jurisich 1998 Proposition 3.2 and positivity).
Hence the generators satisfy the relations of ĝ(A) and π exists; the form pulls back and nondegeneracy on ĝ_n ⊕ ĝ_{−n} shows the kernel lies in ĥ and is central.
If the form is nondegenerate then all h_ij (i ≠ j) vanish and Jurisich 1998 Corollary 4.1 gives g ≅ l/c.
acceptance: For g = sl₂(ℝ) with the grading by the h-eigenvalue/2, ω the Cartan involution and the trace form, the theorem returns A = (2).
Borcherds 1988 Theorem 3.1 and Borcherds 1992 Theorem 4.1 are versions of this statement.

nodes.title: Lazard elimination for free Lie algebras
nodes.statement: Let X be a set, S ⊆ X, and L(X) the free Lie algebra on X over a field (Mathlib FreeLieAlgebra). Then (a) L(X) = L(S) ⊕ 𝔞 as vector spaces, where L(S) is the subalgebra generated by S and 𝔞 is the ideal generated by X ∖ S; (b) 𝔞 is a free Lie algebra: the map (s_1, …, s_n, x) ↦ (ad s_1 ⋯ ad s_n)(x), for n ≥ 0, s_i ∈ S, x ∈ X ∖ S, extends to an isomorphism L(T) ≅ 𝔞 from the free Lie algebra on the set T of such sequences. All statements are compatible with gradings in which X is homogeneous.
hypotheses: X a set, S ⊆ X
proofSteps: Define the Lie algebra map L(X) → L(S) killing X ∖ S (a retraction onto L(S)); its kernel is 𝔞, giving (a).

Construct L(S) ⋉ L(T) with L(S) acting on L(T) by derivations extending s · (s_1,…,s_n,x) = (s, s_1, …, s_n, x); the universal property of L(X) gives a map L(X) → L(S) ⋉ L(T), inverse to the map induced by (ad s_1⋯ad s_n)(x); restrict to 𝔞 (Bourbaki, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras II §2.9).
acceptance: For X = {s, x}, S = {s}: the ideal generated by x is free on {x, [s,x], [s,[s,x]], …}.

sources.excerpt: (a) The Lie algebra L(X) is the direct sum as a vector space of the subalgebra L(S) of L(X) and the ideal a of L(X) generated by X∖S. (b) There exists a Lie algebra isomorphism φ of L(T) onto a which maps (s1, . . . , sn, x) to (ad s1 · · · ad sn)(x).
sources.match: Statement (from Bourbaki).

nodes.title: Traces on exterior, symmetric and tensor powers (Adams operations)
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0. (a) For a finite-dimensional k-vector space U and g ∈ End(U), in k[[t]]: Σ_{n≥0} (−1)ⁿ tr(g|Λⁿ U) tⁿ = det(1 − tg) = exp(−Σ_{m≥1} tr(g^m) t^m/m), Σ_{n≥0} tr(g|Sⁿ U) tⁿ = det(1 − tg)^{−1} = exp(Σ_{m≥1} tr(g^m) t^m/m), and Σ_{n≥0} tr(g|U^{⊗n}) tⁿ = (1 − tr(g) t)^{−1}. (b) Let Γ be a finitely generated free abelian group with a homomorphism deg : Γ → ℤ, U = ⊕_{γ∈Γ} U_γ with U_γ finite-dimensional and U_γ = 0 unless deg γ > 0, finitely many γ of each degree, and g a graded endomorphism. In the completed group ring k[[Γ_{>0}]] (series Σ a_γ e^γ over deg γ > 0 ∪ {0}), with ch_g(U) := Σ_γ tr(g|U_γ)e^γ and the Adams operation ψ^m(Σ a_γ e^γ)[g] := Σ tr(g^m|U_γ) e^{mγ}: ch_g Λ_{−1}(U) := Σ_n (−1)ⁿ ch_g(Λⁿ U) = exp(−Σ_{m≥1} ψ^m ch_g(U)/m), ch_g S(U) = exp(Σ_m ψ^m ch_g(U)/m), ch_g T(U) = (1 − ch_g U)^{−1}.
hypotheses: k field of characteristic 0
U finite-dimensional, or graded with finite-dimensional pieces of positive degree
proofSteps: (a) Extend scalars to an algebraic closure and triangularize g with eigenvalues λ_1, …, λ_d: tr(g|Λⁿ) = e_n(λ), tr(g|Sⁿ) = h_n(λ), and Π(1 − λ_i t) = exp(Σ_i log(1 − λ_i t)) = exp(−Σ_m p_m(λ)t^m/m) with p_m(λ) = tr(g^m); the tensor power statement is tr(g^{⊗n}) = tr(g)ⁿ.

(b) Truncate to degrees ≤ N: finitely many U_γ contribute; Λ(⊕U_γ) = ⊗Λ(U_γ) as graded g-modules, so characters multiply; apply (a) to each U_γ with t replaced by e^γ (the splitting principle of Borcherds 1992 §8).

nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0, Γ, deg as in node graded-trace-exterior-symmetric-power, W = ⊕_γ W_γ a Γ-graded vector space with W_γ finite-dimensional, zero unless deg γ > 0, finitely many γ of each degree, and g a graded linear automorphism of W. Let L(W) be the free Lie algebra on W (graded, with g acting by the induced Lie algebra automorphism). Then each L(W)_γ is finite-dimensional and, in k[[Γ_{>0}]], exp(−Σ_{m≥1} ψ^m ch_g(L(W))/m) = 1 − ch_g(W); for g = 1: Π_{γ} (1 − e^γ)^{dim L(W)_γ} = 1 − Σ_γ dim(W_γ) e^γ, and by Möbius inversion dim L(W)_β = Σ_{mγ=β} (μ(m)/m) Σ_{a∈P(γ)} ((|a|−1)!/a!) Π_α (dim W_α)^{a_α}, where P(γ) is the set of multi-indices a = (a_α) with Σ a_α α = γ.

nodes.title: Free subalgebras of Borcherds algebras (Jurisich)
nodes.statement: Let A satisfy (C1)–(C3), J := {i ∈ I : a_ii > 0} (real simple roots) and g_J the Kac–Moody subalgebra generated by e_i, f_i (i ∈ J), g_J = n_J⁺ ⊕ h_J ⊕ n_J⁻. Assume that a_ij < 0 for all distinct i, j ∈ I ∖ J (no two imaginary simple roots are orthogonal). Then g(A) = u⁺ ⊕ (g_J + h) ⊕ u⁻, where u⁻ is the free Lie algebra on ⊕_{j∈I∖J} U(n_J⁻)·f_j and u⁺ the free Lie algebra on ⊕_{j∈I∖J} U(n_J⁺)·e_j; each U(n_J⁻)·f_j is an integrable highest-weight g_J-module and each U(n_J⁺)·e_j an integrable lowest-weight g_J-module (quotients of U(n_J^±)e_j by the Serre relations (ad e_i)^{1−2a_ij/a_ii}e_j, i ∈ J). u^± are g_J-stable ideals of n^±.
hypotheses: A satisfies (C1)–(C3)
a_ij < 0 for i ≠ j in I ∖ J
proofSteps: n⁺ = L({e_i}_{i∈I})/k_0⁺ with k_0⁺ generated by the Serre elements with i ∈ J (no relations of type [e_i,e_j] = 0 occur among imaginary indices by hypothesis).
Eliminate S = {e_i}_{i∈J} (Lazard): L({e_i}) = L({e_i}_{i∈J}) ⋉ L(W), W = ⊕_{j∉J} U(l)e_j with l = L({e_i}_{i∈J}).
Split W = ⊕_j (U(l)e_j/R_j ⊕ R_j) with R_j generated by the Serre elements, and eliminate again twice (the ideals b, c generated by R_j and K e_j lie in k_0⁺).
Conclude n⁺ = n_J⁺ ⋉ L(⊕_j U(n_J⁺)·e_j) and similarly for n⁻ (apply η).

Corollary: for such A the radical of g(A) is zero (Jurisich 1998 Corollary 5.3).

nodes.title: The Monster Lie algebra is a Borcherds algebra
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module and m = m(V). Grade m by i := 2a + b on m_{(a,b)} and let θ be the induced involution. Then m satisfies hypotheses (1)–(4) of Borcherds' characterisation with nondegenerate form, hence m ≅ g(A)/c for a matrix A satisfying (C1)–(C3), c the centre of g(A); under this isomorphism m_{(0,0)} is the image of the Cartan subalgebra, the II_{1,1}-grading of m is the root grading, and the simple roots have degrees (a,b) with 2a + b > 0.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
proofSteps: (1): m_{(a,b)} ≠ 0 forces ab ≥ −1, so for i ≠ 0 only finitely many (a,b) with 2a + b = i contribute, each finite-dimensional; i = 0 forces (a,b) = (0,0). m is diagonalizable for m_{(0,0)} by the scalar action ⟨α, r⟩ (Monster Lie algebra API (4)), which separates degrees.
(2),(3): θ maps m_r to m_{−r}, is −1 on m_{(0,0)}, preserves the form; the contravariant form is positive definite off degree 0 (Monster Lie algebra API).

(4): the brackets [u ⊗ e^{(1,1)}, v ⊗ e^{−(1,1)}] = (u_3 v) ⊗ (1,1)(−1)1 (u, v ∈ V_2 with u_3v = c1, c ≠ 0) and [e^{(1,−1)}, e^{−(1,−1)}] = (1,−1)(−1)1 are linearly independent in the two-dimensional m_{(0,0)} (Jurisich 1998 (25)–(26)).
The radical of the form on m is zero by construction; apply the nondegenerate case of the characterisation theorem.

nodes.title: Simple roots and denominator formula of the Monster Lie algebra
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module. The Monster Lie algebra m = m(V) is isomorphic to g(M)/c, where M is Jurisich's matrix indexed by pairs (j,k) with j ∈ {−1} ∪ ℤ_{≥1}, 1 ≤ k ≤ c(j), with entries −(j + j') (so the simple roots are (1,−1), real of norm 2, and (1,n) for n ≥ 1, imaginary of norm −2n, each with multiplicity c(n)); the isomorphism matches root spaces with II_{1,1}-graded pieces. Its denominator formula is p·(J(p) − J(q)) = Π_{m≥1, n≥−1} (1 − p^m q^n)^{c(mn)}, where p, q stand for e^{(1,0)}, e^{(0,1)} and J = Σ c(n)qⁿ.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
proofSteps: By the previous theorem m ≅ g(A)/c with simple roots in degrees of positive 2a + b. Real roots have norm −2ab > 0 and m_{(a,b)} ≠ 0 needs ab ≥ −1, so the only positive real root is (1,−1), which is simple; imaginary simple roots have degrees (a,b) with a, b ≥ 1 (m_{(a,0)} ≅ V_1 = 0), and two of them have inner product −(ab' + a'b) < 0.

Hence the free-subalgebra theorem applies with g_J = sl₂: u⁺ = L(W) with W = ⊕_j U(n_J⁺)e_j, the sl₂-string of a simple root (a,b) (b ≥ a, since ⟨(1,−1),(a,b)⟩ = a − b ≤ 0) consisting of the degrees (a+k, b−k), 0 ≤ k ≤ b − a.
Free Lie character formula for u⁺ = ⊕_{a,b≥1} m_{(a,b)} with dim m_{(a,b)} = c(ab) (no-ghost): 1 − ch W = Π_{a,b≥1}(1 − p^a q^b)^{c(ab)}.

The j product formula p(J(p) − J(q)) = (1 − pq^{−1})·Π_{a,b≥1}(1 − p^aq^b)^{c(ab)} (the only factor with n = −1 is 1 − pq^{−1}, and the factors with n = 0 have exponent c(0) = 0) together with the telescoping identity p(J(p) − J(q)) = (1 − pq^{−1})(1 − Σ_{a,b≥1} c(a+b−1)p^aq^b) gives ch W = Σ_{a,b≥1} c(a+b−1)p^aq^b.

Induction on a: the coefficient at (1,n) comes only from strings starting at (1,n), so the multiplicity of the simple root (1,n) is c(n); the string from (1, a+b−1) already accounts for (a,b), so there are no simple roots with a ≥ 2.
The denominator formula is the j product formula with (1 − p/q) = the factor of the real simple root.
acceptance: The matrix M has first row 2, 0 (c(1) times), −1 (c(2) times), −2, …; the simple root spaces sum to V (Borcherds 1992 §1).
The coefficient of p q^1 in the denominator formula gives −c(1) on both sides.

nodes.title: m = u⁺ ⊕ gl₂ ⊕ u⁻ with u⁻ free, equivariantly
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module, G ≤ Aut(V, ω, (·,·)) and m = m(V). Then m = u⁺ ⊕ gl₂ ⊕ u⁻ where gl₂ = m_{(−1,1)} ⊕ m_{(0,0)} ⊕ m_{(1,−1)} and u⁻ = ⊕_{a,b≥1} m_{(−a,−b)}, u⁺ = ⊕_{a,b≥1} m_{(a,b)} are free Lie algebras. Let W ⊆ u⁻ be the orthogonal complement of [u⁻,u⁻] for the contravariant form, degree by degree. Then W is G-stable, the inclusion induces a G-equivariant Lie algebra isomorphism L(W) ≅ u⁻ (G acting on L(W) through W), W is stable under gl₂, and for all a, b ≥ 1 there is a G-equivariant linear isomorphism W_{−(a,b)} ≅ V_{a+b} (VOA weight a + b), while W_{−(a,b)} = 0 unless a, b ≥ 1.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
proofSteps: By the simple-roots theorem and the free-subalgebra theorem (via m ≅ g(M)/c, an isomorphism on n^±) u⁻ is free on ⊕_j U(n_J⁻)f_j, and gl₂ = sl₂ + m_{(0,0)} normalizes u⁻.

A positively graded Lie algebra that is free on some graded subspace is free on every graded complement W of its derived algebra: W generates (induction on degree) and L(W) → u⁻ is injective by comparing graded dimensions through the free Lie character formula (g = 1).

The contravariant form is positive definite and G-invariant on each finite-dimensional m_r, r ≠ 0, and [u⁻,u⁻] is G-stable, so the orthogonal complement W is G-stable; hence L(W) ≅ u⁻ is G-equivariant.
W ≅ u⁻/[u⁻,u⁻] as G × gl₂-modules. For n ≥ 1, W_{−(1,n)} = u⁻_{−(1,n)} = m_{−(1,n)} ≅ V_{n+1} (no bracket of two elements of u⁻ has first coordinate −1).

By the free Lie character formula and the j product formula (as in the simple-roots proof) dim W_{−(a,b)} = c(a+b−1) for a,b ≥ 1. As an sl₂-module (raising operator f_{(−1,1)} of degree (−1,1)), W is finite-dimensional in each string {−(a,b) : a + b = s} with constant multiplicity c(s−1) from weight a − b = −(s−2) to s−2, so it is c(s−1) copies of the s−1-dimensional irreducible, and the powers of the lowering operator give isomorphisms W_{−(1,s−1)} ≅ W_{−(a,s−a)} (sl₂ theory, request to LieHighestWeight Layer 0).
These isomorphisms commute with G because G fixes the one-dimensional spaces m_{±(1,−1)} ≅ V_0 = ℝ1 pointwise.

nodes.title: Borcherds' twisted denominator identity
nodes.statement: Let V be a moonshine module and g ∈ Aut(V, ω, (·,·)); write c_h(n) := tr(h|V_{n+1}) for h = g^i (so c_h(−1) = 1, c_h(0) = 0 and c_h(n) = 0 for n < −1) and T_g = Σ_n c_g(n)qⁿ. Then in the ring ℝ((q))((p)) of formal Laurent series in p with coefficients in ℝ((q)): p^{−1} exp(−Σ_{i≥1} Σ_{m≥1, n∈ℤ} c_{g^i}(mn) p^{mi} q^{ni}/i) = T_g(p) − T_g(q). Equivalently, in ℝ[[p,q]]: exp(−Σ_{i≥1} Σ_{a,b≥1} c_{g^i}(ab) p^{ai}q^{bi}/i) = 1 − Σ_{a,b≥1} c_g(a+b−1) p^a q^b.
hypotheses: V moonshine module
g conformal automorphism preserving the form
proofSteps: Apply the free-decomposition theorem with G = ⟨g⟩: u⁻ ≅ L(W) g-equivariantly with W_{−(a,b)} ≅ V_{a+b}.

The equivariant free Lie character formula (p, q recording the degrees −(1,0), −(0,1)) with ch_g(u⁻) = Σ_{a,b≥1} c_g(ab)p^aq^b (Monster Lie algebra: m_{(−a,−b)} ≅ V_{ab+1} g-equivariantly) and ch_g(W) = Σ c_g(a+b−1)p^aq^b gives the second form (ψ^i ch_g(u⁻) = Σ c_{g^i}(ab)p^{ai}q^{bi}).

Multiply by p^{−1}(1 − p/q) = p^{−1}exp(−Σ_i p^iq^{−i}/i) (the terms with n = −1, m = 1; the terms with n = 0 vanish as c(0) = 0; terms with mn < −1 vanish) and use the telescoping identity (p^{−1} − q^{−1})(1 − Σ c_g(a+b−1)p^aq^b) = T_g(p) − T_g(q).
acceptance: For g = 1 the identity is the j product formula p^{−1}Π(1 − p^mqⁿ)^{c(mn)} = J(p) − J(q).
Comparing coefficients of p²q^2 gives c_g(4) = c_g(3) + (c_g(1)² − c_{g²}(1))/2.
